mastery.sub: 12 months. Prompt engineering as a discipline. Google AI Studio + Vertex to mastery. Four phases, twelve months, forty-eight weekly sprints, twelve gated checkpoints.

quarters.subtitle: Establish rigor. Build the evaluation mindset.

months.title: Prompt engineering as a discipline
months.why: Before any platform, treat prompts as engineered artifacts with tests, not incantations.
weeks: Rebuild vocabulary: context vs. prompt vs. instruction vs. system message. Write your own definitions.
Advanced patterns: CoT, few-shot, self-consistency, role-based, task decomposition. One example each, from your own work.
Structured output comparative: JSON mode, Pydantic/Zod schemas, grammars. Same task, three providers.
Build your first eval harness: 20 prompts, pass/fail rubric, version-controlled.
months.gate: You can defend any prompt with evidence, not aesthetics.

months.title: Gemini API fundamentals via AI Studio
months.why: Leave the playground. Make Gemini a first-class citizen in your stack.
weeks: AI Studio tour: model lineup, safety settings, token counter, get/generate APIs.
SDK integration (Python + JS). First production call from n8n or a Cloudflare Worker.
System instructions, temperature/top-k/top-p calibration. Document what actually moves output.
Migrate one existing Claude prompt to Gemini. Diff results. Write the migration notes.
months.gate: Ship one working Gemini-powered feature inside FlashFusion or Intinc.

months.title: Structured output + function calling
months.why: This is where production agents live or die. Learn both providers cold.
weeks: response_schema deep dive. Pydantic/Zod-first authoring workflow.
Function calling: single tool, multi-tool, parallel tool use.
Gemini vs. Claude tool-use bake-off: latency, reliability, schema adherence, cost per turn.
Build a provider-agnostic tool-calling agent. Same logic, two backends.
months.gate: Portable agent pattern documented and runnable on either provider.

quarters.subtitle: Move from fundamentals into applied agentic patterns.

months.title: Agentic prompting patterns
months.why: Single-shot is done. Multi-step, reflection, and recovery are the real skill.
weeks: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection loops. Implement each from scratch before reaching for a framework.
Thinking models: Gemini Thinking vs. Claude extended thinking. When does reasoning budget pay off?
Error handling, retries, fallback chains. Fail modes you will actually see in prod.
Build a 3-step agent with guardrails. Instrument it.
months.gate: Your agent recovers from its own mistakes at least 80% of the time.

months.title: Context engineering + long context
months.why: Context caching is the single biggest cost lever in Gemini. Most people miss it.
weeks: Context windows in practice: what fits, what retrieves better, when to chunk.
Gemini context caching: how it works, when it pays back, how to monitor hit rate.
Files API: documents, images, video, audio. Pick one non-text modality and ship something.
Long-doc agent comparison: 1M+ tokens full-context vs. retrieval. Measure and decide.
months.gate: Cost model for long-context workloads, in a spreadsheet, defensible to Daniel.

months.title: Evaluation + red-teaming
months.why: This connects to your AppSec/SecAI+ track. Dual-purpose month.
weeks: Promptfoo or LangSmith. Pick one, learn it deeply. Stop rotating tools.
LLM-as-judge patterns. Rubric design. Inter-rater reliability.
OWASP LLM Top 10 as a red-team checklist. Run it against your own prompts.
Jailbreak resistance + safety setting tuning. Document the tradeoffs.
months.gate: Public write-up: "What I broke in my own prompts." The Prompt edition-worthy.

quarters.subtitle: Platform mastery. Vertex AI ramp. Provider portability.

months.title: Vertex AI ramp (GCP foundation)
months.why: This is the 3–6 month GCP ramp you already flagged. Start it here, not later.
weeks: GCP fundamentals: IAM, projects, billing, quotas. Mirror what you know from Azure.
Vertex AI vs. AI Studio. Decision matrix for when to use which.
Model Garden + deployment basics. Endpoint vs. serverless.
First Google ML Engineer practice exam. Record baseline score honestly.
months.gate: Baseline cert score recorded. Gap list written.

months.title: Advanced Gemini features
months.why: The features nobody else is using yet. Early-mover differentiation.
weeks: Grounding with Google Search. Measure when it helps and when it hurts.
Live API (multimodal streaming). Prototype one voice or video use case.
Code execution tool. Compare to Claude code interpreter behavior.
Batch API for cost-heavy workflows. Plug into one real job.
months.gate: One advanced feature shipped in production, not in a demo.

months.title: Multi-provider + prompt versioning
months.why: The discipline that separates hobbyist from platform-aware practitioner.
weeks: Prompt portability layers (BAML, Inspect, LangChain abstractions). Weigh tradeoffs honestly.
Prompt versioning in git. Eval regression tests on every change.
Cost/latency/quality routing between Gemini, Claude, GPT. Write the router.
Build a provider-agnostic prompt library for your own use across lanes.
months.gate: Switching providers is a config change, not a rewrite.

quarters.subtitle: Synthesis. Cert. Publish. Teach what you know.

months.title: Capstone build
months.why: Everything before this was practice. This is the proof.
weeks: Spec a real production system. FlashFusion agent, newsletter automation, or Intinc internal tool.
Build it. Real data, real users, real failure modes.
Evaluate it with the harness from Month 1. Ship with monitoring.
Write the architecture decision record. This becomes a portfolio artifact.
months.gate: System running in production with telemetry and a rollback plan.

months.title: Google Professional ML Engineer cert
months.why: Already on your list. This is the month to close it.
weeks: Practice exam loops. Rotate question pools.
Address remaining gaps: pipelines, feature stores, MLOps concepts.
Schedule the exam. Public commitment to yourself.
Take it. Pass it.
months.gate: Cert in hand. Second GCP credential warranted? Decide.

months.title: Teach + publish
months.why: You do not own knowledge until you can transfer it without the safety net.
weeks: Synthesize: what actually changed in your mental model over 12 months?
Publish a prompt engineering guide. LinkedIn series or Substack, your choice.
Run one workshop: "Gemini vs. Claude for technical teams" — at CLC or Intinc.
Retrospective. What is the next 12-month arc? (Advanced Architect? Deeper MLOps? Pivot?)
months.gate: You can teach this. You have credible, current, shipped work to point to.

claude.sub: 12 months. The deepening play. From Architect Foundations through Agent SDK, MCP authorship, multi-agent orchestration, and a public capstone. Four phases, forty-eight weekly sprints, twelve gated checkpoints.

quarters.subtitle: Close known gaps. Pass Architect Foundations. Cement the base.

months.title: Close the exam gaps
months.why: You already know what you do not know. Time to fix it before the exam window closes the early-mover edge.
weeks: Gap audit week: Agent SDK (Task tool, hooks, fork_session), CLAUDE.md hierarchy, MCP scoping, Message Batches API.
Hands-on Agent SDK: rebuild every example from docs from scratch. No copy-paste.
MCP scoping deep dive — write a one-pager you could teach from.
Mock exam loop. Score honestly. Identify the last 10% of weakness.
months.gate: Sit Claude Certified Architect Foundations. Pass at ≥720/1000.

months.title: Tool design at production grade
months.why: This is where most agents fail in prod. Make tool interfaces a craft.
weeks: Tool interface design principles: shape, naming, error semantics, idempotency.
Structured output mastery: XML, JSON mode, response_format, tool_choice.
Error shapes + retry loops + CI/CD flags for tool-using agents.
Build a 5-tool agent with a full eval harness. 100 adversarial inputs.
months.gate: A tool agent that survives 100 adversarial inputs without breaking.

months.title: Plan mode, few-shot, escalation
months.why: Production agents fail gracefully. They ask for help. They do not just retry forever.
weeks: Plan mode: when it pays, when it costs more than it returns.
Few-shot orchestration patterns. Selecting examples that actually move behavior.
Escalation patterns: when the agent should stop and hand off to a human.
Build a plan-and-execute agent with explicit escalation paths.
months.gate: An agent that fails gracefully and asks for help — not just retries.

quarters.subtitle: Agent SDK depth. MCP authorship. Skills mastery.

months.title: Agent SDK depth
months.why: The Agent SDK is the rare-skill differentiator inside the Claude ecosystem right now.
weeks: Task tool: when to spawn, how to compose, when not to.
Hooks lifecycle: pre, post, error. Build three useful ones.
fork_session strategies: parallel exploration vs. context isolation.
Sub-agents + delegation. Build a parent/child system with separate context.
months.gate: A multi-agent system where parent and child have measurably separate context.

months.title: MCP server authorship
months.why: You have used 50+ connectors. Time to write your own and own the abstraction.
weeks: Build your first MCP server. Local. Working. Tested.
Auth patterns + tool design for MCP. Service auth, OAuth, scoped tokens.
Multi-server orchestration. Compose three of your own MCP servers in one Claude session.
Publish one MCP server you actually use weekly to the registry.
months.gate: One MCP server live, public, used by you in production.

months.title: Skills + Claude Code workflows
months.why: Your skill library already exists. Make it elite.
weeks: Skill authoring: gerund naming, progressive disclosure, trigger phrase density.
skill-rules.json + hooks + SLASH commands. The full surface area.
Claude Code subagents — when to use, how to scope.
Audit your existing skills. Cut the bottom 30%. Promote the top 3.
months.gate: Three production skills you genuinely use weekly. The rest archived.

quarters.subtitle: Orchestration. Evaluation. Safety as your AppSec edge.

months.title: Multi-agent orchestration
months.why: Patterns most engineers reach for badly. You will reach for them well.
weeks: Orchestrator/worker patterns. When the overhead pays back.
Routing patterns: model-as-router vs. code-as-router.
Map-reduce for agents. Long-running state management.
Ship a multi-agent system at Intinc OR FlashFusion.
months.gate: A multi-agent system shipped, instrumented, and recoverable.

months.title: Evaluation + observability
months.why: You cannot improve what you cannot measure. This is the discipline gap.
weeks: Eval harness for agents (not just prompts). Trace-level evaluation.
LLM-as-judge for agent traces. Rubric design + inter-rater reliability.
Observability stack: Langfuse, Helicone, or a custom roll-up. Pick one.
Prompt + agent versioning in git. Regression tests on every change.
months.gate: You can answer "did this change make it better or worse?" with data.

months.title: Constitutional AI + safety as your edge
months.why: This is where AppSec Kyle becomes "the rare AI engineer who actually understands safety."
weeks: Constitutional AI mental model. Read the papers. Internalize.
OWASP LLM Top 10 against your own production Claude builds.
Jailbreak resistance + prompt-injection hardening. Test it.
Multi-tenant isolation patterns for agentic Claude. Document the playbook.
months.gate: A red-team report on your own production agent. Make it public.

quarters.subtitle: Capstone. Advanced credential. Teach the playbook.

months.title: Capstone — flagship multi-agent system
months.why: The artifact every Partner Network reviewer and every future hire will look at.
weeks: Spec a flagship system. Real users. Real failure modes. Real scope.
Build it at Intinc OR FlashFusion. Real data, real telemetry.
Production telemetry + rollback plan. Run a chaos test.
Architecture Decision Record + post-mortem. Public-shareable.
months.gate: Running in production. Telemetry shareable. ADR linked from your bio.

months.title: Advanced cert OR specialization deepening
months.why: When Anthropic releases the advanced track, you are first in line. Until then, deepen.
weeks: If advanced track is live: practice exam loop. Close gaps. Sit it.
If not: pick a depth lane (agentic systems architect, evaluation, safety) and ship a public artifact.
Either path: produce one piece of definitive content in that lane.
Sit exam OR publish artifact.
months.gate: Second Anthropic credential OR equivalent shipped artifact with reach.

months.title: Teach + publish the playbook
months.why: You do not own knowledge until you can transfer it without notes.
weeks: Run a workshop at CLC — your Community Ambassador anchor event.
Record a talk for The Prompt + LinkedIn distribution.
Write the playbook ("How I built X with Claude") — long-form.
Retrospective. Define Y2 arc: deeper Claude vs. broader portfolio.
months.gate: You teach this without notes. Three people are using your patterns.

copilot.sub: 12 months. The paycheck lane. From M365 fluency through Copilot Studio depth, Power Platform integration, governance, and the AIaaS service-line pitch. Four phases, forty-eight weekly sprints, twelve gated checkpoints.

quarters.subtitle: M365 Copilot fluency. Copilot Studio fundamentals beyond what you already ship.

months.title: M365 Copilot fluency
months.why: Most of Intinc lives here. If you cannot teach Word, Excel, Outlook, and Teams Copilot cold, the AIaaS pitch dies.
weeks: M365 Copilot Chat patterns: work data scope, web grounding, prompt patterns by app.
In-app Copilot fluency: Word drafting, Excel analysis, Outlook triage, Teams meeting recap.
Copilot Pages — collaborative AI documents. Where it shines, where it fails.
Onboard a 5-person team. Watch them. Document the friction.
months.gate: A team of 5+ daily users you personally onboarded. Adoption documented.

months.title: Copilot Studio agent fundamentals — beyond what you already know
months.why: You shipped LastPass→Bitwarden. Now go deeper than the happy path.
weeks: Agent designer architecture: when to use the visual designer vs. authoring directly.
Topics vs. generative answers: the strategic decision and its tradeoffs.
System prompts at production grade. Channels (Teams, web, M365 Copilot).
Ship one new non-trivial agent at Intinc beyond the migration agent.
months.gate: A second production Copilot Studio agent shipped at Intinc. Different domain.

months.title: Knowledge sources mastery
months.why: Knowledge grounding is where most enterprise Copilot deployments fail quietly.
weeks: SharePoint connections: indexing, permissions, freshness. The real-world traps.
Dataverse-backed knowledge: when structured data beats documents.
Web sources + filtering. Allow-listing and trust patterns.
Document upload patterns + versioning. Build a knowledge governance posture.
months.gate: An agent grounded in 4+ knowledge source types with measured retrieval quality.

quarters.subtitle: Custom agents. Plugins. Power Platform integration.

months.title: Declarative vs. custom agents — the strategic choice
months.why: Pick wrong here and you are rebuilding in 6 months. This is the architecture decision that compounds.
weeks: Declarative agents (M365 surface): when they win.
Custom agents (Copilot Studio): when the extra surface area pays back.
Decision framework: cost, governance, capability, reach. Document it.
Migrate one existing agent if the original choice was wrong.
months.gate: A decision framework Daniel could sign off on. Documented in writing.

months.title: Plugins, connectors, custom actions
months.why: The surface area where Copilot Studio stops being a chatbot and starts being a platform.
weeks: Connector library: what is prebuilt, what to never trust without testing.
Custom connectors: building, certifying, sharing.
HTTP actions: the escape hatch when no connector exists.
Auth patterns: OAuth, API keys, service principals, managed identity.
months.gate: Three custom connectors in production. One of them used by another team.

months.title: Power Platform integration
months.why: Copilot Studio without Power Automate is a toy. With it, it is an enterprise automation platform.
weeks: Power Automate flows triggered from agents. Sync vs. async patterns.
Dataverse as agent memory and state store.
AI Builder for prebuilt models (form processing, sentiment, etc.).
Power Apps for agent-fronting UIs. When to build one.
months.gate: An agent that triggers a multi-step automation across 3+ MS services.

quarters.subtitle: Governance. Security. Azure AI Foundry as the graduation path.

months.title: Governance + ALM
months.why: This is where enterprise Copilot Studio gets serious — and where most agencies fall flat.
weeks: Environments + solutions: the foundational pattern most people skip.
Managed environments: when the premium pays back.
CoE Starter Kit: deploy it, learn what it surfaces.
Deployment pipelines from dev to test to prod with sign-offs.
months.gate: ALM workflow that promotes from dev to test to prod with documented sign-offs.

months.title: Security + compliance for AI
months.why: This is your AppSec edge expressed in Microsoft language. CISOs will hire you for this.
weeks: Purview + DLP for Copilot. Sensitivity labels and AI inheritance.
Customer Lockbox + data residency for Copilot.
Audit logs for agents: what gets logged, what does not, what to alert on.
Build a compliance posture document. CISO-ready.
months.gate: A compliance posture document you would ship to a CISO. Reviewed by Dave or Jackie.

months.title: Azure AI Foundry — when to graduate
months.why: Knowing when Copilot Studio is the wrong tool is a more valuable skill than knowing how to use it.
weeks: Foundry vs. Copilot Studio: decision matrix on cost, control, capability.
Prompt flow: the more code-forward authoring path.
Model catalog: Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, others — inside Microsoft.
Bring-your-own-model patterns. Migrate one workload deliberately.
months.gate: One workload migrated from Copilot Studio to Foundry with documented rationale.

quarters.subtitle: Enterprise capstone. Microsoft cert. The AIaaS playbook lands.

months.title: Enterprise capstone — multi-agent rollout
months.why: The Head of AIaaS proof point. This is the artifact that justifies the role.
weeks: Spec the rollout. Stakeholders, success metrics, risk register.
Deploy in stages. Pilot, expand, generalize.
Instrument adoption: who uses it, when, for what.
Manage change. Document the friction. Fix the bottom 20%.
months.gate: 50+ active users at Intinc. Adoption telemetry public to leadership.

months.title: Microsoft AI cert
months.why: Logos matter for the AIaaS pitch. Two paths, one decision.
weeks: Decide path: AI-102 (Azure AI Engineer Associate, broader) vs. MB-820 (Copilot Studio Maker, focused).
Practice exam loop. Track scores. Identify gaps.
Close gaps. No new material in week 4.
Sit the exam.
months.gate: MS cert in hand. Logos updated everywhere.

months.title: Build the AIaaS playbook
months.why: Twelve months of work either becomes a service line — or it does not. This is where you make it real.
weeks: Synthesize the year into a service-line offering. Pricing, packaging, delivery.
SOW templates. Discovery script. Implementation runbook.
Pitch to Daniel + Dave + Jackie internally. Get the AIaaS dept on the roadmap.
Teach it: train the next person at Intinc to do what you do.
months.gate: AIaaS service line proposal in front of leadership. Decision: yes, no, or pilot.

openai.sub: 12 months. The lingua franca play. From Responses API and reasoning models through the Agents SDK, Realtime voice, fine-tuning, and a multi-provider capstone. Four phases, forty-eight weekly sprints, twelve gated checkpoints.

quarters.subtitle: Current-state APIs. Structured outputs. Reasoning models when they earn their cost.

months.title: Responses API + current-state fluency
months.why: OpenAI has multiple overlapping APIs. Pick a default, learn it cold, migrate one real prompt.
weeks: Map the API landscape: Responses API vs. Chat Completions vs. Assistants. Pick your default.
SDK fluency in Python and JS. First production call from your stack.
Migrate one Claude prompt to OpenAI. Diff outputs. Write the migration notes.
Cost + latency baseline against Claude on the same task.
months.gate: A working OpenAI-backed feature in your stack. Not a notebook — a feature.

months.title: Structured outputs + function calling, OpenAI-native
months.why: OpenAI structured outputs differ from Claude tool use in subtle, expensive ways. Learn the differences.
weeks: response_format: json_schema vs json_object. Strict mode behaviors.
Tool calling: single, parallel, choice-forced. Latency implications.
Schema authoring discipline: Pydantic/Zod-first, then JSON Schema export.
Build a 5-tool agent with strict schema compliance. 100 adversarial inputs.
months.gate: A 5-tool agent with strict schema compliance under adversarial load.

months.title: o-series reasoning models
months.why: Reasoning models unlock problem classes Claude and Gemini cannot always match. Knowing when is the skill.
weeks: Model selection: o-series tiers, when each makes sense.
Reasoning effort tuning. The cost vs. quality curve, measured.
Tasks where reasoning models beat non-reasoning by ≥20%. Identify yours.
Move one real workload to a reasoning model. Document the win.
months.gate: One workload measurably better on a reasoning model than on standard.

quarters.subtitle: Agents SDK. Realtime API. Multimodal patterns.

months.title: OpenAI Agents SDK
months.why: OpenAI's native agent framework. Required for any serious multi-agent OpenAI work.
weeks: Agents SDK primitives: agent, tool, runner, session.
Handoffs and routing patterns.
Sessions and state persistence.
Tracing + debugging at the agent level. Build a 3-agent system with handoffs.
months.gate: A multi-agent system with at least two clean handoffs. Traced and recoverable.

months.title: Realtime API — voice and streaming
months.why: OpenAI's Realtime API is genuinely best-in-class for voice agents. Underused even by veterans.
weeks: WebRTC vs. WebSocket transport. Pick by use case.
Voice agent fundamentals: turn-taking, interruption, barge-in.
Latency budgeting. Where the milliseconds go and how to claw them back.
Ship one working voice agent prototype. Real microphone, real responses.
months.gate: A working voice agent prototype. Sub-700ms turn latency.

months.title: Vision + multimodal
months.why: Vision is now table stakes. Multimodal agents are the next plateau.
weeks: Image input patterns. Detail levels. Token costs at high-detail mode.
Image generation: gpt-image / DALL·E. When to use which.
Audio in and out. STT + TTS pipelines vs. native multimodal.
Ship one multimodal feature. Not a demo — a feature.
months.gate: A multimodal feature shipped to real users.

quarters.subtitle: Fine-tuning. Evals. Provider portability.

months.title: Fine-tuning + distillation
months.why: Most engineers reach for fine-tuning when prompting would have worked. Learn when it actually wins.
weeks: Decision framework: when fine-tuning beats prompting. The honest version.
Data prep + dataset hygiene. The 80% of the work.
SFT vs. DPO. Method selection by problem shape.
Run one fine-tune. Evaluate against the prompted baseline.
months.gate: One fine-tune that beats prompting on a clear, measurable metric.

months.title: OpenAI Evals + production observability
months.why: Without evals, every prompt change is a guess. This is the discipline gap.
weeks: OpenAI Evals platform. Custom graders.
LLM-as-judge for OpenAI specifically. Calibration patterns.
Production observability: cost telemetry, latency p95, quality drift.
Build an eval suite that runs on every prompt change. CI integration.
months.gate: An eval suite that runs on every prompt change with regression alerts.

months.title: Provider-portable patterns
months.why: This is where your Claude + Gemini work compounds. Multi-provider fluency is the partner-network differentiator.
weeks: Portability layers: BAML, Vercel AI SDK, LangChain abstractions. Honest tradeoffs.
Cost / latency / quality routing. Build the policy.
Build a provider router: same logic, OpenAI / Claude / Gemini backends.
Document the comparison. This becomes a publishable artifact.
months.gate: A working provider router with documented routing policy. Switch is a config change.

quarters.subtitle: Multi-provider capstone. Specialization. The comparative playbook.

months.title: Multi-provider capstone
months.why: The single artifact that proves you are a multi-model practitioner, not a single-vendor enthusiast.
weeks: Spec a system: OpenAI primary, Claude/Gemini fallback by policy.
Build it. Real users. Real failure modes.
Instrument cost telemetry. Tune the routing policy on real traffic.
ADR + cost report. Public-shareable.
months.gate: Multi-provider system in production with measurable cost optimization.

months.title: Specialization or recognized depth
months.why: OpenAI does not currently offer an official cert. Pivot to a deep specialization that produces a public artifact.
weeks: Pick a specialty: voice agents, fine-tuning, evals, or realtime/multimodal.
Go deep. Produce a definitive artifact in that lane.
Engage publicly: forum posts, GitHub repo, a workshop.
Land recognition: cited, used, or referenced by someone outside your circle.
months.gate: Recognized depth in one OpenAI specialty. Public artifact with reach.

months.title: Publish the multi-provider playbook
months.why: You now have Claude + Gemini + OpenAI in production. That comparative knowledge is rare. Publish it.
weeks: Synthesize 12+ months of cross-provider learning. The honest version.
Publish: long-form guide, talk, or workshop series. Pick one channel.
Run a workshop: "Claude vs. Gemini vs. OpenAI for technical teams" — at CLC, Intinc, or a meetup.
Retrospective. Define Y2: deeper in one provider, or platform-agnostic architect track?
months.gate: A definitive multi-provider practitioner guide. Yours, public, dated, cited.

practitioner.sub: All five platforms. One year. Claude, Gemini, Copilot, OpenAI — sequenced by priority, exam-collision-aware, with per-week platform tagging and load meters so you know exactly what you are committing to each month.

quarters.subtitle: Close Architect Foundations. Stand up all four platforms. Lay the eval foundation.

months.title: Claude cert sprint
months.why: Everything else is deferred until Architect Foundations closes. It is the early-mover window that does not reopen.
weeks: Gap audit: Agent SDK (Task, hooks, fork_session), CLAUDE.md hierarchy, MCP scoping, Message Batches. Write the study plan.
Hands-on Agent SDK exercises — rebuild every example from docs from scratch. No copy-paste.
Mock exam loop × 3. Score each. Document the final weak spots.
Sit Claude Certified Architect Foundations. Pass at ≥720/1000.
months.gate: Architect Foundations cert in hand. Everything else unblocked.

months.title: Three platforms, first production calls
months.why: Cert is closed. Now stand up Gemini and prove Copilot depth beyond what you already ship.
weeks: AI Studio onboarding — model lineup, SDK integration, first production call from your stack.
M365 Copilot fluency: Chat, in-app (Word/Excel/Outlook/Teams), Copilot Pages. Onboard 5+ users.
Post-cert tool design — production-grade tool interfaces, error shapes, tool_choice.
First Gemini feature in production. Diff the output against equivalent Claude call.
months.gate: Three platforms each with at least one production call. Not notebooks.

months.title: OpenAI starts. Agent foundations across all four.
months.why: The full platform surface is now active. Every platform gets its first agentic pattern.
weeks: Copilot Studio depth: topics vs. generative, system prompts, channels. New agent shipped.
Agent SDK: Task tool, hooks, fork_session — production patterns, not docs.
Function calling + structured output comparative — same task, Claude vs. Gemini. Document diff.
OpenAI setup: Responses API as default, first production call, SDK fluency in JS and Python.
months.gate: All four platforms with working integration in your stack. One agent per platform.

quarters.subtitle: Each platform earns its advanced unlock. Eval discipline built across all four.

months.title: Context, MCP, and tool mastery
months.why: The features that separate production practitioners from demo builders. One advanced unlock per platform.
weeks: Gemini context caching deep dive — measure hit rate, model the cost savings. Document the threshold.
MCP server #1. Build it. Use it weekly. Not a tutorial project.
OpenAI structured outputs strict mode + parallel tool use. 5-tool agent, 100 adversarial inputs.
Copilot plugins + custom connectors. Three connectors in production, one used by another team.
months.gate: Each platform has one advanced feature shipped in production.

months.title: Multimodal, multi-agent, Power Platform
months.why: Multi-step and multimodal capabilities per platform. This is where demo-grade ends.
weeks: Gemini Files API + multimodal — one non-text use case (doc, image, or audio) shipped.
Multi-agent orchestration: orchestrator/worker pattern. Ship it at Intinc or FlashFusion.
Power Platform: agent triggering multi-step Automate flow across 3+ M365 services.
OpenAI Agents SDK: multi-agent with clean handoffs. Traced and recoverable.
months.gate: Each platform has one multi-step or multimodal feature. Four features, four platforms.

months.title: Evaluation discipline — the cross-platform layer
months.why: Without evals, every change to every platform is a guess. This month installs the discipline system-wide.
weeks: Pick one eval tool (promptfoo or LangSmith). Learn it cold for all four providers.
LLM-as-judge calibration across providers. Rubric design. Inter-rater reliability check.
OWASP LLM Top 10 red-team run against your own Claude and OpenAI builds. Publish the report.
Prompt + agent versioning in git. CI eval run on every change. Regression alerts live.
months.gate: Eval suite running across all active platforms. Every prompt change gets scored.

quarters.subtitle: Security posture. MS and GCP exams. Provider portability layer built.

months.title: Governance, security, and exam prep
months.why: Copilot governance + Claude safety together is rare. MS exam prep starts here.
weeks: Copilot Studio governance: environments, solutions, ALM pipeline. Dev → test → prod with sign-offs.
Security: Purview, DLP, audit logs, sensitivity labels for AI. Draft CISO-ready posture doc.
Constitutional AI + safety patterns. Red-team your own production Claude agent. Make it public.
MS cert practice exam #1 (AI-102 or MB-820). Record baseline score honestly.
months.gate: MS cert baseline recorded. Security posture doc drafted. Red-team report published.

months.title: Advanced features + MS cert close
months.why: Advanced platform features compound, and the MS cert closes this month.
weeks: Gemini grounding with Google Search + Live API prototype. Measure when grounding helps vs. hurts.
OpenAI Realtime API voice agent prototype. Sub-700ms turn latency goal.
Azure AI Foundry orientation. Decision matrix vs. Copilot Studio. One workload migrated.
Sit AI-102 or MB-820. MS AI cert closes this month.
months.gate: MS AI cert in hand. Advanced feature per platform shipped.

months.title: Provider portability + Vertex ramp
months.why: The bridge month. Multi-provider routing, Vertex foundation, fine-tuning experiment.
weeks: Vertex AI ramp: IAM, projects, billing, quotas. First Vertex endpoint. GCP ML Eng baseline exam.
OpenAI fine-tuning: one SFT that beats prompting on a clear, measurable metric.
Provider router: Claude / Gemini / OpenAI backends, policy-based switching. Build it.
Cost / latency / quality model across all providers. Spreadsheet defensible to Daniel.
months.gate: Provider router working. Switching providers is a config change, not a rewrite.

quarters.subtitle: Multi-provider capstone. Google ML Eng cert. Teach everything.

months.title: Capstone — multi-provider production system
months.why: The single artifact that proves you are a multi-model practitioner. Everything before this was practice.
weeks: Spec the system: real users, real scope, provider assignments by routing policy.
Build. OpenAI primary, Claude/Gemini fallback by policy. Real data, real failure modes.
Instrument. Cost telemetry, latency p95, quality drift. Tune routing on real traffic.
ADR + cost report. Public-shareable. Architecture Decision Record linked from your bio.
months.gate: Multi-provider system in production. Cost report published. ADR live.

months.title: Google Professional ML Engineer cert
months.why: Already on your list. Already started in M9. Close it.
weeks: Practice exam loops. Pull the current exam guide. Rotate question pools.
Close remaining gaps: pipelines, feature stores, MLOps, data engineering patterns.
Publish: synthesize cross-platform learnings into one public artifact before exam week.
Sit Google Professional ML Engineer. Two certs on the year.
months.gate: Google ML Eng cert in hand. Two certs closed in 12 months.

months.title: Teach, publish, pitch
months.why: Twelve months of multi-platform work becomes a community event, a published guide, and a service-line pitch.
weeks: Workshop at CLC: "The Multi-Provider AI Practitioner." Community Ambassador anchor event.
Publish the comparative playbook: Claude vs. Gemini vs. Copilot vs. OpenAI. Practitioner-grade.
AIaaS service-line pitch to Daniel + Dave + Jackie. Multi-platform depth = higher enterprise value.
Retrospective. What changed in your mental model? Define Y2. What is the next arc?
months.gate: Workshop done. Playbook public. AIaaS pitch made. Year synthesized.

aiaas.sub: 12 months. The business lane. From a vague "AI consulting" offer to a defined service line, a closed pilot, an external client, and a formal department decision from Intinc leadership. Four phases, forty-eight weekly activities, twelve gated business checkpoints.

quarters.subtitle: Name what you sell. Build the evidence base. Systematize the proposal.

months.title: Service architecture — what you actually sell
months.why: Most consultants never clearly define their offer. Vague services attract vague clients and produce variable margins. You have 45+ builds. Pick three to five things you will actually sell — not "AI consulting."
weeks: Service taxonomy: name 3–5 specific SKUs with defined deliverables, timelines, and out-of-scope clauses. Not categories — sellable units.
Pricing model decision: project-based vs. retainer vs. productized service. Pick one as your primary motion and write down why.
Ideal client profile: who can write the check, who benefits, who signs the SOW. Not demographics — write the pain profile in their words.
Competitive positioning: why you over a Big 4 AI practice, a freelancer, or an internal hire. Write it in two sentences. If you cannot, the positioning is not clear yet.
months.gate: A one-page service catalog: 3 SKUs, each with a price, a deliverable, and what is explicitly not included.

months.title: Build the evidence base
months.why: You have 45+ products. Almost none of them are positioned as case studies. Every pitch without proof is a trust ask. Every pitch with proof is a demonstration.
weeks: Portfolio audit: identify the 5 builds that best demonstrate AIaaS value. Score each on: measurable outcome, client recognizability, and replicability.
Write a case study for each of the top 3: problem stated in client language, approach in one paragraph, outcome with a number — even an internal estimate.
Build the credibility stack: cert logos, case study PDFs, 2–3 testimonial-style quotes from real colleagues or stakeholders.
One-page capability brief — the thing you send before a discovery call. Problem you solve → proof you can → next step. No more than one page.
months.gate: 3 publishable case studies and a capability brief you would not be embarrassed to send to Dave or Jackie.

months.title: Proposal and SOW infrastructure
months.why: Every hour you spend writing a custom proposal from scratch is margin erosion. The proposal is a product. Build it once, deploy it repeatedly.
weeks: Discovery call script: 10 questions that qualify AND scope simultaneously. The goal is to walk out knowing whether to write a proposal.
SOW template per SKU: fixed scope, explicit change order protocol, acceptance criteria, payment schedule. One template per SKU from month 1.
Proposal deck template: 8 slides max. Problem → approach → proof → team → pricing → timeline → risk → next step.
Mock run: run a discovery call + proposal cycle against a real or simulated client need. Time it. Fix what is slow.
months.gate: A proposal packet — discovery script, SOW template, deck — that you could send Monday morning without editing the structure.

quarters.subtitle: The Intinc business case. The pilot engagement. The delivery operating system.

months.title: The Intinc AIaaS business case
months.why: The department does not exist until leadership approves it. This month is the political and financial work. Daniel is the first gate. Dave and Jackie are the second. You need a business case, not a conversation.
weeks: Market framing: what is the addressable opportunity for an AIaaS service line inside a mid-sized engineering org? Use real numbers — Gartner 75%/50% stats are verified; use them.
Internal audit: how much AI work is Intinc doing today that is unbilled or under-leveraged? Estimate the revenue gap.
Department structure proposal: headcount year one, reporting line under Daniel, cost center vs. profit center decision, success metrics for 12 months.
Present to Daniel. This is a real meeting with a real proposal document. Document the outcome, objections, and what he needs to see next.
months.gate: A written business case in front of Daniel with a clear yes / no / revisit decision recorded.

months.title: Pilot engagement — real client, real scope
months.why: Theory about what you sell is worthless without a real engagement. The pilot client can be an internal Intinc team, CLC, or a warm external contact — but it must involve a real deliverable and a real timeline.
weeks: Identify the pilot client. Low risk, high learning. Internal teams count if they have a real problem. CLC is a natural warm relationship.
Run the discovery call using your script from M3. Document what you learned versus what you assumed going in.
Deliver the engagement. Track actual hours versus estimated. Note every scope-creep moment.
Post-mortem: what was the real margin? Where did scope creep? What would you change in the SOW? Write it down before you forget.
months.gate: One completed pilot engagement with a written post-mortem. Margin calculated on actual hours, not estimate.

months.title: Delivery systems and repeatability
months.why: A freelancer delivers work. A service line delivers a repeatable experience. The difference is a delivery system. This month you build the operating system for every future engagement.
weeks: Project management framework: kickoff agenda, weekly check-in format, status report template, close-out process. One document.
Quality checklist per SKU: what does "done" look like? Who signs off? What does the client receive at the end?
Subcontracting model: if volume exceeds your capacity, what does bringing in help look like? Rate, vetting criteria, client communication protocol.
Client onboarding and offboarding templates: the experience from first invoice to final deliverable. Someone else should be able to run it.
months.gate: A delivery playbook another person could use to run an engagement without you in the room for 80% of it.

quarters.subtitle: First external client. Price on real data. Partner Network as a lead source.

months.title: First external client acquisition
months.why: Internal and warm leads are training wheels. An external client tests the full market proposition — cold positioning, real objection handling, competitive pressure. You need this data regardless of outcome.
weeks: Outreach channel decision: LinkedIn, Partner Network directory, referral from existing contact. Pick one and commit — do not spread thin across all three.
First 5 qualified discovery conversations. Not pitches. Discovery calls where you ask all 10 questions and listen more than you talk.
First external proposal sent. Track time from discovery to proposal, time to response, objections raised, and decision-maker access.
Close or lose — document why either way. A lost deal with documented objections is worth more than a won deal you do not understand.
months.gate: A closed or formally lost external deal with documented objections and a one-page deal debrief.

months.title: Pricing optimization — adjust on real data
months.why: Your M1 prices were informed guesses. After a pilot and an external deal, you have actual data on margin, perceived value, and what clients push back on. Use it.
weeks: Margin analysis across all delivered work so far. Actual hours versus estimated, scope delivered versus scoped, effective hourly rate per engagement.
Value pricing calibration: what would the pilot client have paid for the outcome if they had known the result in advance? Compare to what you charged.
Raise at least one SKU price or create a premium tier. Document the rationale — not "I deserve more" but "the market data supports this."
Update all SOW templates, proposal decks, and the service catalog to reflect new pricing. Old pricing documents are a liability.
months.gate: At least one SKU repriced upward with a written rationale based on actual margin and value data.

months.title: Partner Network and referral infrastructure
months.why: The Claude Partner Network directory is a passive lead source. Referrals from complementary practitioners are an active one. Both require infrastructure you do not currently have.
weeks: Claude Partner Network profile: complete, specific, case study links live. Not a placeholder. The kind of profile an enterprise buyer would click.
Referral partner map: who else serves your ideal client without competing directly? Systems integrators, IT consultancies, fractional CTOs.
First referral partner conversation: informal, exploratory. What would a mutual referral arrangement look like for both sides?
CLC and community pipeline: convert the teaching relationship and ambassador credibility into client conversations. One explicit ask.
months.gate: One active referral relationship documented and a Partner Network profile a stranger could use to evaluate you.

quarters.subtitle: Revenue milestone. Department decision. Systems for Y2.

months.title: Revenue milestone — the real number
months.why: You set a target of $300K–$500K Y1. This month you compare reality to that target, understand the gap, and decide whether the model works or needs to change. Numbers are not judgment — they are information.
weeks: Revenue audit: total billed in months 1–9, categorized by SKU, client type (internal/external), and acquisition channel. Build a simple spreadsheet.
Pipeline review: every active deal by stage, estimated close date, and deal size. What is the realistic 90-day number?
Gap analysis: if you are behind the $300K target, what would close the gap — more volume, higher price, a different SKU mix, or a different client profile?
Course correction decision: adjust one variable deliberately. Not everything. One lever, clearly stated, for Q4 execution.
months.gate: A revenue number you can defend to Daniel with a source spreadsheet. Gap to target stated plainly.

months.title: Department formation pitch — Dave and Jackie
months.why: The AIaaS department either forms this year or it does not. You now have 10 months of real data — case studies, margins, a pipeline, and a delivery system. This is the pitch that matters.
weeks: Updated business case for Dave and Jackie: what happened in months 1–10? Real numbers, real clients, real outcomes. Not projections — actuals.
Department charter draft: formal name, scope, headcount plan for Y2, first hire criteria and role description, reporting line.
Full leadership presentation: 15 slides max. Market opportunity → Intinc position → what you built → what it costs to scale → what leadership decides today.
The meeting. Document the decision and the exact conditions attached to it — even a "yes with conditions" is a yes.
months.gate: A formal decision from Dave and/or Jackie: yes (department forms), no (stay as internal practice), or pilot (time-boxed with named conditions).

months.title: Systems, playbook, and Y2 plan
months.why: A department without documentation is a person. Build the operating system for what you created — so it can survive a busy quarter, a new hire, or a week you are sick.
weeks: Documentation sprint: all templates, processes, delivery checklists, and pricing in one organized location. Notion, Craft, or a SharePoint folder — pick one.
Y2 revenue target and product roadmap: which new SKUs, which new client segments, which new acquisition channels. With assumptions exposed.
Hire or partner plan: if the department forms, who is the first hire? What is the job description? If not, what is the subcontracting plan?
Retrospective: what changed in your mental model of what this business is? What did you get wrong in M1 that you know now?
months.gate: A Y2 plan with a target, three stated assumptions, and the first three actions to execute in January.

mcp.sub: 12 months. From 50+ connector consumer to ecosystem contributor. Protocol foundations, production auth, the full primitive surface, a five-server portfolio, and a flagship reference implementation. Four phases, forty-eight weekly sprints, twelve gated artifacts.

quarters.subtitle: Read the spec before touching the keyboard. First server working. Tool design as craft.

months.title: Read the spec — all of it
months.why: You have used 50+ MCP connectors. You know the surface. You do not know the protocol. People who build servers without reading the spec build fragile, subtly wrong tools. Forty-five minutes with the spec saves you forty-five hours of debugging.
weeks: Read the MCP specification end to end. Document every concept you could not have defined before: transport lifecycle, capability negotiation, session management, progress notifications.
Transport deep dive: stdio vs. HTTP+SSE vs. WebSocket. Why HTTP+SSE is the default for remote servers, when stdio is correct for local, and what WebSocket buys you.
The three primitives mapped to your existing experience: for each of Tools, Resources, and Prompts, identify one connector in your existing 50+ that uses each well and one that uses it badly.
Capability negotiation and the MCP handshake — document the full exchange from client hello to server ready in a sequence diagram you could teach from.
months.gate: A spec summary in your own words — transport, lifecycle, three primitives, capability negotiation. Something you could use to onboard another developer.

months.title: First server — local, working, tested
months.why: Theory ends here. Your first server will not be elegant. That is correct. The goal is working and tested — not beautiful. Pick a real problem you have right now, not a tutorial toy.
weeks: Environment setup: Node/TypeScript MCP SDK AND Python FastMCP. Both connected to a local Claude Desktop session. Understand which SDK to reach for by use case.
First Tool — something you actually use. Not a "get weather" tutorial. A tool that solves a problem in your current stack. One tool, working end to end, with the correct input schema.
First Resource — expose a real data source. Your Supabase schema, a Notion document, or a local file you reference regularly. Static is fine for now.
Write tests before shipping anything. Unit tests for tool execution logic. One integration test that runs the full round-trip against a real Claude Desktop session.
months.gate: A working MCP server — 2 tools and 1 resource, with tests — connected to Claude Desktop and solving a real problem.

months.title: Tool design as craft
months.why: Anyone can wrap a function in a tool call. Designing tools that work well with LLMs is a different skill. The description field is a prompt. Schema shape affects reasoning quality. Error responses either help Claude recover or confuse it.
weeks: Description discipline: rewrite the descriptions on your M2 tools as if each one is a system prompt instruction. Test whether Claude uses the tool more accurately after the rewrite.
Input schema design rules: required vs. optional fields, enum vs. open string, nested objects vs. flat. Write down the rules you derive — you will apply them to every tool you build.
Error response design: build a tool that returns structured error shapes. Test which error formats Claude handles gracefully vs. gets confused by. Document the pattern.
Idempotency: build one tool that is safe to call twice and one that is not. Write the side-effect documentation for each. This becomes part of your tool design checklist.
months.gate: A tool design checklist — at least 10 rules you can apply to every tool you write. Applied to your M2 server before moving on.

quarters.subtitle: Auth at production grade. The full primitive surface. Multi-server composition.

months.title: Authentication patterns
months.why: Every server that connects to a real external service needs auth. Most tutorial MCP servers hardcode an API key in an env file and call it done. Production auth means no key exposure, least-privilege by default, and token rotation that does not break sessions.
weeks: API key auth — the simplest pattern done correctly: key in env, never logged, never echoed in tool responses, never returned in resource content. Build one and audit it deliberately.
OAuth 2.0 for MCP servers — the full flow: authorization endpoint, token exchange, refresh handling, and what happens when the token expires mid-session.
Service principal + managed identity (Microsoft ecosystem) — directly relevant to your Copilot/Azure stack. Build an MCP server that authenticates against a Microsoft API using a service principal.
Scoped token patterns: build a server where different users or contexts get access to different tools. The least-privilege design pattern applied to MCP.
months.gate: Three working auth patterns in your codebase. One documented failure mode per pattern — the thing that will go wrong in production.

months.title: Resources and Prompts — the underused surface
months.why: Most public MCP servers are tools-only. Resources and Prompts are underused, which means servers that implement them well stand out in the registry. The full primitive set is also how you build servers that degrade gracefully when a tool is unavailable.
weeks: Resources deep dive — static vs. dynamic resources, subscriptions (resource change notifications), the list-then-read pattern. Build a server where resources update in real time.
Expose a genuinely useful resource from your stack: your Supabase schema as a resource, a live n8n workflow status feed, or a Cloudflare Worker health endpoint.
Prompts primitive — templated prompt patterns exposed via MCP. Build one prompt that encodes a workflow you use repeatedly. Test whether it actually speeds up your Claude usage.
Sampling — the MCP pattern where a server requests LLM completions from the client. Edge case, but essential to understand for agentic server designs. Build a toy implementation.
months.gate: A server using all three primitives (tools + resources + prompts) with a written rationale for why each was the right primitive for its use case.

months.title: Multi-server composition
months.why: The real leverage in MCP is composing multiple servers in one session. You have done this as a consumer with 50+ connectors. Doing it with servers you authored is a different experience — you control both sides of every interaction.
weeks: Compose three of your own servers in a single Claude session. Document every namespace collision, every unexpected tool interaction, every capability overlap.
Server naming conventions and namespace design — the decisions that prevent collisions at scale. Write the convention you will use for every server going forward.
Context window pressure under multi-server load — how resource-heavy servers affect reasoning quality when composed with tool-heavy ones. Test it, measure it, write up what you find.
Build a routing server: one MCP server that inspects the request context and delegates to other servers based on domain. The meta-orchestration pattern.
months.gate: A working multi-server composition where you authored all three servers. The routing server is working and dispatching correctly.

quarters.subtitle: Production-ready. First registry publish. Five-server portfolio across real domains.

months.title: Production-readiness checklist
months.why: Local servers are practice. Production means versioning, changelog, backwards compatibility, graceful degradation, and observability. Most public MCP servers in the registry skip every single one of these. Yours will not.
weeks: Versioning strategy: semantic versioning for MCP servers, changelog format, how you communicate breaking changes to consumers. Write the policy before you publish anything.
Error handling at production grade: timeouts with sensible defaults, retry semantics, partial failure handling. What does a consumer do when your tool returns a 503?
Observability: what to log (request shape, response latency, error rate), what never to log (input fields that might contain credentials or PII), and how to surface logs without exposing them.
Backwards compatibility test suite: a set of tests that verify your v2 does not break any v1 consumer. Run this before every release. Automate it.
months.gate: A production-readiness checklist applied to every server you built in Q1–Q2. At least two servers updated as a result.

months.title: First public registry publish
months.why: Private servers are practice. A public registry listing is the first real ecosystem contribution — and the thing that makes your Partner Network profile, your Community Ambassador application, and your LinkedIn bio mean something concrete.
weeks: Registry options and submission: Anthropic registry, npm (for TypeScript), PyPI (for Python). Understand each — discoverability, maintenance expectations, versioning policy.
Documentation that actually works: README with a working quick-start that takes under 5 minutes, schema documentation for every tool, example Claude prompts that demonstrate correct usage.
Publish your strongest server — not your first, not your most complex, the one that solves the clearest problem for the widest audience. Run the production checklist from M7 first.
Usage signal: star count, npm/PyPI download count, GitHub issues. Set up a simple way to know if anyone other than you is using it.
months.gate: One server live in a public registry. Complete documentation. At least one person other than you has successfully used it.

months.title: The portfolio — five servers, five domains
months.why: One server is a demo. Five servers across distinct domains is a portfolio. Breadth signals that you understand the protocol well enough to apply it to different problem shapes — not just the one you practiced on.
weeks: Portfolio plan: map your stack (Supabase, Microsoft Teams/M365, n8n, Cloudflare Workers, Claude API itself) to four more servers. Each in a different domain, each with a different auth pattern.
Build servers 2 and 3. Different auth patterns from each other. Different primary primitive from server 1. Ship both.
Build servers 4 and 5. At least one must solve a problem you have personally — not a problem you invented for this exercise. Both shipped.
Portfolio presentation: a GitHub repo or landing page that shows all five with a one-paragraph design rationale for each. This is the artifact you link from your bio.
months.gate: Five servers published. Each documented. At least three with measurable external usage (not just your own sessions).

quarters.subtitle: Flagship reference implementation. Ecosystem contribution. Teach the full arc.

months.title: Flagship server — the reference implementation
months.why: The portfolio proves breadth. The flagship proves depth. This is the server other developers study — the one that shows what a production-grade, thoughtfully designed MCP server looks like from the inside.
weeks: Spec the flagship: a server that uses tools + resources + prompts + real auth, solves a genuine enterprise problem, and handles failure modes explicitly. Write the spec before writing a line of code.
Build it. Real data, real auth, real error handling, real observability. Every shortcut you would not ship to a client gets fixed before this one goes out.
Architecture Decision Record: why these design choices? Where did you trade simplicity for correctness? What would you do differently in a v2? Published alongside the server.
Write the companion post: "How I designed this MCP server and what I learned." The design rationale, the mistakes, the things the spec does not tell you. Publish it.
months.gate: A flagship server that a thoughtful engineer would study as a reference implementation. ADR and companion post both live.

months.title: Ecosystem contribution — beyond your own servers
months.why: The MCP ecosystem is early. The developers who help others get unstuck in year one are remembered in year three. Contributing to others' work, reviewing designs, and writing the guides that do not exist yet — this is the reputation work that compounds.
weeks: Review five public MCP servers from the registry. Write honest, specific public feedback on at least two — not "great work" but "this error shape will confuse the model because..."
Contribute to one open-source MCP server that is not yours. A real PR that fixes a real problem. Not a typo fix.
Write "MCP server design patterns" — the guide you wish had existed in M1. The naming conventions, the auth patterns, the tool design rules, the multi-server composition patterns. All of it.
Submit a talk or workshop proposal: "MCP server authorship for enterprise developers." CLC, a local tech meetup, or a conference CFP. Get it on a calendar.
months.gate: A public contribution beyond your own servers. A submitted talk proposal with a confirmed date or a live CFP submission.

months.title: Teach, publish, close the arc
months.why: You do not own this knowledge until you can transfer it without notes. The workshop closes the Community Ambassador loop, the published guide closes the Partner Network loop, and the retrospective tells you what the next arc actually is.
weeks: Run the MCP server authorship workshop — at CLC, Intinc, or a Community Ambassador event. Use M1–M11 as the curriculum backbone. The spec, the first server, tool design, auth, portfolio.
Publish the complete MCP builder guide: spec → first server → auth → full primitive set → production → portfolio. The definitive practitioner guide. Yours, dated, with real examples.
Update everything: Partner Network profile with portfolio links and the guide, LinkedIn with the five servers and the workshop, Community Ambassador impact report if applicable.

Retrospective: what changed in your mental model of how Claude actually uses tools? What surprised you about the ecosystem? What is Y2 — deeper MCP (framework contributions, spec feedback), or pivot to RAG and the data layer?
months.gate: Workshop delivered. Guide published. Portfolio and Partner Network profile updated. Three developers are building MCP servers because of your work.

security.sub: 12 months. Three frameworks cold. Two certs in hand. A red-team report, a multi-tenant isolation design, a prompt injection hardening guide, and a CISO-ready posture template — all published. The AppSec brand formalized into credentials no one else in the partner ecosystem carries together.

quarters.subtitle: Three frameworks cold. Applied to your own stack, not to hypotheticals.

months.title: OWASP LLM Top 10 — applied, not theoretical
months.why: This is the framework enterprise security teams reach for first when evaluating AI deployments. You already cite it. Citing it and owning it are different. Every vulnerability needs a test run against something you actually shipped.
weeks: Read the OWASP LLM Top 10 end to end. For each vulnerability, name one system you have shipped where that class of bug could exist. No hypotheticals.
LLM01 — Prompt Injection: build a structured test harness that attempts direct and indirect injection against one of your Claude or Copilot Studio deployments. Document every finding.
LLM02 through LLM06 (Insecure Output Handling, Training Data Poisoning, Model DoS, Supply Chain, Sensitive Info Disclosure): one practical test per vulnerability against real infrastructure.
LLM07 through LLM10 (Insecure Plugin Design, Excessive Agency, Overreliance, Model Theft): finish the set. Score each finding by severity. Remediate anything critical before moving on.
months.gate: A completed OWASP LLM Top 10 vulnerability assessment against one of your own production systems. Published publicly — this is the first proof artifact.

months.title: MITRE ATLAS — the adversarial ML threat matrix
months.why: ATLAS is the ATT&CK equivalent for AI systems. It covers the attack surfaces OWASP LLM Top 10 does not: model evasion, data poisoning at training time, model inversion, and extraction. If you want to brief a red team or a CISO, you need fluency in both.
weeks: Read the full MITRE ATLAS technique catalog. Map every technique to the adversarial ML attack lifecycle: reconnaissance → initial access → execution → exfiltration. One diagram.
Attack surface map for your stack: which ATLAS techniques apply to your Claude, Copilot Studio, and n8n deployments? Be specific about which component each technique targets.
ATLAS vs. OWASP LLM Top 10 crosswalk: where do they complement each other, where do they conflict, and where does one cover gaps the other misses? Write the comparison you would use to brief a CISO.
Simulate two ATLAS techniques in a test environment (not production). Document what you found, what you could not fully test, and what would require a dedicated red-team engagement.
months.gate: An ATLAS attack surface map for your own stack, mapped to real deployment components. A CISO-ready crosswalk of ATLAS and OWASP LLM Top 10.

months.title: NIST AI RMF — governance as practitioner fluency
months.why: SecAI+ and CAISP both reference NIST AI RMF. Enterprise buyers use it as an evaluation checklist. Understanding it as a practitioner — not just as a test-taker — is what makes your security posture documents land with people who sign purchase orders.
weeks: NIST AI RMF 1.0 core structure: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE. Each function, its outcomes, and the specific relevance to deployed agentic AI systems. Not a summary — a working model.
Map the RMF to a real AI deployment you own: which controls are implemented, which are explicitly missing, which genuinely do not apply. Honest assessment.
Create a basic AI RMF organizational profile for Intinc or FlashFusion. This is a deliverable you will use in a real sales or procurement conversation within 12 months.
Full crosswalk: NIST AI RMF ↔ OWASP LLM Top 10 ↔ MITRE ATLAS. Where do all three align? Where are the gaps none of them cover? This document becomes your exam reference sheet.
months.gate: A NIST AI RMF profile for one real deployment. The three-framework crosswalk document. Both referenced in your Q2 exam prep.

quarters.subtitle: Domain coverage, practice loops, and the first cert in hand by end of quarter.

months.title: SecAI+ domain mapping and gap closure
months.why: Sitting an exam without mapping the objectives to your knowledge first is expensive guessing. You already have Q1 framework depth. This month is about finding the 20% of exam coverage that Q1 did not handle.
weeks: Pull the current CompTIA SecAI+ exam objectives. Map every domain and sub-objective to one of three buckets: strong (Q1 covered it), needs work (partially covered), unknown (not touched yet).
SecAI+ domains 1 and 2: AI concepts in security contexts and core security fundamentals with AI implications. Focus exclusively on the intersections — not the pure-security basics you already know.
SecAI+ domains 3 and 4: AI-specific risk management, governance, and attack surfaces. These are the most exam-weighted domains. Depth here, not breadth.
Practice exam #1. Score honestly. Write down the specific topic of every question you got wrong or guessed correctly. That list is your M5 study plan.
months.gate: A practice exam baseline score. A gap list with specific topics, not just domain names. A study plan for M5 built from actual wrong answers.

months.title: SecAI+ final prep and sit
months.why: The exam is this month. The single rule for exam week: no new material. Reviewing what you know beats cramming what you do not.
weeks: Close the gaps from M4. Targeted study on identified weak topics only. If a topic did not appear on the M4 practice exam, it is lower priority this week.
Practice exam #2. If your score is within 10% of the passing threshold, you are ready. If not, identify which single domain is dragging the score and fix it.
Review the three-framework crosswalk from M3. The frameworks appear throughout SecAI+ — your Q1 work is the study material here, not new content.
Sit CompTIA SecAI+. No new material this week. Schedule the exam for early in the week so you have buffer days if you need to reschedule.
months.gate: CompTIA SecAI+ cert in hand. First AI security credential. Update LinkedIn, capability brief, and Claude Partner Network profile immediately.

months.title: Prompt injection hardening — applied post-exam
months.why: The exam is closed. Now make the knowledge useful. Prompt injection is the most common LLM attack vector in real deployments — LLM01 from M1. Your AppSec background means you already understand injection classes. Translate that into LLM-specific hardening that you can publish.
weeks: Prompt injection taxonomy: direct injection, indirect injection (via retrieved content), payload injection via tool outputs, and context manipulation. Build a named test case for each type.
Defense patterns in practice: input validation layers, output sanitization, instruction hierarchy enforcement, and system prompt isolation. Apply each to one of your Claude deployments.
Jailbreak resistance: run a structured jailbreak attempt against your own system prompts using published jailbreak taxonomies. Document what breaks, what holds, and why.
Write and publish the hardening guide: "Prompt injection defense for Claude deployments." Practical, opinionated, with the real test cases you ran. Not a summary of OWASP — your own findings.
months.gate: A published prompt injection hardening guide with named test cases run against your own system. Referenced in your SecAI+ credential post.

quarters.subtitle: Multi-tenant isolation. Full adversarial engagement. CISO-ready posture documentation.

months.title: Multi-tenant isolation — your strongest lane
months.why: This is the failure mode that ends enterprise AI deployments. When one tenant's data leaks into another's context, it is a breach, not a bug. Your AppSec background and your Supabase/RLS experience make this your most credible technical specialization in AI security.
weeks: Multi-tenant threat model for AI systems: enumerate every failure mode — context bleed between sessions, shared cache exposure, tool output leakage, system prompt exposure across tenants. All of them, in writing.

Row-level security in Supabase applied to AI workloads: build a test that attempts to retrieve another tenant's data through a Claude agent. Verify that RLS holds under adversarial inputs — not just normal usage.

Context isolation patterns for agent sessions: how do you prevent conversation context from one tenant bleeding into another's session? Test the boundary explicitly. Document what the MCP server layer needs to enforce.
Permission scoping for multi-tenant MCP servers: which tools should be available to which tenants, at which privilege levels? Build the policy document and implement at least one enforcement check.
months.gate: A multi-tenant isolation design document and a test suite that verifies isolation holds under 20 adversarial inputs. Publishable — this becomes your most-cited security artifact.

months.title: Full red-team engagement — your own production system
months.why: Vulnerability assessments find known classes of bugs. Red-teaming finds the ones you did not know to look for because you were not thinking like an attacker. This month you apply adversarial thinking systematically. The target is your most sensitive Claude or Copilot deployment.
weeks: Red-team planning: scope definition, threat actor profile (script kiddie / insider threat / nation-state — pick the one most relevant to Intinc's actual risk), attack path enumeration, and rules of engagement in writing before touching anything.
Execute. Document every finding as you find it — not after. Include the attack path, the payload, the observed behavior, and whether it is exploitable in practice.
Score and prioritize findings using CVSS or a simplified severity matrix. What is critical, what is a medium, what is informational? Be honest — a finding you downplay will get exploited.

Write the red-team report to a publishable standard: executive summary for non-technical readers, technical findings section, remediation steps with owners and timelines. This is your flagship public security artifact.
months.gate: A published red-team report on your own production AI system. Every finding documented. Every remediation specified with a timeline. Your most concrete public proof of security depth.

months.title: Security posture documentation
months.why: A red-team report proves you can find problems. A posture document proves you can govern them. Enterprise procurement requires both. This month you build the artifact that pre-answers the "how do we know your AI deployments are safe?" question in any sales or partner conversation.
weeks: Security posture framework for AI systems: define the domains (data governance, access control, model behavior monitoring, incident response) and map each to controls you actually have in place — not aspirational ones.
CISO-ready posture document for one of your deployments: what a security team needs to see before approving an AI system for enterprise use. Written for Intinc's actual risk profile.
Incident response playbook for AI systems: what do you do when a deployed Claude agent exhibits unexpected behavior? Detection triggers, containment steps, rollback procedure, communication protocol.

Publish a general-purpose posture document template: a version other practitioners can adapt for their own deployments. This becomes a Partner Network artifact and a Community Ambassador workshop handout.
months.gate: A CISO-ready posture document for one real deployment and a published general-purpose template. Both linked from your bio and Partner Network profile.

quarters.subtitle: Second cert closed. The complete AI security playbook published. The AppSec brand anchor event.

months.title: CAISP domain coverage
months.why: CAISP goes deeper than SecAI+ on AI governance, ethics frameworks, and regulatory landscape. Your Q1 NIST AI RMF work is your strongest preparation. The genuine gaps are likely: AI ethics review processes, international regulatory landscape, and accountability structures.
weeks: Pull the current CAISP exam objectives. Map every domain to your knowledge. The honest gaps are likely non-technical: ethics frameworks, accountability structures, international regulations (EU AI Act, sector-specific rules).
CAISP-specific depth: AI governance models, accountability chain from developer to deployer to user, ethics review processes for AI systems. Not abstract — applied to your own deployments.

International regulatory landscape: EU AI Act risk tiers, CCPA implications for AI systems, HIPAA considerations for healthcare AI, and financial sector AI guidance. Enough to speak credibly to a compliance team, not enough to practice law.
Practice exam #1. Score honestly. Flag any domain where your score is more than 15 points below passing — those get M11 week 1.
months.gate: CAISP practice exam baseline. Gap list by specific topic. Study plan for M11 built from wrong answers, not from domain names.

months.title: CAISP final prep and sit
months.why: Same rule as SecAI+: no new material in the final week. The SecAI+ cert already proves technical AI security depth. CAISP adds governance and ethics breadth. Together they are a credential stack almost no AI practitioner carries.
weeks: Close M10 gaps. Targeted study on identified weak topics only. If the gap is regulatory, use the EU AI Act official text and NIST AI RMF — not third-party summaries.
Practice exam #2. Verify gaps from M10 are closing. If overall score is at or above passing, stop studying new material.
Review your Q1 NIST AI RMF crosswalk — CAISP exam questions map closely to the RMF's GOVERN and MAP functions. Your M3 work is the best exam prep you have.
Sit CAISP. Two AI security certs closed in one arc. Update every surface immediately: LinkedIn, Partner Network, capability brief, Claude Ambassador profile.
months.gate: CAISP cert in hand. SecAI+ + CAISP credential stack complete. The combination is rare — almost no one in the partner ecosystem carries both.

months.title: Publish the security playbook and close the arc
months.why: Twelve months of framework study, two certs, a red-team report, a hardening guide, a posture document, and a multi-tenant isolation design. You do not own this body of knowledge until it is synthesized, published, and someone else is using it.
weeks: Synthesize the complete "security-first AI deployment" playbook: OWASP LLM Top 10 → ATLAS → NIST RMF → prompt injection hardening → multi-tenant isolation → red-team methodology → posture documentation. One document, your voice.
Workshop: "Securing AI deployments for enterprise engineering teams" — at CLC, Intinc, or a security community event. The AppSec brand anchor event. Use the posture template as the hands-on artifact.

Update every positioning surface: LinkedIn headline to include SecAI+ and CAISP, Partner Network profile with the playbook and red-team report linked, capability brief updated with the security posture offering as a named SKU.

Retrospective: what changed in your threat model? Was the SecAI+ + CAISP path the right order? What does Y2 look like — offensive security depth, regulatory compliance specialization, or security tooling built on top of this arc?
months.gate: The playbook is published. The workshop is delivered. Three security teams are using your posture template. Your credential stack is updated on every surface.

rag.sub: 12 months. The knowledge layer underneath every agent you have ever shipped. Embeddings, chunking strategy, hybrid search, reranking, cross-modal retrieval, and production evaluation — all applied to your real stack, with the Bitwarden migration KB as the capstone target.

quarters.subtitle: Understand the vector space before touching a database. Ship on Supabase pgvector. Master chunking.

months.title: Embeddings — what they actually are
months.why: Most RAG tutorials tell you to call embed() and move on. If you do not understand what embeddings encode, why cosine similarity works, or what dimensionality means in practice — you will not know why your retrieval is failing or how to fix it.
weeks: Vector space and semantic similarity from first principles: what does it mean for two text chunks to be "close"? Build the intuition with toy examples and cosine similarity by hand before touching any API.

Embedding model comparison on your own corpus: text-embedding-3-small, text-embedding-3-large, Gemini text-embedding-004, Voyage AI (Anthropic's recommended embedder). Same 200 chunks, same 20 queries. Measure quality, cost, and latency for each.

Embed a real document set you use: the Bitwarden migration KB, The Prompt newsletter archive, or Intinc SOP documents. Store the embeddings in flat files first — no vector DB yet. Understand the raw representation.

Semantic search without a database: cosine similarity in Python or JS, top-5 retrieval for 10 real queries from your corpus. Score the results honestly. This baseline becomes your benchmark for every improvement made in Q2 and Q3.
months.gate: A working embedding pipeline on a real document corpus. Semantic search returning results without a vector DB. Embedding model chosen with a documented rationale you could defend to a client.

months.title: Supabase pgvector — your natural first vector DB
months.why: You already run Supabase. pgvector turns it into a vector database without adding a new system to your stack. Start here — not with Pinecone, not with a new hosted service. Build on infrastructure you already understand, own, and pay for.
weeks: pgvector setup in your existing Supabase instance: enable the extension, create your first vector column, run your first similarity query with the results you embedded in M1.
Schema design for RAG: how do you store embeddings alongside source metadata (document ID, chunk index, source URL, created_at, content hash) so retrieval is fast and filterable? Write the migration.
Index selection: ivfflat vs. hnsw on your data size and query pattern. Run both. Measure query latency at 10K, 50K, and 100K rows. Document the crossover point.

First RAG-backed Claude agent: knowledge base in Supabase pgvector, retrieval in a Supabase function or Edge Function, generation in Claude. End to end, working, on the Bitwarden migration KB or equivalent real document set.
months.gate: A working RAG pipeline backed by Supabase pgvector. A Claude agent using it in production or staging. Retrieval latency at p95 measured and documented.

months.title: Chunking — the factor that moves quality most
months.why: Chunking strategy determines retrieval quality more than any other single decision. Fixed-size is the default and it is often wrong. The right strategy depends on document structure, query patterns, and how your model uses retrieved context. Most RAG tutorials skip this almost entirely.
weeks: Fixed-size chunking baselines: 256, 512, and 1024 tokens with 10–20% overlap. Measure retrieval quality at each size on your corpus using the M1 query set. The number that surprises you is the one to investigate.

Semantic chunking: split on meaning boundaries using an LLM or sentence transformer, not on token counts. More expensive, often better for narrative documents. Measure whether it beats your best fixed-size on your actual queries.

Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking: embed small chunks (128–256 tokens) for retrieval precision, return larger parent chunks (512–1024 tokens) for generation context. The pattern that reduces fragmentation without losing recall.

Chunking decision matrix: build the rule set you apply when a new document type arrives. Columns: document type (narrative / structured / code / table), query type (factual / exploratory / comparative), and the recommended strategy. This becomes your reusable reference artifact.
months.gate: Three chunking strategies benchmarked on the same corpus with the same 20 queries, scored by a consistent metric. A documented decision matrix for when to use each strategy.

quarters.subtitle: Hybrid search. Reranking. Advanced patterns for the queries basic RAG fails on.

months.title: Hybrid search and metadata filtering
