months.why: Similarity search alone fails on queries with specific entities, dates, product names, or structured facts. Hybrid search (dense + sparse) and metadata filtering close most of the gap between a demo RAG system and a production one.
weeks: Sparse retrieval: BM25 and keyword search as a complement to dense embeddings. Build a BM25 baseline on your corpus. Measure whether it beats semantic search on entity-heavy queries — it usually does.

Hybrid search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: merge dense and sparse result lists using RRF. Implement it from scratch before reaching for a library. Measure whether it beats either baseline alone on your query set.

Metadata filtering: pre-filter before vector search by date range, document type, source, status, or any structured field. Build a retrieval function that accepts a filter object and applies it efficiently against your Supabase schema.

Query analysis: build a classifier that routes queries to different retrieval strategies based on query type. Entity-heavy queries → hybrid with sparse boost. Abstract queries → dense only. Date-bounded queries → metadata filter first.
months.gate: A hybrid search pipeline (dense + BM25 + RRF) with metadata filtering. Benchmarked against pure similarity search on your real query set. Quality delta documented.

months.title: Reranking — the improvement most people skip
months.why: Embedding similarity is a proxy for relevance, not relevance itself. A cross-encoder reranker scores query-chunk pairs directly and consistently improves end-to-end answer quality. It is slower and more expensive — but the quality delta justifies the cost in almost every production deployment.
weeks: Bi-encoder vs. cross-encoder architecture: why embedders (bi-encoders) are fast but approximate, and why rerankers (cross-encoders) are slower but more accurate. The quality/latency tradeoff in plain terms.
Cohere Rerank and Voyage Rerank: API setup, latency at different top-k values (retrieve top-20, rerank to top-5 vs. top-3), cost per query. Run both on your query set.
Two-stage pipeline: retrieval (fast, high recall, top-20) → reranking (slow, high precision, top-5) → generation. Build it. Measure end-to-end latency. Verify it fits your latency budget from M2.

LLM-as-judge evaluation: score 50 answers with and without reranking using Claude as judge. Document the quality delta. If reranking does not improve scores on your corpus, investigate why — the answer is usually in the chunking.
months.gate: A two-stage retrieval pipeline with reranking. Quality improvement measured over pure similarity search on at least 50 real queries, scored by LLM-as-judge.

months.title: Advanced retrieval — HyDE, multi-query, compression
months.why: These are not exotic techniques — they are the patterns you reach for when basic RAG returns the wrong chunks on well-formed queries. Knowing when each helps and when each hurts is the practitioner skill that separates you from someone who just followed a tutorial.
weeks: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings): generate a hypothetical perfect-answer document, embed it, retrieve by that embedding instead of the raw query. Test on abstract and exploratory queries. Measure whether it helps on your corpus.

Multi-query retrieval: generate 3–5 reformulations of the user query using Claude, retrieve for each, deduplicate with RRF. More expensive, more robust on ambiguous queries. Measure cost overhead vs. quality gain.

Contextual compression: after retrieval, use Claude to extract only the query-relevant sentences from each chunk before passing to generation. Reduces context window noise. Measure whether it improves faithfulness scores.

Configurable retrieval module: one function, strategy selectable by config flag (base / hybrid / HyDE / multi-query / compressed). Every pipeline from this month forward uses this module. Standardize the interface.
months.gate: A configurable retrieval module with at least four selectable strategies. Strategy selection documented with the query types each strategy is best suited for.

quarters.subtitle: Evaluation harness. Latency and cost budgets. Cross-modal and multi-vector retrieval.

months.title: Evaluation — RAG quality measured end to end
months.why: Without evaluation, every pipeline change is a guess. RAG eval has two distinct measurement problems: retrieval quality (did you find the right chunks?) and generation quality (did the model use them faithfully?). Both require separate metrics and different golden datasets.
weeks: Retrieval metrics from scratch: precision@k, recall@k, Mean Reciprocal Rank, NDCG. Build a golden dataset of (query, expected chunk IDs) from 50 real queries against your corpus. Score your current best pipeline.

Generation metrics: faithfulness (is the answer grounded in the retrieved context?), answer relevance (does it address the query?), context utilization (did it actually use the chunks?). LLM-as-judge rubric for each.
RAGAs or ARES: pick one evaluation framework, implement it on your production pipeline, and run a full sweep across your golden dataset. Document the baseline scores.

CI regression suite: a test set that runs automatically on every pipeline change — chunking config, retrieval strategy, model swap — and flags quality regressions before they reach production. The RAG equivalent of a test suite.
months.gate: An end-to-end RAG evaluation pipeline with a golden dataset, automated regression tests, and baseline scores documented for every pipeline variant built so far.

months.title: Production patterns — latency, cost, freshness
months.why: A RAG system that works in a notebook is not a RAG system. Production means SLA-defensible latency, cost telemetry per query, document freshness tracking, and graceful degradation that does not hallucinate when retrieval fails.
weeks: Latency profiling per stage: embed query → retrieve (DB query) → rerank → generate. Where is the time going? What is the p50 and p95 for each stage? Which stage has the most variance?

Cost modeling per query: embedding tokens + vector DB queries + reranker API calls + generation tokens. Build a spreadsheet defensible to Daniel for any deployment decision. Cost at 100, 1K, 10K queries per day.
Document freshness: how do you detect when a source document changes and a stored chunk is stale? Change detection triggers, re-embedding queues, and content hash comparison in Supabase.

Graceful degradation: what does your agent return when retrieval confidence is low? Explicit "I did not find enough context" responses beat hallucinated confident answers. Build the fallback. Test it deliberately.
months.gate: A production-readiness checklist for your RAG pipeline: latency p95 measured, cost per query modeled, freshness monitoring live, degradation path tested and documented.

months.title: Cross-modal and multi-vector retrieval
months.why: Most RAG systems embed plain text. Your real document corpus — Intinc SOPs, migration KB, newsletter archives — includes tables, structured data, and sometimes images. Single-vector text search handles these badly. Cross-modal retrieval is where the next quality gains are.
weeks: Table retrieval: how do you embed and retrieve structured records, spreadsheet rows, or database tables? Text serialization strategies (row-as-sentence, column headers as context) vs. structured query hybrid approaches.

Multi-vector retrieval (ColBERT / late interaction models): embed queries and documents into multiple token-level vectors instead of one chunk-level vector. When it outperforms single-vector and at what latency and cost.
Image retrieval (CLIP-style): multimodal embeddings for document screenshots, diagrams, and images. Experimental in most stacks but directionally important. Build a minimal prototype.

Pick the one cross-modal type most relevant to your actual corpus — likely tables or structured records from Supabase — and build a production retrieval path for it. Benchmark against text-only retrieval.
months.gate: A working retrieval pipeline for at least one non-text document type from your real corpus. Benchmarked against text-only on the same queries.

quarters.subtitle: Production system shipped. Provider comparison published. The RAG playbook in the world.

months.title: Capstone — upgrade the Bitwarden migration agent
months.why: Everything before this was practice. The capstone is a real system with real users and real consequences if retrieval fails. The Bitwarden migration agent is the natural target — it has a knowledge base, real queries from staff, and a measurable success condition: does the agent return the right migration step?
weeks: Audit the current migration agent retrieval layer. What is the existing chunking strategy, retrieval method, and (if any) evaluation baseline? Document the pre-capstone state honestly.

Rebuild the retrieval layer: hybrid search on the migration KB, parent-child chunking for the longer procedural documents, reranking before generation. Apply every pattern from Q1–Q3 that is appropriate.
Instrument and deploy: p95 latency, cost per query, retrieval quality score from the evaluation harness. Measure the pre/post delta explicitly.
Architecture Decision Record: why these chunking, retrieval, and reranking choices for this specific corpus and query distribution? What would v3 look like? Published alongside the deployment.
months.gate: The upgraded migration agent in production with measured retrieval quality improvement over the pre-capstone baseline. ADR published. Real users using it.

months.title: Vector DB comparison — the honest benchmark
months.why: You have built your RAG skills on Supabase pgvector. You now need to know when to recommend a different vector DB and how to defend that recommendation to a client who is already paying for something else.
weeks: Pinecone: setup, indexing, query patterns, managed namespace model, cost at three scale tiers. Run your M1 benchmark corpus through it. Compare to pgvector on latency, quality, and cost.
Qdrant: self-hosted or cloud, payload filtering, named vectors, on-disk indexes for large corpora. Run the same benchmark. What does it do better than pgvector and at what operational cost?
Weaviate and brief coverage of Chroma, LanceDB, and Milvus: not deep dives — enough to place each on the decision matrix.

Publish the comparison: "Which vector database for which problem?" — a practitioner guide built from your own benchmarks, not from vendor documentation. The decision matrix, the benchmark data, your honest recommendation.
months.gate: A published vector database comparison built from your own benchmark data. A decision matrix you would use in a real client engagement.

months.title: Teach the knowledge layer and close the arc
months.why: Twelve months of applied knowledge: embeddings, chunking, hybrid search, reranking, HyDE, multi-query, evaluation, production patterns, cross-modal retrieval, and a live capstone. You do not own this until you have transferred it to someone who did not already know it.
weeks: Workshop at CLC, Intinc, or a Community Ambassador event: "Knowledge layers for AI engineers." Hands-on: the chunking decision matrix, a live retrieval quality comparison, and the cost-per-query spreadsheet from M8.

Publish the complete RAG practitioner guide: embeddings → chunking → hybrid search → reranking → evaluation → production → cross-modal. Every pattern you actually shipped. Real numbers, real tradeoffs.
Update Partner Network profile, LinkedIn, and the AIaaS capability brief: link the capstone ADR, the vector DB comparison, and the playbook. "RAG-backed deployments" as a named service SKU.

Retrospective: what surprised you most about where RAG fails in practice? Was it chunking, reranking, or evaluation that moved quality most on your actual corpus? What is Y2 — GraphRAG, agentic RAG, or pivot to the broader data engineering layer?
months.gate: Workshop delivered. Playbook published. Three practitioners are using your chunking decision matrix. The migration agent retrieval quality is measurably better than it was in M1.

n8n.sub: 12 months. From functional to production-grade. Error handling, AI agent loops, parallel orchestration, self-hosted ops, Make and Zapier comparative knowledge, custom node authorship, and the Drive Automation Chain as the flagship reference. One cert. One template library. Everything teachable.

quarters.subtitle: Make your existing workflows production-grade. AI as orchestration layer. Parallel and sub-workflow patterns.

months.title: Production-grade error handling and reliability
months.why: Your existing n8n workflows are functional but fragile. Production means retry logic, error notifications, idempotency, and circuit breakers — the things that keep a workflow running at 3am without your intervention. Audit what you have before building anything new.
weeks: Production audit: run your top 5 existing workflows through a 10-point checklist (error workflow attached, retry logic configured, execution logging on, notification on failure, idempotency guaranteed, sensitive data not logged, timeout set, dead-letter path defined, documentation exists, tested against failure). Score each honestly.

Error workflow pattern: build a reusable error-handling sub-workflow that logs to Supabase, sends a Teams or Slack notification with context, and retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff. Attach it to every workflow you audited.

Idempotency: pick your most-used scheduled workflow and make it safe to run twice. What identifier does it need to store to know it has already processed a record? Implement a deduplication layer in Supabase.
Dead-letter queue: build a Supabase table that captures every failed execution payload with enough context to replay it manually or automatically. Wire it to the error workflow from week 2.
months.gate: All 5 audited workflows pass the 10-point production checklist. Error workflow, idempotency, and dead-letter queue live on at least one critical workflow.

months.title: AI-native workflows — Claude as orchestration layer
months.why: You have connected Claude to n8n as a text-generation node. That is not the same as using Claude as the reasoning and routing layer. This month is the shift from "Claude generates output" to "Claude decides what happens next."
weeks: Claude as a routing node: incoming webhook payload → Claude classifies intent → IF node routes to the correct branch based on classification. Zero hard-coded routing logic. Build one from a real Intinc or FlashFusion use case.

Structured output from Claude into downstream nodes: JSON mode output from Claude populates an Airtable record, a Supabase row, or a Notion page. The schema is defined in the system prompt. Test robustness against 20 varied inputs.

Context chaining across sequential Claude nodes: how do you pass conversation history or accumulated context between Claude calls without hitting the context window ceiling? Build a sliding-window context management pattern.

The AI agent loop in n8n: trigger → Claude reasons about what tool to call → n8n executes the tool → result feeds back to Claude → repeat until Claude signals completion. Build this pattern for a real Intinc problem — ticket triage, email routing, or document classification.
months.gate: An AI agent loop workflow at Intinc or FlashFusion where Claude routes, reasons, and decides — not just generates text. At least one human-in-the-loop escalation path built in.

months.title: Parallel execution, sub-workflows, and orchestration
months.why: Most n8n workflows are linear. The patterns that make automation genuinely powerful — parallel fan-out, sub-workflow composition, dynamic routing — are underused because they require a mental model shift. This month is the shift.
weeks: Parallel execution with SplitInBatches and merge: fan out across a list of items (5, 50, 500), process in parallel, collect results, continue. Build one that processes a real batch (newsletter recipients, client list, document set).
Sub-workflow extraction: identify 3 patterns you have duplicated across multiple workflows. Extract each as a reusable sub-workflow with a clean input/output contract. Call them from a parent.

Dynamic routing: workflow branches determined at runtime by data values, not by hard-coded IF nodes. Use a Switch node with expressions or a Code node with a routing table. Build one that can route to N branches without touching the workflow to add a new route.

Master orchestrator pattern: one workflow that receives a payload, determines the correct sub-workflow to call, calls it, and handles the result. The architecture your production workflows should move toward.
months.gate: A master orchestrator workflow calling at least 3 sub-workflows dynamically. Parallel execution demonstrated on a real batch. Sub-workflows documented with input/output contracts.

quarters.subtitle: Self-hosted n8n operations. Make comparative knowledge. Zapier and the three-platform decision framework.

months.title: n8n self-hosted operations
months.why: Intinc clients running n8n on their own infrastructure need someone who can deploy, secure, back up, and monitor it. n8n Cloud is easy. Self-hosted is where the real ops knowledge — and the billable differentiation — lives.
weeks: Docker deployment from scratch: n8n in Docker Compose with PostgreSQL backend (not SQLite), environment variables, volume mounts, log rotation. Deploy a fresh instance without following a tutorial.
Reverse proxy and TLS: n8n behind nginx or Caddy with Let's Encrypt. Basic auth on the UI. Firewall rules that expose only what needs to be exposed. Document every port and why it is open.
Backup and recovery: PostgreSQL backup script on a cron, workflow export/import automation, execution history retention policy. Run a full restore from backup before calling this week done.
Monitoring: failed execution alerting to Teams or Slack, disk space and container health checks, a simple execution success-rate dashboard. You should know a workflow failed before anyone else does.
months.gate: A self-hosted n8n instance deployed from scratch — Dockerized, TLS-terminated, backed up, monitored. A runbook someone else could use to redeploy it.

months.title: Make (Integromat) — learn it well enough to recommend it honestly
months.why: Your default recommendation is n8n. That is usually correct. But Make has a different cost model, a larger built-in app library, and a visual paradigm that some non-technical users navigate better. Knowing when to recommend Make over n8n is a service differentiator — it signals you are solving for the client, not for your stack preference.
weeks: Make fundamentals in depth: scenarios, modules, operations, routers, iterators, aggregators, error handlers. Rebuild 3 workflows you have already shipped in n8n. Feel where Make is easier and where it frustrates you.
Make-specific features: Data Stores (key-value persistence), custom HTTP modules, built-in app count vs. n8n. The things Make does that n8n does not have a direct equivalent for, and vice versa.

Make pricing model: operations vs. n8n executions vs. Zapier tasks. Cost at 10K, 100K, and 1M operations per month. Build the comparison spreadsheet you would show a client who asks "which one should we use?"

Make vs. n8n decision matrix: team technical level, monthly operation volume, required integrations, self-hosting preference, budget ceiling. Write the rules in plain language — not a matrix that requires interpretation.
months.gate: Three real workflows built in both n8n and Make. A documented recommendation framework for when to use each, written to be shown to a non-technical client.

months.title: Zapier and the three-platform decision framework
months.why: Zapier is the market leader. Most of your clients have heard of it. Some are already using it and paying too much for it. Understanding Zapier's strengths and limits — and being able to articulate them without just saying "n8n is better" — is what makes you a platform-agnostic automation consultant.
weeks: Zapier fundamentals with hands-on depth: Zaps, multi-step actions, Paths (conditional branching), Filters, Delays, Formatter. Rebuild 3 workflows from your n8n portfolio in Zapier. Note every place where Zapier forced a different architectural choice.
Zapier Tables and Interfaces: the newer product surface beyond basic automations. When this matters for non-technical teams who need lightweight apps without a developer.

Zapier cost at scale: tasks vs. operations vs. executions. The price crossover points where n8n self-hosted wins on cost, where Make wins on value, where Zapier wins on accessibility. A spreadsheet with the actual numbers.

Three-platform decision framework — write the final version: Zapier (non-technical, speed over control, limited budget for developer time), Make (mid-technical, visual, good operations value), n8n (technical team, self-hosted option needed, full control required). One page. Use it in every future client discovery.
months.gate: A three-platform comparison built from your own hands-on work with all three. A one-page decision framework you would hand to a client in a discovery call.

quarters.subtitle: Custom node authorship. Webhook-native architecture. n8n as AI agent backbone.

months.title: Custom node development
months.why: You have hit the ceiling of built-in nodes. Every time you reach for the HTTP Request node to call a service that should have a proper node, you are leaving usability — and marketability — on the table. Custom nodes are how your n8n work becomes impossible to replicate without you.
weeks: Custom node architecture: declarative vs. programmatic node types, credentials types, the n8n node development kit (n8n-node-dev). Set up the dev environment. Read one published community node's source code before writing a line of your own.

Build your first custom node: a service from your actual stack that has no built-in n8n integration. Start with one action and one trigger. The test is: does it work identically to how a built-in node would?
Custom credentials type: build a proper credentials implementation for your custom node. Handle OAuth2, API key, and bearer token patterns — not a hardcoded string in the node.
Publish to the n8n community registry: the submission process, documentation requirements (README, parameter descriptions, error messages), and what makes a community node get used vs. ignored.
months.gate: One custom n8n node submitted to the community registry. Full documentation. At least one install from someone other than you.

months.title: Webhook architecture and event-driven design
months.why: Most n8n workflows are scheduled. Scheduled workflows are always late. Event-driven workflows respond when something happens — they are faster, more resource-efficient, and more production-grade. The mental model shift from polling to pushing changes what you build and what you sell.
weeks: Webhook security fundamentals: signature verification (HMAC-SHA256), secret token validation, replay attack prevention. Every webhook endpoint you expose should verify the sender. Build and test the pattern.

Webhook relay with Cloudflare Workers: a lightweight worker that verifies, pre-processes, and routes incoming webhook payloads to the correct n8n workflow before they reach n8n. Decouples your n8n instance from the public internet.

Convert three scheduled workflows to event-driven: identify what event should trigger each one instead of a cron. Implement the webhook source. Measure the improvement in response time and elimination of unnecessary runs.

Webhook-native workflow system: inbound events from Copilot Studio, Teams, or a client-facing Cloudflare Worker route to the correct n8n sub-workflow based on payload type. The event bus pattern for your stack.
months.gate: Three workflows converted from scheduled to event-driven with verified webhook security. A Cloudflare Worker relay handling at least two source systems.

months.title: AI agent orchestration — n8n as the backbone
months.why: This is the month where everything in the arc converges: parallel execution from M3, sub-workflows from M3, Claude routing from M2, Supabase state from M1, and webhook triggers from M8 — all combined into a multi-agent system. The Drive Automation Chain is the natural reference implementation.
weeks: Agent loop pattern in n8n: trigger → Claude reasons and plans → n8n executes the tool → result returns to Claude → Claude decides next action or signals completion → exit. Build the canonical pattern from scratch, no LangChain or CrewAI wrapper.

Memory management in n8n agents: short-term (execution context in a Set node), long-term (Supabase rows with agent_id and session_id), and episodic (n8n execution logs as a queryable history). Which type for which agent task.

Multi-agent coordination: two n8n workflows acting as two agents, sharing state via a Supabase coordination table, with a mechanism for one to signal the other. Rebuild the Drive Automation Council pattern with proper error handling and observability.

Tool-calling without MCP: Claude receives a structured tool manifest via system prompt, decides which tool to call via structured output, n8n executes the corresponding sub-workflow, result flows back. The pattern for clients who cannot run MCP servers.
months.gate: A multi-agent n8n system with at least two agents coordinating via shared state. One agent calling tools defined in Claude's system prompt. Drive Automation Chain or equivalent is the reference.

quarters.subtitle: Flagship workflow system shipped. n8n cert closed. Template library published. Teach the full arc.

months.title: Capstone — flagship workflow system for Intinc or FlashFusion
months.why: Twelve months of workflow expertise should produce one system that demonstrates the full range: event-driven triggers, AI reasoning, parallel execution, sub-workflow composition, error handling, and monitoring. The newsletter automation pipeline and the AIaaS service delivery flow are both candidates.
weeks: Spec the system: which process at Intinc or FlashFusion has the highest automation surface? The Prompt newsletter pipeline (research → draft → format → distribute), the AIaaS client onboarding flow, or the FlashFusion order-to-delivery process.
Build it. Every shortcut you would not be comfortable demonstrating to Dave and Jackie gets fixed. No scheduled workflows where event-driven is possible. No linear flows where parallel is correct.
Instrument it: execution success rate, average duration per stage, error frequency by node, cost per run. These numbers go into the AIaaS service line pitch.
Architecture Decision Record: why these workflow patterns for this specific use case? What would v2 add? Published alongside the system — this is the proof artifact.
months.gate: A flagship workflow system in production with monitoring, an ADR, and an executive summary ready for Intinc leadership. The numbers tell a clear story without narration.

months.title: n8n certification and template library
months.why: The n8n certification exists and almost no one in the consulting ecosystem has it. The template library is the asset that generates ongoing leads — every download is a potential client who has already seen your work and trusted it enough to use it.
weeks: n8n certification exam prep: pull the current exam objectives, identify the genuine gaps, study those specifically. Do not restudy what you already know.
Sit the n8n certification. Update LinkedIn, Partner Network profile, and capability brief immediately.

Build the template library: 5 production-grade workflow templates covering distinct use cases from your arc (AI routing agent, webhook relay + Cloudflare Worker, parallel document processor, error-handling sub-workflow, multi-agent coordinator). Each with a README that explains the use case and setup.
Publish: n8n template marketplace and your own GitHub repository. Set up a simple landing page or Notion page that presents all 5 templates with the context a new user needs to evaluate them.
months.gate: n8n cert in hand. 5 templates published in the n8n marketplace and on GitHub. At least 3 downloads on the most-used template from someone other than you.

months.title: Teach, publish, and close the arc
months.why: You do not own the knowledge until you can transfer it without the safety net of your own implementation history. The workshop closes the Community Ambassador loop. The automation playbook closes the Partner Network loop. The retrospective tells you what the next arc actually is.
weeks: Workshop at CLC, Intinc, or a Community Ambassador event: "AI-native workflow automation for engineering teams." Live demo of the AI agent loop from M9. Hands-on exercise with the error-handling pattern from M1. The template library as the take-home.

Publish the complete automation playbook: n8n production patterns, three-platform decision framework, AI agent orchestration, custom node development, webhook architecture. Every pattern you actually shipped, with the numbers.

Update every positioning surface: Partner Network profile with the template library and capstone ADR linked, LinkedIn with the n8n cert and the workshop, AIaaS capability brief with "workflow automation" as a named service SKU.

Retrospective: what became automatable that surprised you? What resisted automation more than you expected? What is Y2 — heavier orchestration (Temporal, Prefect, Airflow for complex pipelines), deeper AI agent patterns, or broadening to ETL and data engineering?
months.gate: Workshop delivered. Playbook published. Three clients or colleagues are using your templates or your three-platform framework in a real project.

brand.sub: 12 months. Content that flows from real builds, not from the desire for followers. LinkedIn cadence, The Prompt at scale, CLC formalized, Ambassador activated, a speaking pipeline, and a published Year 1 retrospective that tells the market what you built — and what you are building next.

quarters.subtitle: Design the system before publishing anything. LinkedIn cadence live. The Prompt scaled.

months.title: Brand architecture — design before publishing
months.why: You have three active presence threads right now: Intinc employee, FlashFusion consultant, Community Ambassador applicant. Without a deliberate architecture, you publish whichever project is loudest that week. A stranger reading your last 20 posts should be able to answer: what does he do, who does he help, and why should I listen to him? Right now, that answer is probably unclear.
weeks: Read your last 20 LinkedIn posts as a stranger. Write down: what does this person do? Who do they help? What is their single clearest claim? If the answers are vague or inconsistent, that is the work.

Positioning statement v1: "Kyle Rosebrook is [specific role] who helps [specific audience] do [specific outcome] using [specific approach and differentiator]." One sentence. No buzzwords. No "passionate about AI." Test it against three people who know your work — do they recognize themselves in the audience?

Three content pillars from your playbook — Security-first Claude deployments, Claude in real production stacks, Teaching Claude to technical teams — mapped to your last 12 builds. Which pillar has the most evidence? Which has the least? The answer determines which one needs more published proof before it can carry weight.

Channel map with one purpose per channel: LinkedIn (public thought leadership and proof), The Prompt (internal Intinc, segmented depth), Community events (live, local, relationship-building). One job per channel. No content that belongs in two places without a reason.
months.gate: A one-page personal brand document: positioning statement, three content pillars with mapped evidence, channel map. Read it before publishing anything for the next 11 months.

months.title: LinkedIn — consistent cadence over volume
months.why: Burst publishing — nothing for three weeks, then four posts in two days — signals an audience that you cannot be counted on. Consistency compounds. A stranger landing on your profile in month 11 should see a coherent practitioner who publishes regularly, not someone who posts when inspired.
weeks: Content audit: of your last 20 posts, which 3 got the most meaningful response (DMs, saves, reposts, or comments that led somewhere)? Write down what those three had in common. That is your starting format, not the format you think should work.

Eight-week content calendar: one post per week minimum, each mapped to a content pillar. Variety across formats: a "here is what I built" story, a technical insight from a real project, a counterintuitive observation, a teach-something post. No "here are 5 AI tools you should use" content — that belongs to a different practitioner.

First four posts published on schedule. Not drafts — live. Track reach, comments, and saves at 48 hours. Which format performed above your average? That is the one to repeat before experimenting with others.

Engagement protocol: identify 25 practitioners and security-AI voices worth being in genuine conversation with. Read their posts. When you have something real to add — a specific disagreement, a complementary example, a question that opens the thread — comment. Three per day, substantive. Follower trajectory tracked weekly.
months.gate: Eight posts published over eight weeks without a gap. A documented format that outperforms your average reach. Weekly follower trajectory tracked.

months.title: The Prompt — from internal newsletter to compounding asset
months.why: The Prompt is your most direct audience — people who opted in to receive your thinking on a schedule. Most newsletters stay small because they never have a growth mechanism and never raise their quality bar explicitly. This month does both.
weeks: Newsletter analytics audit: current subscriber count, open rate, click rate, which editions got replies or were forwarded. The data tells you what people actually read, not what you think they should read. Write down the three most surprising findings.

Content quality bar: write the rubric for a 9/10 edition vs. a 7/10. Specific criteria — not "better writing" but "at least one finding from my own builds," "one claim I can back with a number," "one thing the reader cannot get from a general AI newsletter." Apply it before sending the next three editions.

Growth mechanism: one specific path to grow the list from current subscribers to 200+ active readers. A LinkedIn post that links to a standout edition, a workshop sign-up that auto-subscribes, an internal Intinc all-hands mention. One mechanism, consistently executed for 90 days.

Tier rationalization: The Prompt has three audience tiers. Which tier gets the most engagement? Which generates the most replies? If one tier is consistently underperforming, cut it or merge it — a three-tier newsletter you actually ship beats a one-tier newsletter you procrastinate on.
months.gate: The Prompt at 200+ active subscribers or a documented, executing growth path toward it. Open rate above 40%. At least one edition cited or forwarded by someone outside Intinc.

quarters.subtitle: CLC formalized. Ambassador application submitted and activated. Cross-channel content system live.

months.title: CLC relationship formalization
months.why: You have genuine institutional goodwill at CLC — two counselors and the math professor who was central to completing your degree. Most people leave that kind of relationship as "someone I know." You are building a Community Ambassador anchor event and CLC is the natural venue. That requires a formal conversation, not an assumption.
weeks: Warm outreach to the math professor — a real conversation, not a cold email. Context: you are applying to the Community Ambassador program, you want CLC to be the anchor venue for Lake County, and you are asking for their support as an institutional co-sign. What is in it for CLC students and faculty?

Institutional path: who at CLC approves external speakers and community events? The professor is the champion, but someone else is the decision-maker. Map the approval path before you need it urgently.

Event concept brief for CLC: one page. Audience (students and staff), format (90-minute lunch and learn or 3-hour workshop), topic (Claude fluency or security-first AI), what CLC receives (free AI literacy education, faculty upskilling, student career value), what you receive (venue, co-branded event, Ambassador proof point).
Get a confirmed date or a clear next step with a named contact. "We think this is a great idea, let's plan something for Q3" with a specific person's name is a gate-worthy outcome. Silence is not.
months.gate: A confirmed CLC event date or a written next step with a named contact and a timeline. The event is on a calendar, even if it is four months away.

months.title: Community Ambassador — apply with evidence, not intention
months.why: The application is open. Applying without a specific event concept and a documented track record is weaker than applying with both. You have the event concept from M4. You have The Prompt, your builds, and the positioning statement from M1. This month you put it together and submit.
weeks: Write the application. Specific city (Lake County / Zion, IL — distinct from Chicago meetup saturation). Specific event concept (the CLC workshop from M4 with a named venue contact). Specific track record (The Prompt at current subscriber count, workshop delivery history, production Claude builds). No generic AI enthusiasm. The framework from your playbook applies here.
Submit. Document the submission date, the confirmation email, and the expected response timeline. Set a calendar reminder for follow-up.

Build the Ambassador infrastructure regardless of outcome: event checklist, participant workbook template, demo script for the CLC workshop, post-event impact report template. The application decision should not gate any of this work — it is useful whether or not you get the program.

If rejected: identify the specific gap in the feedback (or in the self-assessment if there is no feedback) and address it directly. If accepted: activate all available mechanisms — event sponsorship request, API credits application, Slack community introduction. Neither outcome leaves you passive.
months.gate: Application submitted with a specific event concept and documented track record. Ambassador infrastructure built. A clear response plan for acceptance and for rejection.

months.title: Cross-channel content system
months.why: You are publishing in at least four channels. Without a system, you recreate content for each from scratch and burn time doing it. With one, a single workshop becomes a LinkedIn post, a Prompt edition, a speaker abstract, and an Ambassador impact report. The goal is one creation, multiple publications.
weeks: Content multiplication map: take your last three pieces of content and trace what they could have become in each channel. Workshop → LinkedIn story post → Prompt section → short clip (if applicable) → talk abstract. Most content can be extended this way with 20 minutes of work, not 2 hours.

Repurposing workflow with Claude: a system prompt that takes a LinkedIn post draft and generates a Prompt section, a talk abstract, and a tweet-thread outline. Test it on five real posts. Adjust the prompt until the outputs need only light editing.

Unified content calendar: one view that shows all active channels and every planned publication. The goal is immediate visibility of any gap longer than two weeks where you are silent everywhere simultaneously.

Content batching cadence: one 90-minute content session per week where you produce the majority of that week's content before Monday. Track output per session for four consecutive weeks. The batch that consistently underproduces is the one to investigate.
months.gate: A cross-channel content system with a documented repurposing workflow. Three pieces of content that have successfully been multiplied across at least two channels without starting from scratch.

quarters.subtitle: Flagship long-form published. Speaking pipeline built. Nine-month data review drives Q4 adjustments.

months.title: Publish one definitive long-form piece
months.why: A consistent posting cadence builds familiarity. A definitive long-form piece builds authority. They are different things. The content that gets saved, cited, and referenced months later is almost always specific, opinionated, and based on something only you could have written. This month you write and publish it.
weeks: Choose the flagship topic from your three content pillars: which one do you have the most specific, hard-earned, and genuinely rare knowledge about? The criterion is: could someone else have written this without your specific build history? If yes, it is not the right topic.

Draft: minimum 1,200 words. LinkedIn long-form article or a Substack post with a LinkedIn cross-post. Structure: a specific claim → evidence from your own builds with real numbers → the counterargument you actually believe → the practical takeaway a technical reader can act on by Friday.

Edit to a brutal standard: delete every sentence that could have been written by anyone. Delete every sentence that summarizes something the reader could find on Google. What remains is the piece. If less than 800 words remain, the topic was not specific enough.

Publish, distribute, and measure: LinkedIn article + Prompt edition + Ambassador share if the program is active. Track saves (a save is worth ten likes), inbound DMs, and whether it appears in any searches or external links within 30 days.
months.gate: One definitive long-form piece published. At least 3 inbound messages from people you did not already know who discovered it through search or sharing rather than your direct network.

months.title: Speaking and workshop pipeline
months.why: Written content scales. Live events build trust at a qualitatively different level. The CLC event confirmed in M4 is one slot. A pipeline means having 3–5 events on a rolling 6-month calendar so you are never starting from zero. You already have the workshop material — the gap is the pipeline infrastructure.
weeks: Event inventory: what is realistic in the next 6 months? CLC confirmed, one Intinc internal session, one Chicago-area security or AI meetup (search for active groups — there are several, none are saturating the Claude community space), one conference CFP that closes before Q4.

Abstract library: three talk abstracts ready to submit anywhere at any time. One per content pillar. Each: target audience, stated single outcome the attendee will leave with, and the one thing that makes this talk different from a generic AI talk.
Submit two external CFPs or formally propose two external events. Internal only is a ceiling — getting on a stage outside your immediate network is where the brand compounds.

First event delivered — CLC, Intinc, or external. Post-event survey with three specific questions: what will you do differently as a result of this session? What was most useful? Would you recommend this session to a colleague? Collect three specific outcome statements you can use in future event proposals.
months.gate: Three events confirmed or formally submitted (not just planned) on a rolling 6-month calendar. First external or CLC event delivered with documented participant outcomes.

months.title: Nine-month data review and Q4 adjustment
months.why: Most people who build a personal brand never look at the data. They post what feels right and wonder why it is not compounding. Nine months in, you have enough data to make real decisions — which format gets reach, which pillar generates inbound, which newsletter tier people actually read.
weeks: LinkedIn analytics review: reach, engagement rate, follower growth by month, top-performing posts by pillar and format. Is one pillar consistently outperforming the others on both reach and inbound? Is one format consistently underperforming? Write the findings before drawing conclusions.

Newsletter analytics: open rate, click rate, reply rate, unsubscribe triggers by edition type. Is one tier of The Prompt significantly outperforming? If tier 2 (technical) has 2× the open rate of tier 1 (non-technical), that is a content direction signal.
Event analytics: attendance vs. capacity across all events delivered, post-event survey scores, how many attendees took a specific next step (subscribed to The Prompt, sent a DM, scheduled a call)?

Q4 adjustment plan: based on nine months of actual data — not intuition — what changes? Which format gets more budget? Which channel gets less? Which content pillar gets the flagship treatment in Q4? Document the decisions and the data behind each one.
months.gate: A nine-month analytics review document with at least three specific Q4 changes and the data behind each decision. No adjustments made on instinct alone.

quarters.subtitle: Co-marketing partnerships activated. Brand connected to pipeline. Year 2 strategy written.

months.title: Partnership and co-marketing
months.why: Solo brand building has a ceiling. Every piece of content you publish reaches the same audience. Co-marketing — with Anthropic through the Ambassador program, with CLC institutionally, with adjacent practitioners — multiplies reach without proportionally multiplying effort. This month you activate every available co-marketing path.
weeks: Anthropic Ambassador co-marketing: what does the program actually provide? Event co-promotion, social shares from official channels, directory listing, access to Builders Council. Activate every mechanism you have not already used. If the application is still pending, follow up with a specific ask.

CLC institutional co-marketing: a post-event recap published on CLC's channels or newsletter, a student or faculty testimonial, a quote from the math professor about the program. Ask for each explicitly — institutions will provide assets when asked and rarely volunteer them.

Peer practitioner co-marketing: identify three practitioners in adjacent lanes (AI governance, enterprise ML operations, cloud security) who serve the same enterprise buyer without competing directly. Propose one of: a guest edition of The Prompt, a co-authored LinkedIn post on a shared topic, a joint event.

Inbound source tracking: for every meaningful new connection this month, record how they found you. LinkedIn post? A specific edition of The Prompt? Event attendance? Referral from a previous attendee? The source data tells you which channel has the highest-quality conversion, not just the highest volume.
months.gate: At least one active co-marketing relationship beyond Intinc and CLC. Ambassador co-marketing activated at every available lever. Inbound source tracking live for at least 30 days.

months.title: Brand as business asset — connect the dots
months.why: A personal brand that does not connect to revenue, opportunity, or influence is a hobby. This month you explicitly map what the brand work has produced for the AIaaS pipeline — which posts generated leads, which events produced proposal conversations, which newsletter subscribers became clients or referrers.
weeks: Revenue attribution attempt: map every meaningful business conversation in the last 11 months to its originating brand touchpoint. Even rough attribution — "I think they found me through the OWASP post" — is more useful than no attribution. The goal is a hypothesis you can test, not a precise number.

Brand-to-pipeline conversion rates: what is the rough conversion from LinkedIn follower to discovery call? Event attendee to follow-up? Newsletter subscriber to referral or direct inquiry? Calculate these even if the sample is small. A 2% conversion on 500 followers is 10 conversations — that is a real number to defend.

CTA audit: every active channel should end every piece of content with one specific next step for the audience. LinkedIn post → subscribe to The Prompt. The Prompt → book a discovery call or attend the next event. Event → subscribe and connect. Audit for clarity and consistency. Vague CTAs produce nothing.

Brand investment document for Daniel: one page that shows what the personal brand work produced in 11 months. Not follower counts — conversations started, proposals touched, internal visibility gained, Partner Network leads driven. The document that turns a personal project into a justified business activity.
months.gate: A documented brand-to-pipeline map. At least one traceable connection between brand activity and a business outcome — a conversation, a proposal, or a client. The one-page document for Daniel.

months.title: Year 1 retrospective and Year 2 strategy
months.why: A brand that does not evolve calcifies. Year 1 was about establishing consistent presence and claiming the "security-first Claude practitioner in Lake County" positioning. Year 2 is about compounding that presence, deepening the authority, and deliberately expanding into whatever the data and the market are pointing toward.
weeks: Year 1 retrospective: follower growth, newsletter subscriber growth, events delivered, inbound generated, partnerships formed, deals touched. One honest number per channel. Where did you exceed your own expectations? Where did you fall short of the M1 positioning document?

Positioning review: does "security-first Claude practitioner" still fit? Has the market recognized it? Have unexpected opportunities arrived from a different angle — more from the teaching work, more from the Ambassador program, more from the MCP builder work? The data should inform the Year 2 positioning adjustment if one is needed.

Year 2 strategy: one page. Follower target, newsletter target, events planned, one new channel or format to test (video, podcast guest, conference keynote), and one positioning refinement based on what Year 1 actually rewarded. Specific and time-bounded.

Publish the Year 1 retrospective: a LinkedIn post or dedicated Prompt edition that shares what you built, what you learned, and where you are going. Public accountability compounds — the audience you have built should know what you are doing next, and they should be the first to hear it.
months.gate: A published Year 1 retrospective. A written Year 2 brand strategy document. The audience knows what you are building next before you announce it anywhere else.

teaching.sub: 12 months. Three tier packages built and tested. CLC piloted. Feedback systems live. External delivery pipeline active. Instructor credentials earned. The three-tier curriculum packaged as an AIaaS SKU, the design guide published, and the exercise bank on GitHub for anyone who teaches what you teach.

quarters.subtitle: All three tier packages designed, built, and piloted with at least one real audience each.

months.title: Tier 1 — non-technical curriculum design and materials
months.why: The non-technical format (90 min, any audience) is your widest-reach tier. It is also the feeder into Tiers 2 and 3. "A session that gets skeptics to try Claude once" is a brief, not a curriculum. This month you turn it into a reproducible package that someone other than you could facilitate with a 30-minute briefing.
weeks: Learning objective design: 3–4 verifiable outcomes in SMART format. Not "understand AI" — "write a first prompt that returns something useful for their specific job and iterate it once." Test each objective against a real non-AI person: can they tell you if they achieved it at the end of 90 minutes?

Workshop architecture from the playbook refined: Why this matters (their problem, not AI trends) → What Claude is (honest comparison) → Prompt fundamentals (context, clarity, iteration) → Hands-on (3 guided exercises they build themselves) → Setup → Takeaway. Time every block against a real clock, not an estimate.

Slide deck and participant workbook: the deck is for the room, the workbook is for the participant to keep. The workbook must be self-contained — someone who missed the session should be able to get started from it. Ten copy-paste prompts specific to three different job types: manager, analyst, operations.

Test run with 5+ real non-Claude users: facilitate, do not present. Write down every moment of confusion and every moment of visible delight. The confusion moments are the curriculum gaps. The delight moments are the format to repeat.
months.gate: A complete Tier 1 package — slide deck, participant workbook, facilitator guide — that another capable person could deliver after a 30-minute handoff. Tested with real non-Claude users.

months.title: Tier 2 — technical department curriculum design and materials
months.why: The technical audience (3 hrs, developers + analysts) has one non-negotiable success condition: they must build a working integration before the session ends. A technical workshop that ends with slides and no code is a lecture with a higher registration barrier.
weeks: Technical learning objectives — at least one must be: "they built a working [API call / MCP connection / structured output pipeline] before they leave." The others cover API fundamentals, model selection, token math, system prompt architecture for production.

Environment setup protocol: 30% of technical workshops break in the first 20 minutes because of API keys, package conflicts, or corporate network restrictions. Build a pre-workshop setup guide sent 48 hours before, a day-of troubleshooting checklist, and a fallback demo path for every live coding segment.

The skeleton workflow: the 30-minute build artifact participants take home at the end of Tier 2. A minimal working integration — Claude API call from n8n, a structured output pipeline, or a simple agent loop. Simple enough to complete in 30 minutes, complex enough to adapt to a real problem. Design it and build it yourself first.

Test run with real developers or analysts — not AI practitioners. Observe where they get stuck and for how long. A stack on error handling reveals a gap in the facilitation; a stack on "why would I use this" reveals a gap in the framing. Both are fixable before CLC.
months.gate: A complete Tier 2 package — slides, workbook, setup guide, working code skeleton, facilitator troubleshooting guide. Tested with a real technical audience. Every environment failure has a documented workaround.

months.title: Tier 3 — AI team curriculum design and materials
months.why: The Tier 3 format (6 hours, 8–12 AI-capable people maximum) is your highest-value and most differentiated offering. This audience does not need to be convinced AI is useful. They need to leave with something deployed and a mental model for building things they could not build before.
weeks: Six-session architecture refined from the playbook: Architecture (single vs. multi-agent, tool use) → Extended thinking and long context → Observability (what to log, alert on, never skip) → Security posture (OWASP LLM Top 10, RLS, multi-tenant isolation) → Full build → ADR retrospective. Time every session. The security posture session is your strongest differentiator — it is not in anyone else's Tier 3 format.

The full-day build brief: the agentic workflow the cohort builds together in session 5. Scoped to be completable in 90 minutes by a mixed group. Must include: at least one tool call, one retrieval or context step, and one explicit failure-handling path. Design it, build it yourself, time it, then cut 20% of the scope.

Architecture Decision Record template: the artifact each participant produces alongside the build. What decisions did they make, why, what would they change in v2? The rubric for a strong vs. weak ADR at this level — specific tradeoffs named, not vague claims about quality.

Tier 3 test run: minimum 4 people, AI-capable. The security posture session in particular needs real technical people who will push back. Document every objection raised and how you handled it — these become part of the facilitator guide.
months.gate: A complete Tier 3 package — six session plans, facilitator guide, build brief, ADR template, security posture session materials with objection-handling notes. Tested and timed with a real technical audience.

quarters.subtitle: CLC pilot delivered. Feedback systems live. Materials infrastructure built. First pricing model.

months.title: CLC pilot — Tier 1 delivered to a real CLC audience
months.why: A curriculum tested with colleagues is a hypothesis. A curriculum delivered to CLC students and staff who did not choose to attend and have no professional stake in finding it useful is evidence. The CLC pilot is the moment the curriculum meets the people it was designed for.
weeks: Pre-event logistics: venue confirmed, A/V tested, participant workbooks printed or distributed digitally, pre-workshop setup instructions sent 48 hours before (even for Tier 1 — setup expectations matter). Every logistics failure that can happen in the first 10 minutes should fail in your checklist instead.

Deliver Tier 1 at CLC. Facilitate, do not present. Run the hands-on exercises exactly as designed. Do not improvise unless something is demonstrably not working in the room. The test is: does the curriculum work, not does your improvisation work.

Real-time observation notes: during or immediately after, write down every moment of visible confusion and every moment of visible engagement. The confusion moments are fixable curriculum gaps. The engagement moments tell you which exercises actually work for this audience specifically.

Post-event data: standardized survey (what will you do differently after today, what was most useful, what was confusing), attendance vs. registered count, hands-on completion rate, and one verbatim quote per exercise. These four numbers become your baseline for every future delivery.
months.gate: Tier 1 delivered at CLC with documented outcomes — attendance, survey averages, completion rate, three verbatim quotes. Curriculum revision list from real feedback. Ambassador impact report drafted.

months.title: Feedback architecture and curriculum v2
months.why: One delivery produces intuition. Two deliveries begin to reveal patterns. Three reveal the curriculum — the parts that work for every audience, the parts that need facilitation skill to land, and the parts that simply do not work in the format and should be cut. This month builds the infrastructure to capture that distinction systematically.
weeks: Second Tier 1 delivery to a different audience — Intinc non-technical staff, a professional association, or a second CLC cohort. Deliver the same curriculum version as M4. Do not improvise new content. The test is curriculum consistency, not facilitation creativity.

Feedback system design: standardized post-event survey (same 3–4 questions every time), a self-assessment rubric for your own facilitation (what you would do differently, what worked better than expected, what the room needed that was not in the curriculum), and a running "what broke" log across all deliveries.

Curriculum v2: apply everything from M4 and M5 deliveries. The v2 should measurably improve on the three lowest-scoring survey items from M4. Write down the specific change made for each low-scoring item and the hypothesis for why the change will help.

Tier 2 pilot delivery: a small group of real developers — Intinc engineering, a warm technical contact, or a developer meetup. Not a polished delivery — a test. Every place the setup protocol fails is a place to add a fallback. Every place participants finish early is a place to add depth.
months.gate: Curriculum v2 with a documented change log tied to specific survey data from two deliveries. Tier 2 piloted with a real technical audience. Feedback system documented and reusable across all three tiers.

months.title: Materials infrastructure — the curriculum as a handoff-able product
months.why: A curriculum stored in your personal Drive that only makes sense with your context is not a curriculum product. A product is versioned, accessible, reproducible, and deliverable by someone other than its author. This month you build the infrastructure and price the offering.
weeks: Version control and organization: every deck, workbook, facilitator guide, exercise, and setup instruction in a single folder structure with version numbers and change logs. Rule: you should be able to find the current version of any material in under 30 seconds. If you cannot, the organization is not done.

Facilitator onboarding package: a document that lets a capable but AI-unfamiliar facilitator deliver Tier 1 in two weeks of preparation. It must not assume your context, your build history, or your improvisational skill. Every assumption you make in facilitation that is not in the guide is a gap.

Exercise bank: 15+ exercises across all three tiers, tagged by audience type (non-technical / technical / AI team), Claude familiarity level required (0–3 / 4–7 / 8–10), time required, and whether API access is needed vs. claude.ai only. These are the most reusable curriculum elements — treat them as assets.

Pricing model v1: what does each tier cost when delivered to a paying client? Not CLC (covered by Ambassador sponsorship or donated). A Tier 1 for a 30-person corporate team, a Tier 2 for a developer cohort, a Tier 3 for an AI team. Research comparable corporate AI training pricing. Write the first numbers, however uncomfortable.
months.gate: Materials in versioned, accessible infrastructure. Facilitator onboarding package for Tier 1 complete. Exercise bank with 15+ tagged entries. Pricing model v1 written with documented rationale.

quarters.subtitle: External pipeline active. Teaching methodology documented. Instructor credentials earned.

months.title: External delivery pipeline
months.why: CLC and Intinc are safe audiences. External delivery — at companies, meetups, or conferences where you have no prior relationship — is where you learn whether the curriculum stands without your institutional context. It is also where the testimonials come from that close future sales.
weeks: Target pipeline: five organizations worth approaching for an AI fluency workshop in the next 6 months. One per vertical: a tech company, a professional services firm, a healthcare or financial services team, a community college or university other than CLC, and a corporate L&D department. Brief warm outreach for each that names their specific AI literacy challenge, not a generic "I do AI workshops."

Workshop proposal template: a two-page document a procurement manager or L&D director can circulate internally. Problem statement → curriculum overview → three format options (Tier 1 / Tier 2 / Tier 3) → expected outcomes → evidence (portfolio) → pricing → facilitator bio → next step. Professional enough to send without editing the day of a conversation.

First external outreach to one pipeline target — a warm connection through LinkedIn, the Ambassador network, or a mutual contact. The goal is a discovery call, not a closed deal. Listen for what they actually want vs. what the curriculum offers.

External delivery or confirmed date: deliver to an external audience outside CLC and Intinc — a Chicago-area AI meetup, a professional association session, or a small company workshop. Collect a written testimonial or LinkedIn recommendation from the organizer or a participant.
months.gate: A five-organization pipeline documented. A proposal template ready to send. One external delivery completed or a confirmed external date with written agreement. One specific, attributable external testimonial.

months.title: Teaching methodology — the craft underneath the content
months.why: Knowing Claude deeply is not the same as knowing how to teach Claude effectively. The practitioner who can facilitate an adversarial senior engineer to genuine insight has a skill that is genuinely scarce. This month is about making that skill explicit, documented, and improvable.
weeks: Facilitation methodology documented: the specific techniques that distinguish a workshop from a presentation. Socratic questioning in a technical context, live failure as a teaching tool (breaking something deliberately and debugging it with the audience), the difference between "I will show you" and "you are going to figure this out with my help."

Adult learning principles applied to AI workshops: why a skeptical senior engineer learns differently from a curious junior developer, how to design for two standard deviations of Claude familiarity in the same room, why the "why do I need this" objection disappears when you open with their problem instead of your curriculum.

Differentiation techniques: the extension exercise model — a baseline task that anyone completes plus an extension that stretches the advanced participants. Build one extension exercise per tier. The baseline keeps the room moving; the extension keeps the advanced participants engaged.

Facilitation self-assessment: review detailed notes or recordings from your last four deliveries. Apply the methodology rubric you build this month. Identify two facilitation habits to build and two to eliminate. Write the specific, observable behaviors you are targeting, not vague improvement intentions.
months.gate: A facilitation methodology guide written from your own delivery history — not from a pedagogy textbook. A self-assessment from four deliveries with two specific, named development targets.

months.title: Instructor credentials — the right credential for each context
months.why: "Instructor" means different things in different contexts. At CLC there is a formal path to adjunct or continuing education status. At an enterprise client, the credential is your portfolio and testimonials. At the Ambassador program it is your impact reports. This month you clarify and pursue the right credential for each context simultaneously.
weeks: CLC formal path: the specific conversation with your math professor contact and the relevant CLC administrator about what adjunct or continuing education instructor status requires — minimum delivery hours, a formal application, background check, compensation model. Understand the actual requirements, not the assumed ones. If formal status is not the right path, document why and what informal ongoing relationship makes more sense.

Workshop portfolio: a structured record of every workshop delivered — date, audience, size, tier, survey scores, and at least one specific outcome per delivery. By M9 you should have 6+ documented deliveries. This document is the credential in every context where formal credentials do not apply.

Testimonial collection: a formal request to every significant delivery organizer or participant for a specific written testimonial or LinkedIn recommendation. Specific beats generic. "Kyle ran a 3-hour Tier 2 session with our backend team. Two engineers shipped a Claude integration to production the same week" is a credential. "Great presenter" is not.

Partner Network instructor positioning: update your Partner Network profile to include the three-tier curriculum as a named service line, the delivery portfolio as linked evidence, and the teaching credentials (CLC status + testimonials + Ambassador impact reports) as the proof layer.
months.gate: CLC formal path clarified with a documented next step. A workshop portfolio of 6+ documented deliveries. Three specific, publishable testimonials. Partner Network profile updated with teaching credentials as a named service.

quarters.subtitle: All three tiers delivered in sequence. Curriculum packaged as an AIaaS product. The guide published.

months.title: Full-stack delivery — all three tiers, one quarter
months.why: Each tier has been piloted and iterated independently. This quarter you run all three — ideally in sequence with the same organization or community — to test the thing the curriculum was designed to be: a coherent progression from awareness to depth to capability. The three-tier system only proves itself when delivered as a system.
weeks: Tier 1 delivered to a new audience using curriculum v2 or later. Document outcomes against your M4 CLC baseline. Has the curriculum improved? What specifically moved?

Tier 2 delivered to a technical audience — ideally from the same organization as Tier 1, showing the progression. Document whether participants who came through Tier 1 started Tier 2 with measurably different baseline knowledge.

Tier 3 delivered to an AI-capable team — Intinc's internal AI team, a client engineering cohort, or a Community Ambassador event for advanced practitioners. The full 6-hour format with the build and ADR.

Three-tier retrospective: what happened when all three tiers ran in the same quarter? Did the progression work as designed? What did participants carry from one tier to the next? What does the curriculum teach as a system that individual tiers cannot teach alone? This is the insight that belongs in the published guide.
months.gate: All three tiers delivered in Q4 with documented outcomes. A written three-tier retrospective that captures system behavior, not just individual session metrics.

months.title: Curriculum as an AIaaS product — formalize the service line
months.why: The three-tier curriculum is not just a teaching tool — it is a billable service line. This month you formalize it as an AIaaS SKU with a price, a deliverable, a proposal template, and a conversation with Daniel about what it would take to make it a repeatable Intinc revenue line.
weeks: SKU definitions for all three tiers: formal title, audience description, format (duration, group size range, in-person vs. remote), deliverables the client receives (pre-workshop setup guide, participant workbook, post-workshop resources, survey report), price, and explicit out-of-scope boundaries.

Proposal template: a document that sells the curriculum to a corporate L&D manager or engineering leader without you in the room. Problem → solution → format options → evidence (portfolio, testimonials) → pricing → next step. Five pages maximum. Test it by handing it to someone who has not seen your curriculum and asking if they could make a purchase decision from it.

Pricing validation: what do comparable corporate AI training days cost from other providers? What does a Google or Microsoft corporate workshop cost vs. what you are charging? Adjust if you are more than 30% off market without a reason you can articulate.

Daniel conversation: the three-tier curriculum as an Intinc service offering. Not just Kyle teaching workshops — a packaged training service that Intinc can attach to enterprise client relationships. What does it need to become that? A second facilitator? A platform? Formalized scope? Get his honest reaction.
months.gate: Three SKUs formally defined with prices. A proposal template that closes without a verbal pitch. A documented conversation with Daniel about the Intinc service line path — even a "not now" is a gate-worthy outcome if the reason is documented.

months.title: Publish the curriculum guide and close the arc
months.why: Twelve months of curriculum design, delivery iteration, facilitation methodology, and practitioner learning. You do not own this until someone else can use it. The guide that helps other technical educators design and deliver AI workshops is the compounding asset that outlasts every individual session you ran.
weeks: Write the "AI workshop design guide": not your slide decks — the design principles behind the three-tier curriculum. How to write a verifiable learning objective for a non-technical audience, how to design a hands-on exercise that works on a free claude.ai account, how to handle the top five participant objections in real time, and what makes a Tier 3 security posture session land with an adversarial senior engineer.

Publish: LinkedIn article series or a Substack standalone. One post per tier. The exercise bank as a public GitHub repository. The facilitator methodology as a downloadable PDF. Linked from your Partner Network profile, LinkedIn bio, and The Prompt.

Final CLC delivery: if an adjunct or continuing education formal arrangement is in progress, deliver the qualifying session. If not, deliver one final CLC event as the year's Ambassador anchor — the session that the impact report covers and the professor can formally endorse.

Retrospective: what was harder to teach than you expected? What did participants consistently misunderstand that you had not anticipated? What changed in your own understanding of how technical practitioners learn? What is Y2 — a formal CLC course, a train-the-trainer program, a productized online version, or none of the above?
months.gate: The curriculum design guide published with the exercise bank on GitHub. Final CLC session delivered. Year retrospective written. Three other technical educators are using something from this arc in their own teaching.

gcp.sub: 12 months. From Microsoft-heavy practitioner to Google Cloud fluent. GCP fundamentals, Vertex AI core, ML pipelines and MLOps, the Professional ML Engineer cert sat and passed in M11, and a published multi-cloud comparison capstone that turns the credential into competitive positioning.

quarters.subtitle: Project structure, IAM, networking, compute, data layer — the cloud underneath every later month.

months.title: GCP fundamentals — port the Azure mental model
months.why: Microsoft-heavy practitioners arrive at GCP with Azure muscle memory: resource groups, ARM templates, RBAC, AAD. GCP works differently — orgs/folders/projects, IAM with predefined and custom roles, gcloud CLI, Deployment Manager and Terraform. This month is about building the GCP mental model deliberately, not by accident over six months of confused googling.
weeks: gcloud CLI fundamentals and the GCP resource hierarchy: organization → folders → projects → resources. Practice creating a project structure for a hypothetical multi-tenant client. Learn the "organization-only," "folder-only," and "project-only" boundaries because IAM behaves differently at each layer.

IAM deep dive: predefined roles vs custom roles, service accounts vs user accounts, workload identity federation (the keyless auth pattern that GitHub Actions uses), conditional IAM. Build the principle-of-least-privilege pattern for an ML workload before you have ML workloads to apply it to.

Networking on GCP: VPCs, subnets, firewall rules, Cloud NAT, Private Google Access, VPC Service Controls. Map every concept to the Azure VNet equivalent so you can translate between client conversations on either cloud. The vocabulary differs more than the architecture does.

Operational hygiene: billing setup, budget alerts, quotas, region/zone selection, the cost-tracking labels pattern. A GCP project running for six months without budget alerts is a $400 bill waiting to surprise you. Set them now.
months.gate: A GCP project deployed via Terraform with proper organization placement, IAM with workload identity federation, networking baseline, budget alerts, and cost labels. The foundation that every later month builds on.

months.title: Compute layer — Cloud Run, Functions, Compute Engine
months.why: Most ML workloads on GCP run on serverless compute. Vertex AI itself is built on Cloud Run, GKE, and managed services. This month is the compute layer — knowing when to reach for Cloud Run vs Cloud Functions vs Compute Engine for an ML workload, with cost and operational tradeoffs internalized.
weeks: Cloud Run deep dive: deploying containerized services, request-based scaling, cold start mitigation, custom domains, identity-aware proxy in front. Deploy a Claude API proxy on Cloud Run with proper auth, custom domain, and 99% uptime over a week.

Cloud Functions 2nd gen: triggers (HTTP, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage events), the cost model vs Cloud Run, when functions beat services. Build one Cloud Function that processes a Cloud Storage upload and writes metadata to BigQuery.

Compute Engine fundamentals: when you actually need a VM. GPU instances for ML training, the preemptible VM cost pattern, instance templates and managed instance groups. Most ML training in 2026 runs on Vertex AI managed services rather than raw VMs, but the exam still tests Compute Engine.

Artifact Registry and container lifecycle: push from local docker, push from Cloud Build, image scanning, vulnerability triage, cleanup policies. The container layer that sits between every Cloud Run deploy and the actual running service.
months.gate: A Cloud Run service deployed with custom domain, IAM-authenticated, observability via Cloud Logging. One Cloud Function processing storage events. Artifact Registry with scanning enabled.

months.title: Data layer — BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Dataflow, Pub/Sub
months.why: ML on GCP starts with data, and data on GCP lives in BigQuery and Cloud Storage. The Professional ML Engineer exam weights data preparation pipelines heavily — Dataflow, Pub/Sub, BigQuery transformations. This month is the data layer that every later ML pipeline assumes you have already mastered.
weeks: BigQuery fundamentals: datasets, tables, views, materialized views. Partitioning vs clustering — when to use each. Slot reservation vs on-demand pricing. The query optimizer enough to read EXPLAIN plans. Most ML data prep questions on the exam are BigQuery questions in disguise.

Cloud Storage: buckets, multi-region vs region vs nearline vs coldline storage classes, lifecycle policies, signed URLs, Object Versioning. The storage tier where training data and model artifacts actually live.

Dataflow basics: Apache Beam programming model, batch vs streaming, the templates Google maintains for common patterns (BigQuery → Pub/Sub, GCS → BigQuery, etc.). Build one batch Dataflow job from CSV in GCS to a BigQuery table.
Pub/Sub: topics, subscriptions, push vs pull, dead-letter topics, exactly-once delivery semantics. The event backbone for ML pipelines that react to new data arrival rather than running on schedule.
months.gate: A data pipeline running end-to-end: data lands in Cloud Storage → Pub/Sub event triggers Dataflow → transformed data lands in BigQuery → BigQuery view exposes the analytics. All on a schedule, all monitored.

quarters.subtitle: Notebooks, AutoML, custom training, model deployment, online serving — the ML platform itself.

months.title: Vertex AI Workbench + Pre-trained APIs + AutoML
months.why: Vertex AI is GCP's unified ML platform — the answer to Azure ML and SageMaker. Workbench is the managed Jupyter environment most ML engineers live in day-to-day. Pre-trained APIs cover the vision/speech/language tasks where you should never train a custom model. AutoML covers the cases where managed training beats custom code. Most exam questions assume daily fluency with all three.
weeks: Vertex AI Workbench: instance types, environment management, GitHub integration, the persistent vs ephemeral notebook patterns. Set up a workbench that becomes your daily driver for the rest of the arc — the one where every later experiment runs.

Pre-trained APIs survey: Vision API, Translation API, Speech-to-Text, Natural Language API, Document AI. For each, build a small spike that calls the API on a realistic task. The exam tests "given this scenario, which pre-trained API fits?" repeatedly — internalize the decision tree.

AutoML Tabular for structured data: upload a CSV, train a model, evaluate, deploy to an endpoint. Note training time and cost. AutoML is the floor — your custom models from M5 must beat AutoML to justify the engineering cost.

Model Garden: GCP's catalog of pre-trained models including Gemini, open-source models like Llama, and Google research models. The "which model fits the use case" decision now includes pre-trained Garden models alongside AutoML and custom training.
