months.gate: A Workbench instance running daily. One AutoML model deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint. Pre-trained API decision tree documented. Model Garden surveyed and the three most relevant Garden models for your use cases identified.

months.title: Custom training — bring your own model
months.why: AutoML covers the floor. Custom training is where ML Engineers earn their title. Vertex AI Training supports custom containers, pre-built containers, distributed training, hyperparameter tuning. The exam weights this domain heavily — every "design a training pipeline that..." question is in this territory.
weeks: Custom training jobs: pre-built TensorFlow/PyTorch containers, custom containers from Artifact Registry, training data sources from BigQuery and Cloud Storage. Build a custom training job that fine-tunes a small model on real data.

Hyperparameter tuning with Vertex Vizier: defining the search space, choosing the search algorithm (random, grid, Bayesian), parallel trials, early stopping. Run a tuning job with 20 trials and analyze the convergence pattern.

Distributed training: when to use TPUs vs GPUs vs CPU clusters, the strategy parameter for TensorFlow, PyTorch DDP, the cost-vs-speed tradeoffs. Most ML practitioners never do real distributed training — the exam expects you to know when you would and how it scales.

Training pipelines vs custom jobs vs notebook execution: the three patterns, when each is right, and the lineage tracking that comes free with Vertex AI Pipelines but not with notebook execution. This is the bridge to M7.
months.gate: A custom-trained model with documented hyperparameter tuning, deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint. Cost and training time benchmarked against the M4 AutoML baseline. Distributed training pattern explained in writing even if not run end-to-end.

months.title: Model deployment, monitoring, and serving
months.why: Building models is half the job. Deploying them at scale with proper monitoring, traffic splitting, drift detection, and rollback — the production half — is what separates ML Engineers from data scientists. The exam treats deployment and monitoring as distinct domains. Both are heavily weighted.
weeks: Vertex AI Endpoints: online serving for low-latency, batch prediction for high-throughput. Traffic splitting between model versions for A/B testing. Auto-scaling configuration. The deployment patterns that production ML systems actually use.

Model Registry: versioning, lineage, the deployment workflow from registry to endpoint. Model cards documenting intended use, training data, evaluation metrics, fairness assessment. The governance layer the exam tests as part of deployment.

Vertex AI Model Monitoring: feature skew between training and serving data, prediction drift over time, alerting thresholds, the runbook for "drift detected — what now?" Drift detection is one of the highest-value production patterns and one of the least practiced.

Edge deployment: Vertex AI Edge Manager for on-device inference, the use cases (low-latency, intermittent connectivity, data sovereignty), the tradeoffs vs cloud endpoints. Lightly weighted on the exam but worth the chapter.
months.gate: A model deployed with traffic splitting between v1 and v2. Drift monitoring active and alerting tested. Model Registry populated with versions and model cards. Production runbook documented for "drift detected" and "endpoint failing health check" scenarios.

quarters.subtitle: Vertex AI Pipelines, Cloud Build CI/CD, governance, monitoring, the production ML practice.

months.title: Vertex AI Pipelines (Kubeflow + TFX)
months.why: The exam weights pipelines heavily — the highest-weighted single domain at roughly 23-26% depending on the version. Vertex AI Pipelines (managed Kubeflow Pipelines + TFX components) is how production ML on GCP gets orchestrated. This is the orchestration layer that ties M3 data, M5 training, and M6 deployment into one repeatable system.
weeks: Kubeflow Pipelines fundamentals: components (containerized steps), pipelines (DAGs of components), artifacts (typed inputs/outputs), lineage (the auto-tracked graph of who produced what). The mental model that makes the rest of the month make sense.

Vertex AI Pipelines specifically: the managed runtime, the SDK (kfp.v2), pipeline parameters, conditional branches, parallel execution. Build a small pipeline with three components — data prep, training, evaluation — running end-to-end.

TFX components: ExampleGen, StatisticsGen, SchemaGen, Transform, Trainer, Evaluator, Pusher. The pre-built components that most production ML pipelines use rather than reinventing. Each component is exam-relevant individually.

Pipeline triggers and orchestration: schedule-based (Cloud Scheduler), event-based (Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage triggers), manual triggers from CI/CD. Build one scheduled pipeline that retrains a model weekly and conditionally deploys based on eval metrics.
months.gate: A Vertex AI Pipeline running end-to-end: data ingestion → preparation → training → evaluation → conditional deployment. Scheduled to run weekly. Lineage visible in the GCP console for every artifact produced.

months.title: CI/CD for ML — Cloud Build, GitHub Actions, testing strategies
months.why: ML Engineer is fundamentally an MLOps role. Cloud Build for GCP-native pipelines, GitHub Actions for repos that need broader CI/CD, workload identity federation for keyless authentication, and the testing strategies that make ML systems actually reliable. This month applies engineering discipline to ML systems.
weeks: Cloud Build: build configurations, triggers, custom builders, the integration with Artifact Registry and Cloud Run. The native GCP CI/CD that most exam scenarios assume.

GitHub Actions ↔ GCP via workload identity federation: keyless authentication, the OIDC trust setup, the deployment patterns. For a Microsoft-heavy practitioner with GitHub repos, this is the bridge between worlds.

Container security in the pipeline: Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning, Binary Authorization, the policy that prevents unsigned images from deploying to Cloud Run. Security shifted left in the ML deployment flow.

Testing strategies for ML: unit tests for data transformations, schema validation tests, model performance regression tests, integration tests for end-to-end pipelines. Coverage of the four critical paths that breaking would cause user-facing failures.
months.gate: A complete CI/CD pipeline: PR triggers Cloud Build → tests run → image builds → deploys to staging Vertex AI endpoint → eval tests run → manual approval promotes to prod. Workload identity federation working for GitHub Actions integration.

months.title: Model governance, security, and the cross-arc Security work
months.why: Enterprise ML on GCP runs under governance: who can train, who can deploy, who accesses training data, what gets logged for compliance, who reviews model cards. The exam tests this lightly. Enterprise practice tests it heavily. This month also ties directly into the Security Arc work — the AI security posture you build in the Security Arc applies here.
weeks: Vertex AI Model Cards in production: documentation, intended use, training data sources, evaluation results, fairness assessments, known limitations. The artifact that lets a security or compliance team approve a model for production.

Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), VPC Service Controls perimeters, Private Service Connect for Vertex AI endpoints. The patterns enterprise clients require for any ML workload touching regulated data.

Audit logging and Cloud Logging for ML systems: Admin Activity logs, Data Access logs, the cost vs visibility tradeoff, BigQuery export for long-term retention. The forensic layer that makes incident response possible.

Compliance frameworks on GCP: HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC2, GDPR considerations, the GCP services that are in-scope for each. Lightly weighted on the exam, heavily relevant for any AIaaS client engagement that mentions compliance.
months.gate: A documented model governance pattern applied to your M5-M7 work: model cards filled out, CMEK encryption applied, audit logging enabled and tested, compliance framework alignment documented. The pattern Daniel could hand to a regulated-industry client.

quarters.subtitle: Eight-week prep intensive, sit the exam, multi-cloud comparison capstone published.

months.title: Exam prep intensive — eight weeks before the seat
months.why: The Google Professional ML Engineer exam is 60 multiple-choice questions, 2 hours, passing roughly 70%. The exam guide is published. Microsoft-heavy practitioners typically need 40+ hours of focused prep on top of the M1-M9 hands-on work. This month is the structured preparation window that makes the difference between sitting the exam confident and sitting it hopeful.
weeks: Official Google Cloud Skills Boost ML Engineer learning path: complete every module, every quest, every hands-on lab. The labs in particular are exam-relevant because the exam tests applied knowledge. Skip the labs and you skip the exam preparation.

Practice exams: at least three different practice exam sets (Whizlabs, ExamPro, Tutorials Dojo). Score each, identify the three lowest-scoring domains, do additional labs in each. Practice exams are diagnostic, not predictive.
Weak area drills: for each weak domain identified in week 2, build a 2-hour hands-on drill. Most weak areas resolve with hands-on practice rather than re-reading documentation. Trust the diagnostic.

Mock exam simulation: take a full 60-question, 2-hour exam in one sitting under exam conditions. Score it. If above 75%, schedule the real exam. If below 75%, identify the gap and run the drill cycle one more week before scheduling.
months.gate: Three practice exams scored 75%+ on different days. Weak areas remediated with hands-on labs. Mock exam taken under simulated conditions and passed. Confidence to schedule the real exam.

months.title: Sit the exam
months.why: The cert is paid for, scheduled, and sat in a single month so the prep pressure produces the credential rather than dissipating into endless preparation. Pearson VUE proctored either at a test center or online. The exam is real, and so is the post-exam analysis whether pass or fail.
weeks: Final review week: domain-by-domain checklist of objectives, three-page summary notes that compress everything into a single document. Light review only — heavy cramming the week of the exam costs more than it gains.
Schedule the exam at a Pearson VUE center or remote-proctored online. Time it for early in the week so the rest of the week is buffer. Set up the test environment 24 hours before if remote.

Sit the exam. Document the experience immediately afterward — which questions surprised you, which domains felt under-prepared, what you would do differently. The post-exam writeup is useful whether you passed or not.

Pass: update the Partner Network profile, update LinkedIn, plan the M12 capstone. Fail: identify the specific domain gaps from the score report, plan a 30-day remediation, schedule the retake. Either outcome is a defined next step, not a stall.
months.gate: Google Professional ML Engineer cert credential issued (or a clear remediation plan with retake scheduled). Partner Network profile updated. LinkedIn announcement drafted. The M12 capstone work scoped.

months.title: Multi-cloud comparison capstone and brand leverage
months.why: Holding a cert is one thing. Turning it into competitive positioning — multi-cloud expertise that no single-cloud practitioner can claim — is what makes the cert work for the Personal Brand arc, the AIaaS service line, and the Partner Network listing. This month produces the artifact that Anthropic Partner Network clients actually need.
weeks: Multi-cloud comparison document: "When to use Vertex AI vs Azure ML vs AWS SageMaker." The artifact written from a practitioner who has actually used both Azure ML (from the Copilot/Azure arc) and Vertex AI (this arc). The framework: workload type, compliance requirements, existing stack, team skill set, cost model.

Apply the comparison to a real engagement: pick one Intinc client or FlashFusion engagement and map "if this were on GCP instead of Azure, what would change?" The applied analysis makes the comparison document real, not theoretical.

Publish the comparison: LinkedIn long-form article (the M7 flagship piece in Personal Brand arc terms), Prompt edition, GitHub gist of the architecture diagrams. Cross-link to the Partner Network profile and the AIaaS service offerings.

Year-end retrospective: the 12-month GCP arc, what changed in your practice, what conversations the cert unlocks that were previously closed, what the Y2 plan looks like (advanced certs? specialization? deeper Vertex AI work?). Published as the Personal Brand arc Q4 retrospective material.
months.gate: Published multi-cloud comparison referenced in the Partner Network profile, the AIaaS positioning materials, and at least one client conversation. The cert is now leverage for billable work, not just a credential on a wall.

fullstack.sub: 12 months. The bridge from automation to product. Next.js, FastAPI or Hono, Supabase with multi-tenant RLS, Auth.js or Clerk, Vercel deployment, Stripe payments, real users. Three apps shipped — a foundation v1, a multi-tenant SaaS, and a flagship that earns revenue or significant adoption.

quarters.subtitle: Each stack layer mastered through working spikes — not tutorials. Frontend, backend, data, auth.

months.title: Next.js & React — frontend craft, not just HTML+CSS
months.why: Your existing builds use Copilot Studio chat surfaces, Claude Desktop, or n8n form embeds. None of those required real frontend craft. Next.js App Router with Server Components, Client Components, Server Actions, and proper hydration boundaries is the foundation under every modern AI product. This is the month where your component thinking shifts from "HTML page" to "composable UI tree."
weeks: Next.js App Router fundamentals: app/ directory structure, server vs client components, the rules around use client and where state can live. Build a small spike with three routes, two layouts, and one server action that reads from a database. The spike is the curriculum.

TypeScript foundations applied to React: prop typing, generic components, useState/useReducer with proper types, and the discriminated union pattern for component variants. Your Microsoft-heavy stack has C# muscle memory — TypeScript will feel familiar but the React patterns are different.

Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui setup: the component library that lets you ship without designing from scratch. Install shadcn, add 5 components (button, card, dialog, form, table), build a static dashboard layout with them. This becomes the visual shorthand for every later app.

Deploy spike to Vercel: connect a GitHub repo, push to main, see the preview URL. Configure environment variables. The deploy step should feel routine by the end of week 4 — every later month assumes you can ship to a URL in under five minutes.
months.gate: A small Next.js app deployed to a public Vercel URL with three routes, server actions, shadcn/ui components, and TypeScript typing throughout. Pushed to main = automatically deployed.

months.title: API design & streaming — the backend layer for AI
months.why: Your n8n workflows and Copilot Studio agents handle backend implicitly. A real product has an explicit backend with versioned APIs, rate limiting, error handling, and streaming responses. This month you build that layer once — properly — so every subsequent app reuses the patterns instead of reinventing them.
weeks: API design fundamentals: REST vs RPC vs Server Actions vs tRPC, when each is the right call. For AI products, Server Actions in Next.js cover 70% of cases; the other 30% need a dedicated backend. Build a Server Action that calls Claude and returns structured output.

FastAPI or Hono for the AI backend layer: pick one based on language preference. FastAPI if you want the Python ecosystem and your future ML Engineer cert work; Hono if you want edge-native and the Cloudflare arc compatibility. Build a backend with /chat, /generate, /healthz endpoints, proper status codes, error responses.

Streaming responses (Server-Sent Events): the pattern that makes AI UIs feel alive. SSE from backend, fetch with a ReadableStream on the frontend, token-by-token rendering. This is the hardest pattern in the arc — get it working in week 3, refine through every later project.

Rate limiting, API key management, and observability: Upstash Redis for rate limits, env-based API key management, basic request logging. Send one rate-limited request and watch the 429 come back. Send a malformed request and watch the structured error response.
months.gate: A backend API with at least 3 endpoints, streaming Claude responses via SSE, rate-limiting working, and structured error responses. Tested with curl and from the M1 frontend.

months.title: Supabase & auth — the data layer for multi-tenant products
months.why: You already use Supabase for the Drive Automation Chain. That use is single-tenant — your data, your queries. A user-facing product is multi-tenant by default: every query needs to know who is asking, what they own, and what they can see. This month is when Supabase RLS stops being theory and becomes the default mental model.
weeks: Supabase deeper: Row Level Security policies, Postgres functions, database triggers, realtime subscriptions. Build a schema with users, workspaces, and resources. Write RLS policies that prevent any user from reading another user's data. Test the policies with two real test accounts.

Auth.js (NextAuth) or Clerk: pick based on control vs. speed. Auth.js gives you full control and lives in your codebase; Clerk gives you speed and a hosted UI. For a portfolio of multiple apps, Clerk is the faster path. Build sign-up, sign-in, sign-out, password reset, and a protected dashboard route.

Multi-tenancy at the data layer: workspaces table, workspace_members table, the join pattern for "all resources in workspaces I belong to." Test the SQL queries directly in Supabase before wiring them to the UI. This is the pattern under almost every B2B SaaS product.

Migrations and schema management: Supabase migrations with the CLI, version-controlled schema, the workflow for "I changed the schema in dev, now apply it to prod." Practice the migration apply / rollback cycle three times until it is muscle memory.
months.gate: A Next.js app with Clerk or Auth.js auth, Supabase data layer with RLS policies preventing cross-tenant reads, and a working migration workflow. Two test users cannot see each other's data.

quarters.subtitle: A real product, end-to-end. One Claude-powered feature, real auth, real users, real deployment.

months.title: Build app v1 — vertical slice from auth to AI feature
months.why: The fastest way to learn a stack is to build a real product end-to-end. This month is the v1 of the first app. Pick something narrow: a writing assistant for a specific job role, a structured extractor for a specific document type, a Claude-powered tool for a workflow you already do manually. The narrowness is the point — a focused v1 ships, a broad v1 stalls.
weeks: Pick the problem and write the spec: one paragraph describing what the app does and who uses it. Define the v1 scope as a single Claude-powered feature plus auth plus history. If the spec exceeds three sentences, the scope is too big for v1.

Build vertical slice 1 — auth + landing page + protected dashboard with a "no data yet" empty state. The spine of the app exists before any AI feature is wired up. Most full-stack projects fail because the AI feature is built before the app skeleton.

Build vertical slice 2 — the Claude-powered feature: input form → API call → streamed output → save to database → display in history. End to end. One feature, working all the way through, not three half-features.

Polish week: empty states for new users, error states for Claude API failures, loading states with skeleton UIs from shadcn/ui. The difference between a tutorial app and a real app is what happens when things go wrong. Handle three failure modes: bad input, API timeout, rate limit hit.
months.gate: A v1 app with auth, one working Claude-powered feature, history, and three handled failure modes. Deployed to a Vercel URL. You can demo it to a non-technical person without disclaimers.

months.title: Deployment, observability, and operational hygiene
months.why: Shipping to Vercel once is a milestone. Operating a deployed app — watching errors, managing environments, recovering from failures — is the discipline. This month builds the operational layer that turns a working deploy into a maintainable product.
weeks: Vercel deployment patterns: preview deployments per branch, environment variables per environment (dev/preview/prod), promotion flow from preview to production. Push a feature branch, get a preview URL with isolated env vars, merge to main, watch it promote.

Sentry or similar error tracking: install the Sentry SDK, capture an unhandled error in development, see it in the dashboard. Trigger a real production error, see it tracked. The first time you see a user error you didn't experience yourself is the moment observability earns its weight.

Vercel Analytics or PostHog for user analytics: page views, custom events for "user submitted prompt," "AI response completed," "history viewed." The data tells you what users actually do vs. what you assumed they would do.

Database backups and restore drills: Supabase point-in-time recovery, the manual backup workflow, the restore-to-staging drill. Run the drill once. The backup that has never been tested is not a backup.
months.gate: Sentry catching production errors. Analytics showing real user events. Preview-to-production promotion working. One successful database restore drill documented.

months.title: Polish, accessibility, and the first real user
months.why: The v1 app from M4 works. M5 makes it operationally sound. This month is the difference between "engineer-built" and "professional product." Accessibility, SEO, performance, and one non-Kyle user actually using it for a real task. The first user feedback rewires every assumption you made in M4.
weeks: Accessibility audit: WCAG 2.1 AA basics. Keyboard navigation through every interaction. Screen reader testing on three critical flows. Color contrast checks. Most of this is fixed by using shadcn/ui components correctly — the audit reveals where you went off-pattern.

SEO and metadata: proper page titles, descriptions, og:image, twitter:card. Sitemap and robots.txt. A Google Search Console property verified for the production domain. The product gets indexed before anyone searches for it.

First real user — not Kyle, not Daniel, not someone obligated to give kind feedback. Find one person who has the problem the app solves. Watch them use it without explaining anything. Write down every moment of confusion. The watching is more valuable than the talking.

v1.1 ship: apply the top three changes from the user observation. Re-deploy. Send to the user, see if v1.1 unblocked the confusion. The cycle observation → fix → re-test is the product development loop in miniature.
months.gate: A WCAG 2.1 AA-compliant app with proper SEO. One real user has used it for a real task. Top three friction points fixed and shipped as v1.1. Honest user-observation notes documented.

quarters.subtitle: Streaming UI, multi-tenancy, payments, and the production hardening that separates a product from a prototype.

months.title: Streaming AI UI — the pattern that makes AI feel native
months.why: The M2 SSE backend was infrastructure. This month is the UI layer that consumes it elegantly: token-by-token rendering with smooth transitions, optimistic UI for assistant responses, cancelable streams, partial-render error recovery. The difference between an AI app that feels alive and one that feels like a form submission.
weeks: useStream and Server Actions with streaming: the Vercel AI SDK's useChat / useCompletion hooks, OR custom hooks built on the Fetch ReadableStream API. Build a generation UI where text appears word-by-word as Claude produces it. Smooth, no flicker.

Optimistic UI patterns: when a user sends a message, the UI updates instantly to show their message before the server responds. When Claude responds, the assistant message appears in a "thinking" state, then streams content. The perceived latency drops by 60% even when actual latency is unchanged.

Cancelable streams: a stop button that actually stops the stream. AbortController on the frontend, propagating cancellation to the backend, partial response handling on cancel. Users will stop bad generations — your app needs to handle that gracefully.

Multi-turn conversation UI: the chat-style interface that keeps context across turns. Message history rendering, conversation persistence to the database, scroll-to-bottom behavior, auto-resize input. The Claude.ai pattern, in your own product.
months.gate: A streaming AI UI with token-by-token rendering, optimistic UI, working cancel, and multi-turn conversation. Indistinguishable from Claude.ai or ChatGPT in feel. Deployed and tested with a real user.

months.title: Multi-tenancy and payments — the SaaS layer
months.why: A product that does not collect money is a portfolio piece. A product that does is a business. This month adds the SaaS scaffolding: workspaces, team members, Stripe subscriptions, usage-based billing, quota enforcement. Most of these patterns are well-trodden — execute them correctly once and they become reusable across every future app.
weeks: Workspaces and team patterns: workspaces table, workspace_members table with role enums (owner, admin, member), invitation flow with email tokens, RLS policies that scope every query to "my workspaces." This is the pattern under almost every B2B SaaS.

Stripe integration: Stripe Checkout for subscriptions, Stripe Customer Portal for self-service, webhook handler for subscription lifecycle events (created, updated, canceled, payment_failed). The webhook handler is where 80% of payment bugs live — log every event, replay them in dev.

Quota enforcement: free tier vs paid tier limits, usage tracking in the database, the API-layer guard that returns 402 when over quota. The user must hit the quota wall and see a clear upgrade path, not a confusing error.

The pricing page: a real pricing page with three tiers (free, pro, team). Linked to Stripe products. Users can click "upgrade" and complete checkout in under 90 seconds. Test the full flow in production with a real card and refund yourself afterward.
months.gate: A multi-tenant app with workspaces, Stripe subscriptions working end-to-end, quota enforcement preventing free-tier abuse, and a pricing page that converts at least one real test purchase. Webhook handler logged and tested.

months.title: Production hardening — security, testing, recovery
months.why: Most apps fail in production because of issues nobody tested for. This month applies the Security Arc work to your own codebase, builds the test coverage that catches regressions, and runs the recovery drills that turn "we lost data" into "we restored from backup." The discipline that lets you sleep.
weeks: Security review applied to your own app: OWASP ASVS basic checklist, input validation on every endpoint, output sanitization, rate limiting verified, auth bypass attempts tested. This is the Security Arc M2-M4 work applied to the artifact you built. Every finding becomes a backlog item or a ticket-now item.

Test coverage for critical paths: Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for end-to-end tests of the auth flow + the AI feature flow + the payment flow. Not 100% coverage — coverage of the three paths that breaking would refund the customer.

Backup and recovery drill in production: simulate a database failure, restore from point-in-time backup, verify the data is intact, document the runbook. The first real drill takes 4 hours; the second takes 30 minutes; the third never happens because nothing breaks.

Monitoring and alerting: Sentry alerts for critical errors, uptime monitoring (Better Stack or UptimeRobot), Slack or email notifications for production issues. The alert that wakes you up at 3am should be the same alert you can fix from your phone in 10 minutes.
months.gate: A security review documented with all findings addressed or backlogged. End-to-end tests covering auth, AI, and payment flows. One successful production recovery drill. Alerting working and tested.

quarters.subtitle: The portfolio piece. A product worth paying for, launched publicly, with real users and a public retrospective.

months.title: Build the flagship — the product worth paying for
months.why: The M4 v1 app proved you can ship. The M7-M9 work proved you can operate. This is the product you want in your portfolio when an enterprise client asks "show me what you have built." Pick the problem worth solving — for Intinc, FlashFusion, or your own consulting brand. Build it for real, not as a tutorial output.
weeks: Pick the problem with stakes: an internal Intinc tool that automates a real process, a FlashFusion client tool that delivers real value, or a public product targeting your security-first AI practitioner audience. The problem must have a user willing to pay for the solution — even if "pay" means time saved or budget allocated, not dollars.

Design before code: figure pages or even Excalidraw mockups of every screen before any code. The interaction patterns, the empty states, the error states. The design phase prevents three weeks of "this doesn't feel right" rebuilds in M11.

Build the spine — auth, dashboard, the primary feature working end-to-end with the real Claude integration. Deploy to a custom domain (not a vercel.app subdomain). The product looks and feels like a product, not a project.

Build the secondary features — settings, export, sharing, history, anything the primary user needs beyond the core feature. By the end of M10, every flow a user could plausibly want is implemented at least once.
months.gate: A flagship product on a custom domain with auth, primary feature, secondary features, and the design quality of a real SaaS app. One internal stakeholder (Daniel, a client, or a partner) has used it for a real task and given specific feedback.

months.title: Performance, accessibility, and pre-launch polish
months.why: A product can ship at 70% polish and learn from users, or it can ship at 90% polish and earn trust on day one. For a flagship, the second path matters. This month is the audit and remediation work that turns a working product into a professional one — the difference between "engineer made this" and "you would not know an engineer made this."
weeks: Performance audit: Lighthouse 90+ across performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO. Bundle analysis with @next/bundle-analyzer, code splitting where bundles are large, image optimization with next/image, font optimization with next/font.

Accessibility deep pass: WCAG 2.1 AA verified with automated tools (axe DevTools) and manual keyboard testing on every flow. Screen reader testing on the critical paths. Real disabled users use AI tools — exclusion is a product flaw, not a checkbox.

Copy and content polish: every error message rewritten to be helpful, every empty state given a clear next action, every email template (welcome, password reset, payment receipt) on-brand and clear. The words a user reads define their experience as much as the UI.

Brand and visual polish: a real logo (even if AI-generated and refined), consistent use of brand colors, a polished marketing page that explains what the product is in 10 seconds. The marketing page is the conversion gate — a confused visitor does not sign up.
months.gate: Lighthouse 90+ across all categories. WCAG 2.1 AA verified. Marketing page that converts a non-technical visitor in 10 seconds. Copy reviewed and rewritten for clarity. The product is launch-ready.

months.title: Launch and the year-one retrospective
months.why: The product is built, polished, and operational. The launch is what turns it into something that exists in the world. Public launch, real users, first paying customer (or first equivalent commitment), and a written retrospective that ties the arc to the next year of work — including how the flagship feeds the AIaaS and Personal Brand arcs.
weeks: Soft launch: send to your existing audience first — The Prompt subscribers, LinkedIn followers, Intinc colleagues, Community Ambassador network. Collect 20-50 active users in the first week. Watch the analytics, fix the bugs that emerge, refine onboarding before going broader.

Public launch: ProductHunt, Hacker News (Show HN), LinkedIn announcement, Prompt edition with the full story. The launch post is half "here is what I built" and half "here is what I learned" — the second half is what makes it shareable to other builders.

First paying customer or commitment: a real Stripe charge, an Intinc internal budget allocation, or a FlashFusion client retainer that includes the product. The number on the line item validates the product as a business, not just a portfolio piece.

Year-one retrospective: published as a Prompt edition or LinkedIn post. What you built, what worked, what failed, how the stack feels after 12 months, what the Y2 plan is. Public accountability ties the arc to the next year — and feeds the Personal Brand arc directly.
months.gate: A flagship product launched publicly with at least 50 real users in the first month and at least one paying customer or paid commitment. A published retrospective. The artifact that the AIaaS service line and Partner Network listing both reference as proof of capability.

azure.sub: 12 months. From Copilot Studio implementer to Microsoft AI engineer. Azure resource fluency, Foundry Hub and Projects, Azure OpenAI direct, Prompt Flow orchestration, AI Search retrieval, Semantic Kernel agents, Azure ML model layer, enterprise governance — and the architecture comparison that makes Intinc a credible Microsoft AI partner, not just a Copilot reseller.

quarters.subtitle: Azure resource fluency, AI Foundry Hub setup, Azure OpenAI Service mastered as the engine.

months.title: Azure resource model — past the Copilot Studio surface
months.why: Copilot Studio hides the underlying Azure infrastructure from you. Every Copilot you have built sits on resources you may not have managed directly — App Registrations, managed identities, Key Vaults, Log Analytics workspaces. M1 is the resource layer made explicit. Without this, every later month sits on assumptions you cannot defend in a client architecture conversation.
weeks: Azure CLI and Bicep fundamentals: az login, subscription selection, resource group structure, the Bicep DSL for infrastructure-as-code. Most production Azure work is Bicep, not ARM JSON, not Portal clicks. Build a Bicep template that provisions a resource group, Key Vault, and storage account.

Entra ID + RBAC + managed identities: the auth layer underneath everything. App Registrations vs Service Principals vs Managed Identities — when each is right, what permissions are required for which Foundry operations. The "principle of least privilege" applied to AI workloads.

Key Vault, App Configuration, and secrets discipline: the proper home for API keys, connection strings, model endpoints. Practice the workflow: store a secret, retrieve it from a Function, rotate it, revoke it. Most Copilot Studio integrations leak secrets in custom connectors — fix that pattern now.

Networking baseline: VNets, private endpoints, the "all Azure traffic should travel private network" pattern that enterprise clients require. Most AI Foundry deployments in regulated industries are private-endpoint-only. Document the network architecture before building on it.
months.gate: A Bicep-deployed Azure baseline: resource group, Key Vault, Log Analytics, private VNet. Entra ID auth working with managed identity. The infrastructure foundation that every later Foundry resource will sit on.

months.title: AI Foundry Hub + Project — the Foundry control plane
months.why: Azure AI Foundry (formerly Azure AI Studio) is the unified workspace for Azure OpenAI, Azure ML, AI Search, content safety, and evaluations. The Hub is the org-level container; Projects are the workspaces inside. M2 is setting up the Foundry workspace properly so the next 10 months build on a clean foundation, not a Portal-clicked mess.
weeks: AI Foundry Hub creation via Bicep: the proper way, not the Portal way. Hub configuration, storage account binding, Key Vault binding, container registry binding, Application Insights binding. The five resources every Hub depends on, all provisioned together.

Project structure: one Project per use case vs. one Project for everything. The decision tree based on team size, compliance requirements, and resource separation needs. Build one Project for general-purpose work and one for a regulated-data use case.

Connections and credentials: connecting Azure OpenAI, AI Search, and storage to your Project. The managed-identity-based connection pattern (preferred) vs. API key (lazy, leaky). Practice both, document why one is right.

Compute resources: serverless compute for prototyping, compute instances for development, compute clusters for training. The cost model differs significantly per pattern. Spin one up, run a job, shut it down. Verify the cost in the billing dashboard.
months.gate: An AI Foundry Hub deployed via Bicep with two Projects, managed-identity connections to Azure OpenAI and AI Search, and at least one compute resource lifecycle exercised (create, use, shut down). The workspace is production-grade, not Portal-tinkered.

months.title: Azure OpenAI Service — the engine underneath Copilot Studio
months.why: Every Copilot you have built calls Azure OpenAI Service underneath. M3 is the direct access to that service — your own deployments, your own model selection, your own quota management. This is where you stop being a Copilot user and start being an AOAI engineer.
weeks: Azure OpenAI deployment: model selection (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1, text-embedding-3-large), deployment SKUs (Standard, Provisioned Throughput Units), region selection. Most production deployments are Standard SKU initially; PTU is for predictable high-volume workloads. Deploy GPT-4o and an embedding model.

Quota and rate-limit management: token-per-minute (TPM) quotas per deployment, request-per-minute (RPM) limits, the dynamic quota feature. Production AOAI failures are usually quota failures. Build a small spike that hits the quota limit deliberately and observes the 429 response.

Direct API calls from Python and TypeScript: bypassing Copilot Studio entirely. The SDK patterns (OpenAI Python SDK with Azure config, Azure.AI.OpenAI for .NET), streaming responses, function calling, structured output mode. Build the API patterns once, reuse forever.

Content filtering and safety: AOAI's built-in content filters (categories, severity levels), Prompt Shields for jailbreak detection, custom blocklists. Configure each, test with adversarial inputs, document the safety posture. The compliance layer the platform provides for free.
months.gate: Direct Azure OpenAI access from Python and TypeScript SDKs with streaming, function calling, structured output, and content filtering configured. A deliberate quota-limit test documented. The engine layer is now accessible, not abstracted away.

quarters.subtitle: Prompt Flow mastered as orchestration. AI Search as the RAG layer. Hybrid retrieval shipped.

months.title: Prompt Flow — Foundry's orchestration layer
months.why: Prompt Flow is Microsoft's answer to LangChain and LlamaIndex — a graph-based orchestration tool for multi-step LLM workflows. It runs inside Foundry, integrates with Azure OpenAI, deploys to managed endpoints. M4 is fluency with Prompt Flow as the orchestration layer for non-Copilot-Studio agent work.
weeks: Prompt Flow fundamentals: the graph model (nodes, edges, variants), the built-in node types (LLM, Python, prompt, embedding, vector index lookup), the Visual Studio Code extension for local development. Build one Prompt Flow end-to-end that takes a query, retrieves context, and generates a response.

Variants and evaluation: Prompt Flow's built-in pattern for A/B testing prompts. Define two variants of an LLM node, run evaluation across both with a dataset, compare results in the Foundry UI. This is the eval layer the Eval arc M4 platform decision could also point at.

Custom Python nodes: when the built-in nodes are not enough. Building a custom node that calls an internal API, applies a guardrail, or performs a domain-specific transformation. The extension pattern that makes Prompt Flow viable for real production use cases.

Deployment to managed endpoints: a Prompt Flow deployed as a real-time endpoint, callable via HTTPS, scaled automatically. The deployment that turns a Prompt Flow from a development artifact into a production service. Test it end-to-end with curl.
months.gate: A multi-step Prompt Flow deployed to a managed endpoint, callable via HTTPS, with at least one custom Python node and one A/B variant. The orchestration layer beyond Copilot Studio is now in your toolkit.

months.title: Azure AI Search — the retrieval layer
months.why: Azure AI Search (formerly Cognitive Search) is the retrieval service most enterprise Foundry RAG systems use. Hybrid search (vector + keyword), semantic ranking, integrated vectorization, security trimming for multi-tenant scenarios. M5 is the retrieval layer Foundry RAG sits on.
weeks: AI Search basics: indexes, fields, indexers, skillsets. The data model that lets you ingest documents, extract fields, generate embeddings, and store everything in one searchable index. Build one index with a real document corpus.

Integrated vectorization: AI Search calling Azure OpenAI embedding deployments during indexing. The pattern that eliminates the separate embedding-generation pipeline most RAG architectures need. Configure it and ingest a corpus.

Hybrid search and semantic ranker: the combined retrieval pattern that outperforms either vector or keyword alone for most enterprise use cases. The semantic ranker (an L2 reranker) adds another quality boost. Benchmark hybrid vs. vector-only vs. keyword-only on the same query set.

Security trimming: per-document ACLs that let you build multi-tenant RAG where each user only retrieves documents they have access to. This is the pattern almost every enterprise client requires and almost no demo RAG system implements. Build it correctly on one index.
months.gate: An AI Search index with integrated vectorization, hybrid search with semantic ranker, and security trimming for multi-tenant scenarios. The retrieval layer is production-grade, with documented benchmark comparisons across retrieval strategies.

months.title: RAG end-to-end on Foundry
months.why: M4 built orchestration. M5 built retrieval. M6 combines them into a complete RAG system on Foundry — Prompt Flow orchestrating AI Search retrieval and Azure OpenAI generation, with eval, monitoring, and the production characteristics enterprise clients require.
weeks: End-to-end RAG architecture: ingestion (data → AI Search index with integrated vectorization), retrieval (Prompt Flow node querying AI Search), generation (Prompt Flow LLM node with retrieved context), evaluation (Prompt Flow eval flow scoring relevance and groundedness). Build the architecture diagram before the implementation.

Implementation: every component from M4-M5 connected in one working system. Real corpus, real queries, real evaluation. By the end of week 2, queries flow from input through retrieval through generation back to the caller, all within Foundry.

Groundedness and relevance metrics: Foundry's built-in RAG metrics — groundedness (does the answer cite retrieved context?), relevance (does it answer the question?), retrieval quality. Run the evaluation, document baseline scores, iterate.

Production observability: Application Insights wired up for the RAG endpoint, custom metrics for retrieval latency, generation latency, end-to-end token cost. The observability the M11 polish month will rely on.
months.gate: A complete RAG system on Foundry deployed end-to-end with baseline groundedness, relevance, and retrieval quality metrics measured. Application Insights tracking latency, cost, and quality per request. The pattern that future client engagements will replicate.

quarters.subtitle: Semantic Kernel for agents. Azure ML for model deployment. Enterprise governance and compliance.

months.title: Semantic Kernel — Microsoft's agent framework
months.why: Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open-source SDK for building AI agents, comparable to LangGraph or the Anthropic SDK's agent loop patterns. It is the SDK most Microsoft-stack enterprises will reach for. M7 is fluency with Semantic Kernel as the agent-building primitive for Foundry-stack work.
weeks: Semantic Kernel fundamentals: kernels, plugins, planners, the function-calling pattern. The mental model differs from LangChain — read the docs and the sample repos. Build one kernel with three plugins (a date utility, a search wrapper, an internal API caller).

Multi-step agent patterns: the FunctionCallingStepwisePlanner, the Handlebars planner, custom planners. The "agent decides which tool to call next" pattern that turns SK from an LLM SDK into an agent framework.

Memory and context management: short-term memory (chat history), long-term memory (vector store integration with AI Search or Azure Cosmos DB), the patterns for managing context across conversation turns. Build one agent with persistent memory across sessions.

Process Framework (Semantic Kernel's Q4 2024 addition): structured multi-agent orchestration, the state machine model, multi-agent collaboration patterns. The most recent SK feature — exam-relevant if Microsoft adds agent questions to AI-102, client-relevant for advanced agent architectures.
months.gate: A Semantic Kernel agent built end-to-end with plugins, a planner, persistent memory, and at least one multi-agent orchestration via Process Framework. The agent framework on the Microsoft stack is now in your fingers, not just your reading list.

months.title: Azure ML — the deeper model layer
months.why: Azure OpenAI is the LLM service. Azure ML is the broader ML platform — custom model training, fine-tuning, model registry, real-time and batch endpoints. M8 is the Azure ML layer underneath AOAI for the cases where you need a custom model, a fine-tune, or a deployment pattern AOAI does not support.
weeks: Azure ML workspace and assets: workspaces (different from Foundry Hubs), models, environments, datasets, jobs. The asset model that lets you version everything that goes into a training run.

Fine-tuning patterns: when to fine-tune vs. when to prompt engineer (almost never the former). For Azure OpenAI, the fine-tuning workflow through Foundry. For open-source models, fine-tuning through Azure ML with proper compute clusters. Run one small fine-tune end-to-end so the workflow is real, not theoretical.

Model deployment patterns: managed online endpoints (real-time, auto-scaling), batch endpoints (high-throughput, scheduled), model serving on Azure Kubernetes Service for advanced cases. Deploy one custom model to a managed online endpoint.

MLflow integration: Azure ML uses MLflow as its tracking layer. Experiments, runs, model registry, the workflow that ties training to deployment. The pattern that makes ML reproducible at the engineering level the M9 governance work depends on.
months.gate: A custom model trained or fine-tuned via Azure ML, registered in the model registry with MLflow tracking, deployed to a managed online endpoint. The deeper ML layer beneath AOAI is operational, not abstract.

months.title: Enterprise governance, compliance, content safety
months.why: Enterprise Azure AI work runs under governance that consumer or startup AI work skips entirely. M9 is the governance layer most practitioners learn the hard way — through a client compliance review three months into an engagement. Better to learn it now.
weeks: Content safety in depth: Azure AI Content Safety (text, image, multimodal), Prompt Shields (direct + indirect prompt injection), groundedness detection, protected material detection. Configure each on a real deployment, test with adversarial inputs.

Responsible AI dashboard: Azure ML's tooling for fairness, error analysis, model interpretability, counterfactual analysis. The artifacts an enterprise responsible AI review will request. Build the dashboard for one deployed model and walk through it as if presenting to a compliance team.

Compliance frameworks on Azure: HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, ISO 27001, the EU AI Act considerations. Which Azure services are in-scope for each, what the shared responsibility model looks like. This is the conversation Daniel will need to have with regulated-industry clients — be the one who can have it.

Audit logging and Microsoft Purview integration: tracking who accessed which AI service, which prompts were sent, which data was retrieved. The forensic layer that compliance teams require and most AI deployments skip until forced.
months.gate: A documented enterprise governance posture applied to your M6 RAG system and M8 ML deployment: content safety configured, Responsible AI dashboard built, compliance framework alignment documented, audit logging tested. The compliance-ready pattern Daniel can present to regulated clients.

quarters.subtitle: AI-102 deepening, the architecture comparison published, the Microsoft AI engineer credential earned.

months.title: AI-102 deepening — the cert that validates the credential
months.why: The Copilot arc already targets AI-102 at M11 of its own track. This arc gives that cert real weight — instead of passing AI-102 on memorization, you pass it on the genuine engineering depth M1-M9 built. M10 is the exam prep window that turns nine months of Foundry work into the formal Microsoft credential.
weeks: AI-102 exam blueprint review: the four domains (Plan and manage an Azure AI solution, Implement decision support solutions, Implement language solutions, Implement generative AI solutions). Map each domain to the M1-M9 work — most of M1-M3 covers domain 1, M4-M6 covers domain 4, etc.

Microsoft Learn paths: complete the official AI-102 learning paths in Microsoft Learn. Most of the content will be review at this point, but the exam tests Microsoft-specific terminology that only the official content uses correctly.

Practice exams: at least three different practice exam sets, weak-area identification, hands-on remediation. Same diagnostic pattern as the GCP arc M10 — diagnostic first, drill the weak domains, retest.

Mock exam under conditions: full 60-question simulated exam in one sitting, scored honestly. If above 75%, schedule the real exam for early M11. If below 75%, one more week of remediation before scheduling.
months.gate: Three practice exams scored 75%+ on different days. Weak areas remediated with hands-on work in Foundry. Mock exam taken under simulated conditions and passed. Real exam scheduled.

months.title: Sit AI-102, publish the architecture comparison
months.why: M11 ships two things simultaneously — the cert sat and earned, and the architecture comparison that turns the cert into competitive positioning. "Copilot Studio vs. Azure AI Foundry — when to use which and why" is the artifact Intinc has needed and that no one outside Microsoft itself has published well.
weeks: Sit AI-102. Same workflow as the GCP arc M11 — schedule early in the week, sit it, document the post-exam experience immediately. Pass or fail, document specifically. Failure is recoverable; not learning from it is not.

Draft the architecture comparison: when does Copilot Studio win? When does Foundry win? The decision framework Intinc clients actually need: workflow complexity, governance requirements, team capability, total cost of ownership over 24 months. Specific examples from your Copilot arc and this arc.

Polish and publish: long-form post or Substack standalone, GitHub repo with the example Bicep templates and Prompt Flow YAML files (sanitized of any client-specific data), architecture diagrams. The artifact that makes Intinc a credible Microsoft AI partner, not just a Copilot reseller.

Distribution: cross-post in Microsoft AI community forums, submit to relevant Microsoft MVP-adjacent newsletters, share with Daniel and the Intinc team. Internal distribution matters as much as external — this is the artifact that changes how Daniel positions Intinc in Microsoft Partner conversations.
months.gate: AI-102 cert credential issued (or clear remediation plan with retake scheduled). Architecture comparison published with at least 2,000 views in the first month or one specific cited reference. Daniel has read it and given specific feedback on positioning.

months.title: AIaaS service line + year retrospective
months.why: Twelve months of Foundry work. The cert exists, the architecture comparison exists, the engineering credibility exists. M12 turns the work into business asset — a formal Intinc AIaaS service offering, a Microsoft Partner positioning conversation, and the retrospective that ties this arc to the Head of AIaaS pathway directly.
weeks: AIaaS service line definition: "Enterprise Foundry Implementation" or "Foundry-Based RAG Engagement" as a packaged Intinc offering. The deliverable, the format (8-12 week engagement), the price, the target client profile. Most Microsoft partners offer Copilot Studio implementations — few offer Foundry depth. That is the market.

First Foundry-based client engagement or pitch: pitch the service line to one Intinc client or warm prospect. The deliverable from M6 (RAG end-to-end) and M9 (governance posture) is the demonstrable artifact in the pitch.

Microsoft Partner positioning conversation with Daniel: not a status update, a strategic conversation. What does the Foundry depth add to Intinc's Microsoft Partner status? What additional Partner specializations or competencies should Intinc pursue? Is there an AI Solutions Partner designation worth targeting? The conversation that affects Intinc's 2-3 year Microsoft strategy.

Year retrospective: what changed in your engineering practice when Foundry became muscle memory? What does Y2 look like — deeper Azure ML specialization, multi-cloud AI architecture lead, formal AI Solutions Partner designation? The retrospective feeds the Personal Brand arc Q4 work and the AIaaS arc Q4 work simultaneously.
months.gate: A defined AIaaS Foundry service line. At least one Foundry-based pitch made (closed or pending). A documented strategic conversation with Daniel on Microsoft Partner positioning. Year retrospective published. The Microsoft AI engineer credential is now operational positioning, not just a credential.

eval.sub: 12 months. Eval becomes a first-class discipline rather than a byproduct. Golden dataset design as practice, LangSmith or Braintrust mastered, LLM-as-judge calibrated against human reference, CI/CD eval gates on every change, online drift detection, and a published playbook that turns the discipline into both brand asset and billable AIaaS service line.

quarters.subtitle: Eval mental model, dataset design as the highest-leverage skill, metrics fundamentals.

months.title: The discipline of evaluation — taxonomy and why
months.why: Your existing builds use eval implicitly: did the migration agent route this case correctly? Is the new prompt better? This arc makes eval a deliberate discipline. Most practitioners conflate "I tested it" with "I evaluated it." The difference is the methodology behind whether you can trust the answer when it changes.
weeks: Read the foundational material: Anthropic's evaluation cookbook, OpenAI's evals repo, the eval chapters of the major LLM textbooks. Take notes on the taxonomy: offline vs online, scalar vs preference, exact vs semantic, single-step vs trajectory. The vocabulary is the foundation for every later month.

The eval categories mapped: offline (run-against-fixed-dataset), online (score-production-traffic), A/B (compare-two-systems-on-same-input), human (manual-review), model-graded (LLM-as-judge). For each, write down one example from your existing builds where it would have caught a real failure.

Survey of tooling: LangSmith, Braintrust, Promptfoo, custom-built. For each, read the docs deeply enough to answer: what data model does it use? How does it integrate with your stack? What is the cost model? Don't pick yet — survey first.

The first eval audit: pick one production agent you have shipped (Bitwarden migration, Drive automation, or a Customization Service workflow). Without writing code, list every silent regression that would currently slip past you. The list is the case for the rest of the arc.
months.gate: A written eval taxonomy mapped to your existing builds. A documented audit of one production agent showing at least 5 silent regression risks that current testing does not catch. The case for eval as a discipline written in your own words.

months.title: Golden dataset design — the underrated highest-leverage skill
months.why: Most practitioners think "eval = pick LangSmith and run it." The actual value is in the dataset that captures the right edge cases. A great tool with a bad dataset measures nothing. A simple harness with a great dataset catches real regressions for years. M2 is where eval discipline either becomes serious or stays superficial.
weeks: Dataset sourcing: production logs (real distribution, real edge cases), synthetic generation (cheap volume, suspect realism), hand-curated (highest signal, lowest scale). Build one example dataset using all three sources for the same task. Compare what each catches and what each misses.

Edge case taxonomy: for any LLM task, the failure modes cluster — input length extremes, ambiguous queries, adversarial prompts, format violations, language mixing, malformed structured output. Build a checklist for each task category. Use the checklist to find the cases your current dataset is missing.

Dataset versioning: like code, with changelogs and reasoning. Every change to a golden dataset is a measurement system change. Build a v1 dataset for one task, then a v1.1 with three intentional additions. Document the reasoning for each addition. The versioning discipline matters as much as the dataset itself.

Holdout discipline: dev set for iteration, holdout set for unbiased measurement, never test against the holdout during development. The cardinal eval sin is leaking the holdout into your dev loop. Build the workflow that makes the leak structurally hard.
months.gate: A versioned golden dataset for one production agent task with at least 50 cases including edge cases derived from real production logs. Dev/holdout split documented with the workflow that prevents leakage.

months.title: Metrics fundamentals — what you measure, why, and the calibration problem
months.why: A metric is a measurement system. Bad metrics produce confident wrong answers — the worst possible outcome. This month you build the discipline of choosing the right metric for the task and validating that the metric correlates with what you actually care about.
weeks: Task-specific metrics survey: exact match, F1, BLEU, ROUGE, semantic similarity (embedding-based), structural validity (does the JSON parse?), executable correctness (does the code run?). For each, write down: when it works, when it fails, what kind of error it misses.

Production metrics: latency (p50, p95, p99), cost per request, error rate, hallucination rate (specifically), user satisfaction proxies. The metrics that matter for production are different from the metrics that matter for development. Map both layers.

The calibration problem: how do you know your metric is measuring the right thing? Build a small calibration study — for one task, score 30 examples with both your chosen metric and a human gold label. Compute the agreement. If it's below 70%, the metric is broken even if it produces clean numbers.

Metric composition: most useful eval signals are composite — a weighted score across multiple individual metrics. Build one composite metric for one task with documented weights and the reasoning. Pressure-test it against examples where individual metrics would mislead.
months.gate: Metric specifications documented for one production agent task — task-specific, production, and composite. Calibration study run against human labels with documented agreement rates. The metric is defensible, not just plausible.

quarters.subtitle: Platform mastered. First real eval suite shipping against production agents. LLM-as-judge calibrated.

months.title: Pick a platform — LangSmith vs Braintrust deep evaluation
months.why: After M1 surveying, M4 is the commit. LangSmith ties tightly into the LangChain ecosystem and prioritizes traces. Braintrust is more dataset-and-eval-first, framework-agnostic. Both are real tools. The pick matters less than the depth — most practitioners shop platforms forever and master none. This month you pick one and master it.
weeks: Decision framework: build a comparison matrix across the dimensions that matter for your work — tracing depth, dataset management, LLM-as-judge support, CI/CD integration, cost model, framework-agnostic vs LangChain-tied. Pick based on your stack, not on what other practitioners use.

Tracing setup: every model call in one production agent flows into the chosen platform with proper metadata — input, output, latency, cost, parent-child relationships for multi-step calls. The trace is the foundation; if traces are missing, evals built on top are blind.

Dataset creation in the platform: import the M2 golden dataset into LangSmith or Braintrust as a managed dataset. Connect to versioning. Run one experiment that produces scores. The first end-to-end run is the proof the platform setup is real.

Power-user mode: SDK depth, programmatic dataset management, custom evaluators, the API patterns that go beyond the UI. The UI is for exploration; the SDK is for the production discipline. Spend a week using only the SDK.
months.gate: One platform chosen with a written decision rationale. Traces flowing from one production agent. Datasets managed in the platform. One experiment run end-to-end producing scores. The SDK in your fingers, not just the UI.

months.title: First real eval suite — applied to one production agent
months.why: M1-M4 builds the foundation. M5 ships the first real eval suite. Pick one production agent — the Bitwarden migration agent, the Drive automation chain, or a Customization Service workflow — and build the eval harness that catches regressions on every change. This is the proof that the discipline works.
weeks: Define the eval contract for the chosen agent: what tasks does it perform, what should pass, what should fail, what edge cases are non-negotiable? Write the contract before writing the eval code. The contract is the spec.

Build the test cases: at least 30 covering the happy path, edge cases, adversarial inputs, format violations, and known historical bugs. Each test case includes input, expected output (or expected behavior), the metric used to score, and the rationale for inclusion.
Run baseline evals: score the current production agent against the suite. Document the baseline. The first baseline is the bar — every later change is measured against it.

Make one intentional change to the agent and re-run the suite. Did scores go up? Down? On which cases? The first time you see a regression you wouldn't have caught otherwise is the moment eval discipline earns its weight.
months.gate: A complete eval suite for one production agent with 30+ cases, documented baseline scores, and one demonstrated regression catch. The discipline is proven on a real artifact, not a tutorial example.

months.title: LLM-as-judge calibration — the hardest part of eval
months.why: For tasks without exact-match ground truth — open-ended generation, summarization, conversational quality — LLM-as-judge is often the only viable evaluator. It is also the easiest place to fool yourself. Bias, position effects, length preferences, and self-preference all corrupt the scores. This month you build a calibrated judge or you build evals that lie to you.
weeks: The judge taxonomy: pairwise (A vs B preference), scalar (1-10 score), rubric (structured criteria evaluation), reference-based (matches gold answer). For one task, build all four and run them on the same 30 examples. Compare the conclusions each draws — they often disagree, and the disagreement is the signal.

Bias diagnosis: position bias (judge prefers first answer), length bias (judge prefers longer), self-preference (judge prefers outputs from its own model family), verbosity-equals-quality. Run controlled experiments to detect each bias in your chosen judge configuration.

Calibration with human reference: hand-label 30 examples with the correct judgment, run the LLM judge on the same 30, compute agreement rate (Cohen's kappa or similar). If agreement is below 70%, the judge is unreliable. Iterate on the judge prompt until it climbs.

Multi-judge ensembles and disagreement as signal: when single judges are unreliable, ensembles of differently-prompted judges produce more stable scores. The cases where judges disagree are the cases worth human review. Build the disagreement-flagging workflow.
months.gate: A calibrated LLM-as-judge configuration for one open-ended task with documented bias diagnosis and at least 70% agreement with human reference labels. A disagreement-flagging workflow that surfaces the cases needing human review.

quarters.subtitle: Eval gates in CI/CD. Online eval and drift detection. Multi-agent trace evaluation.

months.title: CI/CD integration — eval gates on every change
months.why: Eval that runs only when you remember to run it is theater. Eval that runs automatically on every change is discipline. This month integrates the M5 eval suite into CI/CD so every PR is scored, every regression is caught before merge, and the eval becomes infrastructure rather than ritual.
weeks: CI/CD pipeline design: which evals run on every PR (fast, cheap, high-signal), which run nightly (expensive, comprehensive), which run weekly (full suite with human review). The cost-vs-coverage tradeoff has to be explicit — running everything everywhere is unaffordable.

GitHub Actions or Cloud Build integration: eval suite triggered by PR, results posted as a PR comment, threshold-based pass/fail. Build the workflow end-to-end. The first time a PR fails because of an eval regression is the cultural moment.

Threshold strategy: hard gates (regression beyond threshold blocks merge) vs soft gates (regression flagged but mergeable with reviewer override). Start with soft, move to hard after the team trusts the system. Hard gates on a noisy eval suite kill the team's trust faster than no gates.

Cost management: eval runs cost API spend. Track cost per PR, cost per merge, cost per month. The eval budget should be defensible — every dollar spent on eval is a dollar of debug time saved later, but the trade has to be visible.
months.gate: CI/CD pipeline running evals on every PR with documented threshold strategy. At least one PR has been blocked by an eval failure that the team agreed was correct. The cost per PR is tracked and within budget.

months.title: Online eval — scoring production traffic in real time
months.why: Offline evals catch regressions before deploy. Online evals catch the gap between dev distribution and production reality. The data your dev set didn't represent — the queries you didn't anticipate — only shows up in production. This month adds the online eval layer that watches production directly.
weeks: Sampling strategy: random sample of production traffic (cheap, broad coverage), anomaly-triggered (expensive, high-signal), user-flagged (highest signal, lowest volume). Pick a strategy and configure it. The right sampling rate balances cost against latency-of-detection.
Online judge configuration: the LLM-as-judge from M6 deployed against sampled production traffic. The traces flow into LangSmith or Braintrust with online scores attached. Set up the dashboards.

Drift detection and alerting: when online eval scores trend down, what triggers? Statistical drift detection on the score distribution, alerting threshold, the on-call workflow when drift fires. The first drift alert that isn't a false positive is the moment online eval earns its weight.

The drift runbook: alert fires → triage (is this real drift, or noise?) → root cause (model change, traffic shift, new data?) → decide (rollback, retrain, accept). Build the runbook before drift fires, not during.
months.gate: Online eval running against production traffic for at least one production agent. Drift detection configured with documented thresholds. A written runbook for "drift alert fired — what now." One drift event handled (real or simulated).

months.title: Multi-agent and trace-level evaluation
months.why: Most production agents are multi-step: tool calls, retrieval, multi-turn conversations, planning. Single-step eval misses the failures that emerge from agent trajectories. This month builds the harness for evaluating multi-step agents — the eval discipline that almost no practitioner has yet.
weeks: The trajectory eval problem: when an agent takes 5 steps to answer a question, where do you score? Per-step (catches local errors) vs end-to-end (catches global drift) vs a mix. Most production systems need both. Build the harness for both layers on one multi-step agent.
Per-step evaluation: tool call correctness, retrieval relevance, intermediate reasoning quality. Build evals for each component independently. The component evals catch class-of-failure early.

Trajectory evaluation: full-conversation outcome scoring, planning quality, recovery from intermediate errors. The trajectory eval is the integration test — does the whole thing work, given the parts work?

Agentic eval patterns: success rate at completing a goal, average steps to completion, error recovery rate, tool selection accuracy. The metrics that matter for agents are different from the metrics that matter for single-call models. Document the metrics for at least two agent types.
months.gate: A multi-agent eval harness covering per-step and trajectory-level evaluation on at least one production agent. Documented agent-specific metrics. The patterns are reusable for the next agent you eval, not just the first.

quarters.subtitle: The playbook drafted, public traces published, eval as an AIaaS service line, brand integration.

months.title: Second eval suite + the playbook drafted
months.why: One eval suite is a project. Two is a discipline. This month applies M5–M9 to a second production agent — different domain, different failure modes — and writes the playbook that captures the cross-cutting lessons. The second suite proves the practice generalizes; the playbook proves you can teach it.
weeks: Pick the second agent — different domain from the M5 agent. If M5 was the Bitwarden migration agent, M10 is the Drive automation chain or a Customization Service workflow. The domain difference is the test of generalization.
Apply the M2-M3 dataset and metric design to the new agent. Document what was reusable from M5 work and what was domain-specific. The reusability map is the heart of the playbook.

Build the second eval suite end-to-end: dataset, metrics, judge, CI/CD integration, online eval, trace evaluation. Faster than M5 because the patterns are now in your fingers. Document the velocity delta — how much faster is the second suite than the first?

Draft the playbook: the practitioner's guide to agentic evaluation. Sections for dataset design, metric selection, judge calibration, CI/CD integration, online eval, multi-agent eval. Specific examples from your two suites. Not academic — operational.
months.gate: A second eval suite shipping against a different production agent. A playbook draft of 5,000+ words covering dataset design, metrics, judges, CI/CD, online, and multi-agent eval. Velocity delta between suite 1 and suite 2 documented.

months.title: Public traces and the playbook published
months.why: The eval discipline is invisible work. The playbook and public traces make it visible. This month publishes the playbook, shares public LangSmith or Braintrust traces (with sensitive data redacted) that demonstrate the methodology, and turns the discipline into a brand asset that recruiters, clients, and Anthropic Partner Network actually see.
weeks: Trace curation: from your two eval suites, select 5–10 traces that best demonstrate methodology — not the cleanest results, the most pedagogically useful ones. Redact sensitive data. Add narrative annotations explaining why each trace matters.

Playbook polish: from M10 draft to publishable. Hire an editor or do three brutal self-edit passes. Add diagrams. Cut every section that summarizes content available elsewhere. What remains is the work nobody else has written.

Publish: LinkedIn long-form article series (3 parts), Prompt edition with the executive summary, GitHub repo with the example code and trace links, Partner Network profile updated to feature "agentic evaluation" as a named service offering.

Distribution: cross-post in relevant practitioner communities (LangChain, Braintrust user groups, ML Twitter/X if applicable), submit the playbook URL to relevant newsletters and aggregators, present the methodology at one external event (conference talk, meetup, podcast).
months.gate: A published agentic eval playbook of 5,000+ words. 5+ public traces with annotations. Partner Network profile updated. At least one external distribution venue (talk, podcast, newsletter feature).

months.title: Eval as a billable AIaaS service line + retrospective
months.why: Twelve months of eval discipline. The credential exists, the playbook exists, the proof exists. This month turns the practice into a business asset — a billable AIaaS service offering, a Partner Network differentiator, and the retrospective that ties the arc to the next year of work.
weeks: Service line definition: "Agentic Eval as a Service" as an Intinc/FlashFusion offering. The deliverable (eval suite + harness + runbook), the format (8-week engagement), the price, the target client. Most enterprises do not eval their AI systems — that is the market.

First paid engagement (or paid commitment): pitch the eval service line to one Intinc client or FlashFusion lead. Even a discounted first engagement is validation. The deliverable from M5 or M10 is the demonstrable artifact in the pitch.

Year retrospective: what changed in your engineering practice when eval became a discipline? What does the next 12 months look like — deeper specialization, broader teaching, an open-source eval framework? The retro feeds the Personal Brand arc Q4 work directly.

Cross-arc integration audit: the eval discipline applied retroactively to the Full-Stack arc apps, the GCP Vertex AI work, the MCP servers from the MCP Builder arc. By M12 you should have eval coverage across at least 5 production artifacts spanning multiple arcs.
months.gate: Eval-as-a-service line defined with at least one paid engagement (or paid commitment) closed. Year retrospective published. Eval coverage across 5+ production artifacts spanning multiple arcs. The discipline is now leverage, not just a credential.

voice.sub: 12 months. Text chat is the current paradigm. Voice is the next. The latency budget, the speech pipeline (ASR · LLM · TTS), the OpenAI Realtime API, Pipecat, WebRTC transport, three voice applications shipped, and a flagship voice product launched publicly with the methodology published as a productized service line.

quarters.subtitle: Latency budget, ASR, TTS — the three components of the speech pipeline mastered before the agent.

months.title: The latency budget — voice begins with milliseconds
months.why: Every other arc treats latency as a "make it fast enough" concern. Voice arcs treat it as the primary engineering constraint. Sub-700ms perceived turn latency is the bar — past 800ms a voice agent feels broken, past 1200ms users disengage entirely. This month establishes the budget mental model: VAD + ASR + LLM + TTS + network = your turn time, and every component competes for the same pool.
weeks: Audio fundamentals: sample rates (16kHz vs 24kHz vs 48kHz), encodings (PCM, Opus, MP3), the tradeoffs each makes for voice agents specifically. Build a spike that records, encodes, and plays back audio. Most voice work assumes 16kHz Opus — know why.

The latency budget exercise: map out a single turn from "user stops speaking" to "assistant starts speaking." Document every component (VAD ~50ms, ASR ~100-200ms, LLM ~200-400ms, TTS ~100-200ms, network ~50-150ms). Your sub-700ms target is the sum of these decisions.

VAD and end-of-turn detection: the underrated hard problem. Silero VAD setup, threshold tuning, the "is the user done speaking?" decision. Bad VAD cuts users off mid-sentence (worst) or waits 2 seconds for them to start over (almost as bad). Tune it on your own voice first.

Streaming Claude text output: the foundation for every voice agent that uses the pipeline approach (vs Realtime API). Server-sent events, partial completion handling, cancelable streams. Measure the time-to-first-token from your closest Anthropic region.
months.gate: A documented latency budget for one voice agent type with target milliseconds per component. Working VAD with tuned thresholds. Streaming Claude output with measured time-to-first-token. The numbers are real, not estimated.

months.title: ASR — speech-to-text, the input layer
months.why: The user's voice becomes text the LLM can reason over. Whisper is the obvious starting point but rarely the production answer for low-latency agents — Deepgram, Google, AssemblyAI all win on real-time transcription latency. This month is the input layer survey, decision, and integration.
weeks: Whisper API basics: synchronous transcription for testing, the cost model, the language support, the accuracy on noisy or accented speech. Build a spike with the OpenAI Whisper API and a self-hosted whisper.cpp variant. Compare latency.

Streaming ASR providers: Deepgram Nova (most popular for voice agents), OpenAI Realtime ASR, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text streaming, AssemblyAI. Pick one based on latency targets and cost. Most production voice agents under 800ms total latency use Deepgram.
Self-hosted vs API decision: at scale, self-hosted Whisper on a GPU can be cheaper than API calls. The break-even is usually 100k+ minutes per month. Document the decision tree for your use cases.

Partial transcript handling: streaming ASR produces hypothesis updates that change as the model gains confidence. The downstream LLM, the UI, and the end-of-turn logic all need to handle partial vs final transcripts. Build the abstraction once, reuse forever.
months.gate: A streaming ASR pipeline with measurable latency under 200ms time-to-first-partial. Partial transcript handling working end-to-end. Cost model documented for both API and self-hosted paths. Decision tree written for each use case type.

months.title: TTS — text-to-speech, the output layer
months.why: TTS is where voice agents either feel professional or feel like 2018 Alexa. Quality matters enormously — bad TTS loses users in the first 30 seconds.
