Latency matters too — streaming TTS that starts playing before the LLM finishes is the production pattern. This month chooses the voice and engineers the streaming.
weeks: TTS provider survey: ElevenLabs (highest quality, premium pricing), OpenAI TTS (good quality, moderate pricing), Cartesia Sonic (newer, fastest), Azure Speech (cheapest, good quality), Google Cloud TTS, self-hosted XTTS. For each, generate the same paragraph and compare quality, latency, cost.

Streaming TTS: the chunk-based generation pattern that lets audio start playing while text is still being generated by the LLM. Cartesia and ElevenLabs both support sub-100ms streaming. Build the streaming integration end-to-end on one provider.

Voice selection and consistency: stock voices vs custom cloned voices. Most enterprise deployments use stock voices for consent and compliance reasons. Pick one stock voice for testing and stick with it across the arc — voice consistency matters.

Audio playback patterns: queue-based playback for streaming TTS chunks, interruption handling (user starts talking — drop the queue, fade the audio), the audio buffer management that prevents stuttering. The hardest production engineering problem in voice agents.
months.gate: A streaming TTS pipeline with chunked output and proper queue management. Interruption handling tested with real user audio. Provider chosen with documented rationale. End-to-end audio quality validated on at least one external listener.

quarters.subtitle: OpenAI Realtime API, Pipecat framework, WebRTC transport — the production voice agent stack.

months.title: OpenAI Realtime API — speech-to-speech model
months.why: The Realtime API bypasses the ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline by directly accepting audio input and producing audio output. Lower latency (sub-300ms achievable), higher cost, less control over each component. This month is the deep evaluation: when does Realtime win vs the pipeline approach?
weeks: Realtime API basics: WebSocket connection, audio in/out streams, function calling, the session model. Build a spike that runs a real voice conversation through the Realtime API. Measure the actual latency vs your M1-M3 pipeline baseline.

Capabilities and limits: what Realtime does well (low latency, natural turn-taking, emotional prosody) and what it doesn't (multi-modal output, deep tool chains, fine-grained voice control, cost predictability at scale). Document the decision tree.

Cost analysis: Realtime API audio tokens cost significantly more than text tokens. For a 10-minute conversation, what's the actual bill? When does Realtime's latency advantage justify the cost premium, and when does the pipeline approach win economically?

Function calling in Realtime: voice agents that take actions (book meetings, query CRM, send messages) ship business value. Voice agents that only chat ship demos. Build one Realtime agent with at least 3 working function calls.
months.gate: A working voice conversation through the OpenAI Realtime API with at least 3 function calls. Measured latency vs M1-M3 pipeline baseline. Cost analysis for representative use cases. Decision tree for Realtime vs pipeline written.

months.title: Pipecat — the voice agent framework
months.why: Building voice agents from scratch means orchestrating ASR + LLM + TTS + VAD + transport + interrupt handling + session state. Pipecat (Daily.co's open-source framework) handles the orchestration so you focus on agent logic. Vocode is the alternative. Most production voice agents that need pipeline-level control use one of these.
weeks: Pipecat architecture: the pipeline model where frames flow through processors, the built-in components (Deepgram, Cartesia, Daily transport, ElevenLabs), the extension points for custom processors. Read the source — it is small enough to read end-to-end.

Wrap an existing agent in voice: take the Bitwarden migration agent, the Drive automation chain, or a Customization Service workflow. Keep the agent logic identical; add a voice interface using Pipecat. The agent logic stays; the interface changes.

Latency optimization in Pipecat: parallel ASR processing, streaming TTS, optimized turn-taking, prompt caching. Measure the latency before and after each optimization. The full optimization pass typically reduces perceived latency by 200-300ms.

Custom processors: when you need behavior not in the framework — a prompt rewriter, a guardrail check, a custom TTS wrapper. Build one custom processor end-to-end. The processor pattern is what makes Pipecat extensible without forking.
months.gate: A production-grade voice agent built on Pipecat wrapping an existing text agent. Sub-800ms perceived latency measured. At least one custom processor extending framework behavior. Latency optimization deltas documented.

months.title: WebRTC transport, telephony, deployment
months.why: A voice agent on your laptop is a demo. A voice agent in production needs WebRTC transport for browser/mobile users, telephony integration for phone calls, session management for disconnects, and real deployment with regional latency considerations. This is the production transport layer.
weeks: WebRTC fundamentals: ICE, STUN, TURN, the connection negotiation. Most voice agents use a managed service (LiveKit, Daily, Agora) rather than raw WebRTC — pick one and integrate. The 80/20 of production voice transport is choosing the right service, not building your own.

Telephony integration: Twilio Programmable Voice for inbound and outbound phone calls, the Stream API for connecting Twilio audio bidirectionally to your voice agent, SIP for enterprise PBX integration. The hardest production transport problem because PSTN audio is 8kHz and lossy.

Session management: handling disconnects, reconnects, conversation persistence across sessions. Voice sessions are typically short and ephemeral, but high-fidelity — losing context mid-call is worse than text agents losing context mid-conversation. Build the state model deliberately.

Deployment and regional latency: voice agents on Cloud Run, Fly.io (excellent for voice — low cold start, easy multi-region), or specialized infra. Multi-region deployment for global latency. Sub-700ms total budget means region selection contributes ~50-100ms — not negotiable.
months.gate: A voice agent deployed on managed WebRTC transport, accessible via web call. Telephony integration tested with a real phone number. Session management with disconnect/reconnect verified. Multi-region deployment plan documented with latency targets per region.

quarters.subtitle: Two real voice applications shipped. Production observability, safety, and compliance.

months.title: Application 1 — meeting assistant
months.why: The first real application. Meeting assistants — bots that join video calls, transcribe, extract action items, generate summaries — are one of the most common enterprise voice use cases and a strong first deliverable. Tests speaker diarization, real-time transcription, action item extraction, and structured output generation in one product.
weeks: Meeting bot architecture: how to get audio out of Zoom/Teams/Meet (recording APIs, bot participants like Recall.ai), the legal/consent layer for recording, the audio processing pipeline. Recall.ai handles the platform integration so you focus on the agent logic.

Real-time transcription with speaker attribution: who said what. Diarization is hard — Daily.co built-in, Pyannote for self-hosted, Deepgram with diarization mode. Pick one and integrate. False speaker attribution erodes trust faster than missing transcription.

Live action item detection: as the meeting progresses, detect commitments and assignments using LLM-as-extractor. The challenge: low false positive rate. False action items destroy trust faster than missing real ones. Calibrate against real meeting recordings before shipping.

Post-meeting structured summary: topic, decisions, action items with owner and due date, follow-ups, the format that makes the summary actually useful. Cross-reference with the Eval arc M2 dataset design — this is the kind of output that needs eval calibration.
months.gate: A working meeting assistant deployed and tested on at least 5 real meetings. Documented accuracy on action item extraction. Generated summaries reviewed by meeting participants and rated useful (or specific feedback collected on what was missed).

months.title: Application 2 — voice-first internal tool
months.why: Application 2 — an Intinc-internal voice-first tool for a workflow that genuinely benefits from being hands-free. Voice agents that replace text-based tools with no real benefit are demos. Voice agents that make a daily workflow faster or possible-while-driving are products. Pick the workflow that meets that bar.
weeks: Use case definition: pick one Intinc workflow where voice would genuinely be better than typing. "What's the status of [client]?" or "Schedule a follow-up with [contact] next Tuesday at 2pm." The workflow has to be simple enough for voice, common enough to justify the build, complete enough to ship.
Build the agent: voice interface, tool calls (CRM lookup, calendar API, ticketing system, internal Intinc systems), response patterns. Use Pipecat or Realtime API based on the M4 decision tree.

Real user deployment: one Intinc colleague uses it for a week of real work. Daily check-ins. What works? What breaks? What is genuinely faster than typing? What is annoying? The feedback loop is the value, not the build.

Iteration and v1.1: based on the week of use, ship v1.1 with the top three changes. Measure whether the changes moved the user's actual usage frequency. If they used it twice in week 1 and once in week 2 of v1.1, the product is not landing — re-scope before continuing.
months.gate: A voice-first internal tool deployed and used by one real Intinc user for a full week. Documented usage frequency, friction points, and iteration cycle. v1.1 shipped with measurable improvements.

months.title: Production hardening — observability, safety, compliance
months.why: Voice agents in production are different from text agents. Audio data has compliance implications (HIPAA, GDPR, recording consent). Latency monitoring is per-component, not per-request. Cost monitoring is critical because voice cost compounds fast — a poorly optimized agent burns hundreds of dollars per day at scale.
weeks: Observability for voice: per-turn latency tracking with component breakdown, per-call cost tracking, quality monitoring (audio dropouts, ASR confidence, TTS errors). Build the dashboards that show what is actually happening in production, not what you assume is happening.

Safety and content moderation: ASR captures everything users say, including PII. TTS generates everything the LLM produces, including potential hallucinations. Build the moderation layer for both directions — input scrubbing for PII, output filtering for harmful content. The Security Arc M2 work applied to audio.

Recording, consent, compliance: what gets recorded, who has access, retention policies, the consent flow. Two-party consent states require explicit notification at call start. HIPAA and GDPR considerations for healthcare and EU users. Document the compliance posture before regulators ask.

The voice agent runbook: alert thresholds for audio quality degradation, TTS provider failures, ASR transcript anomalies, latency spikes. The on-call playbook for "users report the agent sounds choppy" — most voice issues are latency or transport issues, not LLM issues.
months.gate: A voice agent in production with full observability dashboards. Safety moderation in both directions tested with adversarial inputs. Compliance posture documented. Production runbook covering the top 5 voice failure modes.

quarters.subtitle: The flagship voice product launched. Methodology published. Voice as a productized AIaaS service line.

months.title: Build the flagship voice product
months.why: M7 and M8 proved the pattern. M10 builds the flagship — the voice product worth being known for. Pick the highest-value use case from your work that has a real path to revenue or significant adoption. Go deep on the design, not just the technical build.
weeks: Pick the flagship use case: an internal Intinc tool that becomes a service line, a FlashFusion client tool that becomes a referenceable case study, or a public voice product targeting your security-first practitioner audience. The use case must have a path to either revenue or strategic positioning, not just technical demonstration.

Design before build: voice UX patterns specific to this product, agent personality, the failure mode recovery scripts (silence detection, interruption handling, off-topic recovery, repetition handling). Voice agents fail differently from text — the design has to anticipate the failure modes explicitly.

Build the spine: core agent logic, tool integrations, deployment infrastructure, end-to-end happy path working. By the end of week 3, the agent can complete its primary use case in real conditions with at least one real user.

Build the failure modes: the agent has to handle silence (user thinking? user gone? prompt them after 8 seconds), interruption (user starts talking — fade out, listen), off-topic (user asks something unrelated — graceful redirect), confusion (LLM produces something nonsensical — recovery message). Each failure mode is designed, not accidental.
months.gate: A flagship voice product end-to-end with documented failure mode recovery for at least 5 named scenarios. One real user beyond Kyle has used it for a real task. The product feels professional, not engineered.

months.title: Polish, latency optimization, production-grade
months.why: The flagship needs to feel professional. M11 is the optimization pass — every component measured, every latency hot path optimized, every interaction polished. The difference between "AI demo" and "AI product" is largely M11 work.
weeks: Latency optimization deep dive: measure every component end-to-end, identify the bottleneck, optimize it, re-measure. Iterate. Most voice agents have one component consuming 60% of perceived latency — find it, fix it. Common culprits: synchronous TTS waiting for full LLM response, ASR finalization delay, suboptimal region selection.

Voice quality optimization: TTS prompt tuning for natural delivery (proper pauses, emphasis, pacing), pronunciation handling for proper nouns and acronyms, the "this sounds like AI" tells that you can engineer out. Voice quality is harder to fix later than to build correctly.

Conversation design polish: every spoken word the agent says has been read aloud, edited, and tested. The system prompt, the tool descriptions, the error responses, the personality. Voice agents say their words out loud — wooden language is more obvious than in text.

Cost optimization: which API calls can be cached, which can be reduced, which model can be swapped for a smaller one. Voice cost compounds — a 5% per-turn cost reduction is 5% of every minute the agent runs. Document cost-per-minute as a tracked metric.
months.gate: Flagship voice agent at sub-700ms median perceived latency. Polished voice quality validated by external listeners. Documented cost-per-minute as a tracked metric. Production runbook updated with current performance baselines.

months.title: Launch, publish methodology, and the year retrospective
months.why: Twelve months of voice work. The flagship is built and polished. M12 is the public launch, the methodology publication that turns this arc into brand asset, and the retrospective that ties the arc to the next year of voice work — including the multimodal direction the field is moving.
weeks: Launch the flagship: ProductHunt for public products, internal launch at Intinc for company tools, client deployment for FlashFusion engagements. The launch is what turns the build into something that exists in the world rather than something on your laptop.

Publish the methodology: a long-form post or video about building production voice agents — the latency budget worksheet from M1, the framework decision tree from M4-M5, the production hardening checklist from M9, the cost optimization patterns from M11. The artifact other practitioners actually use.

Voice agent service offering: package the methodology as a productized AIaaS service line. "Build a production voice agent in 90 days" with a defined deliverable, defined price, defined client profile. The Partner Network listing updated to feature voice as a named capability.

Year retrospective: what changed in your understanding when voice became a paradigm? What does Y2 look like — multimodal agents, voice-first products, the agentic voice pattern (voice agents that take real-world actions autonomously)? The retro feeds the Personal Brand arc Q4 work.
months.gate: Flagship launched publicly. Methodology published with at least one external practitioner referencing it. Voice service line defined with at least one paid commitment. Year retrospective written and integrated into the Personal Brand arc Q4 retrospective.

strategy.sub: 12 months. From "I build AI systems" to "I advise on which AI systems to build." Discovery as a discipline, PRDs as starting moves, AI-specific metrics, roadmapping under uncertainty, audit deliverables, and the formal strategy advisory service line that turns thinking into billable revenue separate from implementation. The fastest path to the Head of AIaaS strategic layer.

quarters.subtitle: Product thinking as a distinct discipline, AI discovery methods, the artifact library.

months.title: Product thinking — the discipline most engineers underweight
months.why: You can build production AI systems. That is a different skill from deciding which AI systems to build, for whom, with what success criteria. Most engineers conflate "I would use this" with "users will value this" — the discipline of product thinking is the rigor that prevents the conflation. M1 is the foundation, learned deliberately rather than absorbed accidentally.
weeks: Read the core canon: "Inspired" (Cagan), "Continuous Discovery Habits" (Torres), "Lean Startup" (Ries) — the chapters on validated learning. Take notes on the frameworks: opportunity-solution tree, JTBD, problem-solution-validation. This is the vocabulary every later month uses.

Product vs. engineering thinking: the differences in default questions, success metrics, and time horizons. Engineers ask "can we build it?" PMs ask "should we build it, for whom, and how will we know it worked?" Build a side-by-side comparison from your own builds — what was the engineering answer vs. the product question that was actually missed?

AI-specific product thinking: what changes when the system is non-deterministic, when the cost model is per-token, when the user has to learn a new interaction paradigm. Most product frameworks assume deterministic systems — the AI adaptations are what separates "PM" from "AI PM."

The audit: pick three things you have built (Bitwarden migration, Drive automation, one Customization Service deliverable). For each, write the PRD you should have written before building. Notice every assumption you made that a PRD would have surfaced. The audit is the case for the rest of the arc.
months.gate: A documented framework for AI product thinking applied to three of your own past builds. The retrospective PRDs reveal at least five assumptions per build that the engineering work skipped. The case for product discipline is now written in your own examples.

months.title: Discovery — the work that happens before the build
months.why: Most AI engagements start with a solution ("build an agent that does X") and skip the discovery that would have produced a better question. M2 is the discovery toolkit — user interviews, JTBD, opportunity assessment — applied to AI specifically. The interviews that produce real signal rather than confirmation bias.
weeks: User interview methodology: the difference between leading and non-leading questions, the JTBD interview structure ("walk me through the last time you..."), the contextual inquiry pattern. Most engineers conduct user interviews badly — leading the witness, asking about features instead of problems. The methodology matters more than the willingness.

Run three real interviews: an Intinc internal user about an AI workflow, a Customization Service client about their actual problem, a CLC contact about how they think about AI. Not pitches, not feedback sessions — discovery interviews. Document what surprised you.

Opportunity-solution tree: Teresa Torres' framework for connecting business outcomes to user opportunities to solution experiments. Build one for a real Intinc AIaaS opportunity. The exercise of mapping opportunities first, solutions second, is the discipline that prevents premature solution lock-in.

Synthesis pattern: from three interviews to a single insight. The "what did we hear, what surprised us, what does it mean?" workflow. Most discovery dies at the data collection step — synthesis is what turns interviews into decisions. Build the pattern once on the real interviews from week 2.
months.gate: A complete opportunity-solution tree for one real AIaaS opportunity, built from three documented user interviews. The synthesis identifies at least one opportunity Daniel had not articulated and at least one solution candidate that was not yet on the table.

months.title: The PRD as a product artifact
months.why: Every AI product engagement should start with a PRD. Most do not — the work happens in conversation and Slack and gets reconstructed from memory three months in. M3 is the PRD as a deliberate artifact. The format, the depth, the audience, and the discipline of writing it before building rather than after explaining it.
weeks: PRD formats: the one-page PRD (Amazon working backwards), the structured PRD (Linear-style), the longer narrative PRD (Stripe-style). Each is right for different contexts. Build templates for all three. The template is not the PRD — the discipline of using it is.

AI-specific PRD sections: model selection rationale, latency requirements, cost-per-request modeling, evaluation criteria, failure modes and recovery, observability requirements, governance posture. These sections are not in standard PRD templates and they are the sections that prevent the worst engineering surprises.

Write a real PRD: for one current Intinc AIaaS opportunity or one Customization Service deliverable, write the PRD you would want before building. Test it against Daniel or the client — does it answer the questions a thoughtful stakeholder would ask? Iterate until it does.

PRD review patterns: the structured walkthrough, the silent reading + reactions pattern (Amazon-style), the assumption-challenge pass. Build the review protocol that catches gaps before the build, not after. The discipline of "let me push back on this PRD" is the moment product thinking earns its weight.
months.gate: A real PRD written for a real AIaaS opportunity, reviewed by at least one stakeholder, with documented changes from the review. PRD templates for three formats stored as reusable artifacts. The PRD discipline is now a starting move, not a retroactive explanation.

quarters.subtitle: AI-specific success metrics. AI roadmapping under uncertainty. The first strategy document.

months.title: AI metrics — defining what success means for non-deterministic systems
months.why: Standard product metrics (DAU, retention, conversion) translate badly to AI products. Was the agent's answer good? Did the user's job get done? Is the system getting better over time? M4 is the AI-specific metric layer — what to measure, how to define "good," and how to track quality improvement without conflating it with engagement.
weeks: AI metric taxonomy: outcome metrics (user job done), output metrics (quality of AI response), usage metrics (engagement with AI features), efficiency metrics (cost per task completed), quality drift metrics (is the system getting worse?). For each category, define one concrete metric for a real Intinc AIaaS use case.

The "AI success" problem: when the model produces good output that nobody uses, the AI failed at the product level even if it succeeded at the model level. Build the framework for diagnosing "is this an AI quality problem, a product fit problem, or an adoption problem?" Most "the AI isn't working" complaints are not AI quality complaints.

North-star and counter-metrics: every AI product needs both. North-star is the metric that defines success. Counter-metrics prevent the perverse incentives — "shorter responses" alone produces unhelpfully terse outputs; balance with "task completion rate" prevents it. Build north-star + counter for one real product.

Cross-arc tie: the Eval arc M3 metrics work covers engineering eval metrics. This month covers product metrics. Both layers needed; both layers different. Document the layer separation explicitly so the engineering team and the product team are not running different metrics for the same system.
months.gate: A documented AI metrics framework for one real AIaaS use case: outcome, output, usage, efficiency, and drift metrics defined. North-star + counter-metrics articulated. The product-vs-engineering metric layer distinction made explicit.

months.title: AI roadmapping under uncertainty
months.why: Traditional roadmapping assumes feature deterministic outcomes. AI roadmaps face two uncertainties most products do not: model capability uncertainty (will GPT-5 make this whole feature obsolete?) and user adoption uncertainty (will users actually use voice AI?). M5 is roadmapping discipline under these uncertainties.
weeks: Now-next-later roadmapping vs feature-list roadmapping: the format that survives the inevitable changes vs the one that needs constant updating. Build one now-next-later roadmap for an Intinc AIaaS service line. The format itself constrains overcommitting to dates.

Bet-sizing under model capability uncertainty: "what would change if Claude 5 doubles in capability?" vs "what would change if frontier model capability stalls?" The scenario planning that prevents over-investing in capability moats that will not last and under-investing in product moats that compound.

Adoption assumption surfacing: every roadmap has implicit adoption assumptions. "Users will pay for this" is an assumption, not a fact. Surface the assumptions, rate confidence in each, design validation work for the lowest-confidence ones. The roadmap that does not surface its assumptions is theatre.

The opportunity backlog: a prioritized list of opportunities (not solutions) for an AIaaS service line. Each with a brief, a confidence rating, and a "what would have to be true for this to be worth doing?" Document the top 10 opportunities; rank by WSJF (the prioritization framework you already use).
months.gate: A now-next-later roadmap for one Intinc AIaaS service line with explicit scenario planning, surfaced adoption assumptions, and a WSJF-prioritized opportunity backlog of at least 10 items. The roadmap is one Daniel can act on, not one that needs additional context to be useful.

months.title: The first strategy document
months.why: M1-M5 builds the toolkit. M6 ships the first real strategy document — a written artifact that takes a real AIaaS opportunity from problem space to recommended path. Not a PRD (that comes after strategy). Not a deck (that comes for the audience). The strategy document is the artifact that captures the thinking before either is needed.
weeks: Pick the opportunity: an Intinc AIaaS service line that does not yet have a strategy document, a Customization Service direction that needs explicit positioning, or a personal FlashFusion brand direction that needs strategy clarity. The opportunity has real stakes and a real decision-maker.

Draft the strategy document: problem statement, who experiences the problem, current alternatives, our differentiation, the bet we are making, what would have to be true for it to work, the path from current state to bet-validated. 5-10 pages, written in narrative prose, not slide-deck bullets.

Review and iterate: read it to Daniel (or the relevant stakeholder), capture every question, gap, and pushback. The questions are the diagnostic — they reveal the weak parts of the strategy. Iterate based on the questions, not the surface feedback.

Decision and commitment: the strategy document is not done until it produces a decision. Yes, we are pursuing this with these constraints. No, we are not pursuing this because of these reasons. The strategy document that does not lead to a decision was a writing exercise — push for the decision moment.
months.gate: A complete strategy document for a real AIaaS opportunity, reviewed by Daniel or the relevant decision-maker, with documented questions/gaps from review and a recorded decision outcome (proceed, defer, kill). The strategy artifact produced a strategic decision, not just a document.

quarters.subtitle: Multiple PRDs shipped. AI product audits. Advisory engagement patterns. Cross-arc product reviews.

months.title: Shipping multiple PRDs — the pattern that proves the discipline scales
months.why: M3 shipped one PRD. M7 ships three more in one month — different AI use cases, different stakeholders, different formats. The volume reveals which parts of the discipline transfer cleanly and which parts require domain-specific adaptation. The pattern that proves the practice scales, not just the example.
weeks: PRD #2: a fully-internal Intinc PRD — likely something around AI tooling, internal productivity, or operational efficiency. Different audience than the M3 client-facing PRD. Document the differences in format, depth, and stakeholder expectations.

PRD #3: a FlashFusion Customization Service deliverable PRD. Even though Customization Service is more execution than product, a real PRD before each engagement prevents scope creep and surface assumptions. Apply the discipline to the format Customization Service actually needs.

PRD #4: an external pitch PRD — for a prospect, not an existing client. The audience does not yet trust you. The PRD format and depth that builds credibility with a stranger differs from the format that works with Daniel. Adapt explicitly.

PRD review pass on all four: what transferred cleanly? What had to be adapted? Where is the discipline now muscle memory, and where does it still require deliberate effort? The retrospective is the calibration the next quarter's work builds on.
months.gate: Four real PRDs shipped across different contexts (M3 + three new in M7). Documented retrospective on what transferred and what required adaptation. The discipline is now demonstrably reusable, not a one-off output.

months.title: AI product audits — the advisory engagement pattern
months.why: Most AIaaS work is implementation. Higher-leverage work is advisory — the audit, the recommendation, the strategic critique that comes before the implementation. M8 builds the audit deliverable that lets you bill for thinking rather than building. The leverage shift that moves your hourly value substantially.
weeks: The audit format: scope (what we reviewed), method (how we reviewed it), findings (what we found), recommendations (what to do), priorities (what first), risks (what we cannot evaluate). The structure that produces actionable audits, not vague critiques.

AI-specific audit dimensions: model selection, prompt architecture, retrieval pattern (if RAG), evaluation discipline, observability layer, cost model, governance posture, scalability ceiling. Each dimension has specific questions to ask and specific failure patterns to look for.

Run a real audit: of one existing Intinc AI system (Copilot deployment, custom Foundry project, automation workflow) or one Customization Service deliverable. Apply the audit dimensions, write the findings, present to the system owner. The audit produces specific actionable items, not vague suggestions.

Audit as service line: package the audit deliverable as a billable Intinc/FlashFusion service. Format (1-2 weeks), price (defined by audit depth), deliverable (written report + presentation), follow-on (implementation engagement). The audit is the wedge into higher-value advisory work.
months.gate: A complete AI product audit delivered for one real system with documented findings and accepted recommendations. The audit packaged as a named billable service line with format, price, and deliverable defined.

months.title: Cross-arc product reviews — applying the discipline to your own portfolio
months.why: By M9 you have multiple arc artifacts in flight — Full-Stack apps, voice agents, edge AI deployments, MCP servers. Most practitioners ship these and move on. M9 applies the product discipline retroactively to your own portfolio — what does the product layer look like for each, and where are the gaps the engineering work skipped?
weeks: Portfolio inventory: list every "product" you have shipped across all arcs in the past 12 months. Full-Stack apps, voice agents, edge AI deployments, MCP servers, Customization Service deliverables. Each gets a product audit treatment in this month.

Product audits, applied: for each portfolio item, the audit dimensions from M8 applied. Where is the product layer thin? Where is the user understanding shallow? Where are success metrics undefined? The discipline applied to your own work reveals what you would have caught earlier with M1-M3 in place.

Cross-arc product roadmap: which portfolio items are worth deepening? Which are worth retiring? Which need product layer rebuild even if the engineering layer is solid? The roadmap that turns scattered builds into a coherent portfolio.

The PM-self conversation: the documented retrospective on what changed in your engineering work when product discipline arrived. Where did you make different decisions than you would have without M1-M3? Where do you still default to engineering thinking? The honest self-assessment that calibrates Y2 work.
months.gate: Product audits completed for at least 5 portfolio items spanning multiple arcs. A cross-arc product roadmap identifying which to deepen, retire, or rebuild. A written self-assessment of how product discipline changed engineering decisions over the prior 12 months.

quarters.subtitle: The strategy advisory service line. Internal Intinc positioning. The published framework.

months.title: The strategy advisory service line — packaged and priced
months.why: Twelve months of strategy work. M10 turns the practice into a formal Intinc/FlashFusion service line — packaged, priced, marketed, sold. The advisory layer that lets Intinc bill for thinking before building, which is where the higher-leverage revenue lives.
weeks: Service line definition: "AI Strategy Advisory" with three tiers — 1-day strategic workshop, 1-week strategy sprint, 4-week strategy engagement. Each with defined scope, deliverable, price, target client profile. The packaged service that turns advisory from "we also do strategy" into a primary offering.

Pitch materials: a one-pager for each tier, a deck template, a sample deliverable (sanitized from M6 or M9 work). The materials a Daniel or a prospect can use to evaluate the service offering without needing additional context from you.

First strategy advisory engagement (or paid pitch): pitch the service line to one warm prospect or close one internal Intinc engagement. The first dollar of advisory-only revenue validates the service line, even if it is a discounted introductory engagement.

Pricing validation: what do comparable AI strategy advisory engagements cost from competing consultants and firms? Adjust if you are more than 30% off market without a reason you can articulate. The price signals positioning as much as it signals revenue.
months.gate: A formally defined AI Strategy Advisory service line with three tiers, pricing, deliverables, and pitch materials. At least one paid advisory engagement closed (or paid commitment received). The service line is now generating revenue separately from implementation work.

months.title: Internal Intinc positioning + Head of AIaaS pathway
months.why: The Head of AIaaS pathway is partly about credentials (which this arc and the others produce) and partly about internal positioning (which has to be deliberate, not assumed). M11 is the conversation series with Daniel, Dave, and Jackie that positions you for the role rather than waiting to be considered for it.
weeks: Strategy briefing for Daniel: a formal presentation of the AIaaS strategic landscape — current state, opportunities, recommended bets, what Intinc would have to commit to for each. Not a status update, a strategic document delivered as the kind of brief a Head of AIaaS would deliver to a leadership team.

Cross-functional positioning: similar briefings adapted for Dave and Jackie. Each cares about different things — operational fit, financial model, client implications. The same strategic content, three different presentations, three different conversations. Run them in the same week.

The Head of AIaaS conversation: the explicit conversation with Daniel about the path to the role. What evidence does he need? What additional credentials, engagements, or experience? What is the realistic timeline? Get the answer in writing, not assumed. The conversation is the path; the silence is not.

Personal brand integration: the strategy advisory work and the Head of AIaaS conversation become content for the Personal Brand arc Q4 work. The published reflections, the LinkedIn posts about advisory practice, the Prompt edition on AIaaS strategy. The brand work that signals the role before the title.
months.gate: Strategic briefings delivered to Daniel, Dave, and Jackie. A documented Head of AIaaS conversation with Daniel including required evidence, timeline, and decision criteria. Personal brand content drafted that signals the strategic positioning publicly.

months.title: The published framework + year retrospective
months.why: M12 publishes the framework that compresses the year of strategy work into a reusable artifact. "Building AI Products: A Practitioner's Framework" or similar — the published artifact that turns the practice into brand asset and influences how other practitioners think about AI product strategy.
weeks: Draft the framework: the discovery-to-decision workflow for AI products, the PRD adaptations for AI specifically, the metric framework, the roadmapping under capability uncertainty, the audit dimensions. The intellectual content of the year compressed into a usable artifact.

Polish and publish: long-form post or Substack standalone, GitHub repo with PRD templates and audit checklists, slide deck for the framework that can be delivered as a talk. The artifact other practitioners reference when thinking about AI product strategy.

Distribution: cross-post in relevant practitioner communities (Mind the Product, Product School AI track, Pragmatic Engineer audience), submit to relevant newsletters, present the framework at one external venue (conference talk, podcast guest, internal Intinc all-hands).

Year retrospective: what changed in your understanding when strategy became a discipline? What does Y2 look like — deeper specialization in regulated-industry AI strategy, formal product leadership role, or expanded advisory practice? The retrospective is the year's closing artifact and the bridge to whatever comes next.
months.gate: The AI product strategy framework published with at least one external distribution venue secured. Year retrospective written and integrated into Personal Brand arc and AIaaS arc Q4 work. The advisory practice is now demonstrable on a public artifact, not just engagement history.

cloudflare.sub: 12 months. Past webhook relays into production edge AI infrastructure. Workers AI, Vectorize, D1, R2, AI Gateway, Durable Objects, Workflows, Queues. Five production deployments shipped. The "AI at the Edge" architecture guide published. Cloudflare AI added as a named capability on the Partner Network listing.

quarters.subtitle: Workers deeper, the storage primitives, Workers AI + AI Gateway as the inference layer.

months.title: Workers deeper — past webhook relays into production patterns
months.why: You already use Cloudflare Workers for webhook relays and proxy patterns. That use is a fraction of what Workers actually is. This month is the upgrade from "I can deploy a Worker" to "I can architect production systems on the Workers runtime" — TypeScript discipline, observability, secrets management, and the constraint-aware design that edge runtime requires.
weeks: Workers in TypeScript: wrangler with TypeScript scaffolding, types for env bindings, the development loop with wrangler dev. Most production Workers are TypeScript — vanilla JS is fine for spikes but harder to maintain past the first 200 lines. Migrate one of your existing Workers to TypeScript.

Edge runtime constraints as design principles: CPU time per request (10ms free, 50ms paid bundled, longer with paid unbound), no Node.js APIs (use Web APIs or Cloudflare-specific bindings), request-scoped lifecycle (no persistent state between requests). These constrain the design — they are not bugs to work around.

Secrets, environment variables, and bindings: wrangler secret put, environment-specific config, the bindings model (env.AI, env.DB, env.VECTORIZE) that injects services into Workers. Secrets management is more deliberate at the edge than in long-running services.

Observability and debugging: wrangler tail for live logs, Workers Analytics Engine for metrics, Logpush for shipping logs to your aggregator. Edge debugging is harder than centralized debugging because every edge node is its own runtime — observability is non-optional.
months.gate: A Worker deployed in TypeScript with proper bindings, secrets management, and structured logging shipping to an aggregator. Constraint awareness documented — what your design assumes about CPU time, memory, and request lifecycle.

months.title: Storage primitives — D1, R2, KV — when each is right
months.why: Cloudflare has three storage primitives plus Vectorize. Choosing wrong burns a quarter rebuilding. D1 is SQLite-as-a-service for relational workloads. R2 is S3-compatible blob storage with no egress fees. KV is eventually consistent key-value for read-heavy caching. This month is the decision tree internalized through real builds, not docs.
weeks: D1 deep dive: SQLite-based, replicated read replicas, the migration model with wrangler d1 migrations, the limits (10GB per database currently, adjust to actual at the time of building). Build a small CRUD app on D1 with proper migrations. The relational answer for most edge apps under 10GB.

R2 deep dive: S3-compatible API, no egress fees (the actual differentiator from S3), public buckets with custom domains, lifecycle policies. Build one service that uploads and serves files via R2. The storage layer for AI training data, model artifacts, and generated outputs.

KV deep dive: eventually consistent, optimized for high-read workloads, the latency characteristics (writes propagate within 60 seconds globally). KV is wrong for transactional data and right for cached config, session tokens, and feature flags. Build one service that uses KV correctly.

The decision tree: when to use each storage primitive. Build a one-page reference document with concrete examples — "Bitwarden migration metadata: D1 (relational, transactional). User-uploaded files: R2 (binary, no egress). Cached API responses: KV (read-heavy, tolerant of staleness)." The reference becomes muscle memory.
months.gate: Three small services demonstrating D1, R2, and KV in their right contexts. A documented decision tree for storage primitive selection. Migration discipline working for D1 (apply, rollback, redeploy in under 5 minutes).

months.title: Workers AI + AI Gateway — the inference layer
months.why: Workers AI is Cloudflare's managed inference platform — Llama, Mistral, Whisper, embedding models, image models. Pricing is per-token-equivalent, often cheaper than OpenAI/Anthropic for comparable open-source models. AI Gateway sits in front of any AI provider (Workers AI, OpenAI, Anthropic) and adds caching, rate limiting, observability, fallbacks. Together they are the inference control plane.
weeks: Workers AI capabilities survey: text generation models (Llama 3, Mistral), embedding models (BGE, E5), Whisper for transcription, image models for generation and analysis. Build one spike calling each model type. Note latency from your closest Cloudflare PoP.

Workers AI cost vs API providers: Llama 3.1 8B on Workers AI vs Claude Haiku vs GPT-4o-mini. For each, run the same evaluation prompt 100 times and document cost, latency, and quality. The cost-quality tradeoff is real and use-case-specific.

AI Gateway setup: a gateway in front of Workers AI, Claude, and OpenAI. Caching configuration, rate limiting per user/IP, observability dashboards. AI Gateway makes multi-provider AI architecture cheap to implement — the abstraction other arcs assume but rarely build.

Fallback patterns through AI Gateway: if Claude is unavailable, fall back to GPT-4o-mini; if both unavailable, fall back to Workers AI Llama. The reliability pattern that turns AI from "single point of failure" to "graceful degradation."
months.gate: Workers AI integrated with at least 3 model types tested for your use cases. AI Gateway in front of multi-provider AI with caching, rate limiting, and fallback configured. Cost comparison documented across providers for one representative workload.

quarters.subtitle: Vectorize mastered. Edge RAG patterns. First production edge AI app shipped.

months.title: Vectorize — Cloudflare's vector database
months.why: Vector DBs at centralized providers (Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud, Weaviate) add latency to every retrieval — 100-200ms minimum. Vectorize runs at the edge with sub-30ms retrieval. For latency-sensitive RAG and semantic search, edge vector DB changes the architecture. This month is Vectorize fluency.
weeks: Vectorize fundamentals: index creation, dimension specification, metric selection (cosine, dot product, euclidean), the wrangler vectorize commands. Build one index with a small dataset. Note the dimensions and metric tradeoffs.

Embedding generation strategies: Workers AI embedding models (BGE-small, E5) for in-platform generation, OpenAI/Cohere/Voyage embeddings for higher quality. The cost vs quality vs latency tradeoff for embeddings is different from the LLM tradeoff. Build one of each pattern.

Hybrid search patterns: Vectorize for semantic similarity + D1 full-text search for keyword matching. The combined retrieval pattern that outperforms either alone for most production RAG. Implement the hybrid retrieval and benchmark against pure vector search.

Vectorize at scale: index size limits, query throughput, the cost model. Vectorize is priced per-query and per-stored-vector — at large scale the math differs from self-hosted alternatives. Document the break-even points for your likely use cases.
months.gate: A working Vectorize index with embeddings generated via at least two providers compared. Hybrid search (vector + full-text) pattern implemented and benchmarked against pure vector search. Cost model documented for scaling scenarios.

months.title: Edge RAG — sub-50ms retrieval + generation
months.why: Most RAG systems run with 200-500ms time-to-first-token because retrieval happens at a centralized DB and generation happens at a centralized model. Edge RAG runs both at the edge — Vectorize retrieval (sub-30ms) + Workers AI generation (sub-100ms first token) = a different architecture entirely. This month builds the edge RAG pattern that almost no practitioner has built well yet.
weeks: The edge RAG architecture: ingestion pipeline (offline, runs anywhere), retrieval at the edge (Vectorize), generation at the edge (Workers AI or AI Gateway to Anthropic). Build the architecture diagram and identify the latency budget for each component.

Ingestion pipeline: documents → chunking → embedding → Vectorize index. The ingestion can run offline on any platform; only the serving runs at the edge. Build one pipeline that ingests a real document corpus (Intinc internal docs, your existing project documentation, or a public dataset).

Retrieval pattern: query → embedding → Vectorize search → re-ranking (if needed) → context assembly. Measure end-to-end retrieval latency from at least three geographic locations. The latency win over centralized vector DB should be visible.

Generation pattern: assembled context + user query → Workers AI or AI Gateway → streaming response back to the user. End-to-end edge RAG measured at sub-700ms time-to-first-token. The architecture that makes RAG feel instant rather than laggy.
months.gate: A working edge RAG system end-to-end with measured sub-700ms time-to-first-token from three geographic locations. Documented architecture with latency budget per component. Comparison against centralized RAG showing the latency delta.

months.title: First production edge AI app
months.why: M1-M5 builds the foundation. M6 ships the first real production app on the edge AI stack. Pick a use case where edge latency genuinely matters — internal tool that runs everywhere, public-facing semantic search, AI middleware that wraps an existing API. The use case must justify the edge architecture, not just deploy to it.
weeks: Pick the use case: an internal Intinc tool that benefits from low latency globally, a Customization Service deliverable that needs sub-100ms response times, a public AI middleware product. The latency advantage must be the differentiator, not an afterthought.

Architecture and build: combining M1-M5 components into one production app. Workers + D1 + Vectorize + Workers AI + AI Gateway working together. The architecture is the product — the choices about which primitive does what define the system.

Deployment and observability: production deployment with proper environment management (dev, staging, prod), Workers Analytics Engine dashboards, error tracking, cost monitoring. Edge cost is per-request — track it per-feature to know where the spend goes.

First user and iteration: deploy to one real user (Intinc colleague, FlashFusion client, or one external user). Measure usage, gather feedback, ship v1.1. The iteration cycle proves the edge stack works for real workloads, not just demos.
months.gate: A first production edge AI app deployed and used by at least one real user. Documented architecture with measured latency. Cost-per-request tracked. v1.1 shipped based on real feedback.

quarters.subtitle: Durable Objects, Workflows, Queues, AI middleware patterns — the advanced edge primitives.

months.title: Durable Objects — stateful coordination at the edge
months.why: Workers are stateless by design. Durable Objects are the escape hatch when stateful coordination is required — chat rooms, real-time multi-user state, agent session management, rate limiters that need consistency. Durable Objects are the most powerful and most misunderstood Cloudflare primitive. This month makes them muscle memory.
weeks: Durable Objects fundamentals: the actor model, single-instance consistency, the storage API, the lifecycle (sleep, wake, eviction). Most edge developers never reach for Durable Objects because the mental model is unfamiliar. Build one DO that maintains a counter across requests.

Real-time patterns with WebSockets: a chat room or live collaboration session backed by a Durable Object. WebSocket hibernation for connections that idle. The pattern that makes real-time AI agents possible at the edge.

Agent session management: a voice agent or chat agent backed by one Durable Object per session. The DO holds conversation state, tool call history, and session metadata. The pattern that makes the Voice arc M6 deployment patterns work at the edge.

Rate limiting and quota enforcement: per-user rate limits backed by Durable Objects (consistent, exact) vs KV (eventually consistent, approximate). When each is appropriate. Build one strict-consistency rate limiter using Durable Objects.
months.gate: At least three Durable Objects implementations covering counter/state, real-time WebSockets, and agent session management. The patterns documented as reusable templates. The mental model is in your fingers, not just the docs.

months.title: Workflows + Queues — durable async work at the edge
months.why: Workers run for milliseconds. Real systems often need work that runs for minutes, hours, or days — document processing, model retraining triggers, batch operations, multi-step agent flows. Cloudflare Workflows (durable execution) and Queues (message-based async) are the answer. This month is the async layer.
weeks: Cloudflare Workflows fundamentals: durable execution, automatic retries, sleep/wait primitives, the programming model. Workflows is Cloudflare's answer to Temporal — long-running work with guaranteed completion, but with edge-native pricing and integration.

Build a multi-step workflow: document ingestion that runs across hours — chunk, embed, index, summarize, notify. Each step is a durable function that survives Worker restarts and platform failures. The pattern that makes batch ML pipelines at the edge possible.

Cloudflare Queues: message-based async with FIFO ordering, batch consumption, dead-letter queues. The pattern for "this work needs to happen but does not need to happen synchronously." Build one Queue-backed service that processes events asynchronously.

Workflows vs Queues vs Durable Objects: the decision tree. Each solves a different async problem. Durable Objects: stateful coordination. Queues: message-based async. Workflows: long-running multi-step durable execution. Document when each is right with concrete examples from your work.
months.gate: One Workflows-based multi-step pipeline running end-to-end. One Queues-based async service. A decision tree document for choosing between Workflows, Queues, and Durable Objects with concrete examples.

months.title: AI middleware patterns — the edge as control plane
months.why: Cloudflare's most underused capability for AI is as middleware — the layer that sits between client and AI provider, adding auth, caching, rate limiting, transformations, fallbacks, and observability. AI middleware at the edge runs in front of every AI request without latency penalty. This month is the middleware patterns that turn the edge into the AI control plane.
weeks: Authentication middleware: Workers in front of AI APIs that handle auth, user identification, quota enforcement before forwarding to the upstream AI provider. The pattern that prevents API key leakage and enables per-user quota.

Caching middleware: AI Gateway caching for deterministic prompts, custom Worker caching for semi-deterministic patterns, the cache hit rate optimization. Real-world caching can reduce AI cost by 30-50% on production workloads — most practitioners under-implement this.

Transformation middleware: Workers that intercept AI requests and responses to add system prompts, redact PII, enforce output formats, or apply guardrails. The "every AI request goes through our quality gate" pattern that makes safety policies enforceable at infrastructure level.

Fallback and circuit-breaker middleware: when the upstream AI fails or is slow, route to a backup. AI Gateway handles basic fallbacks; advanced patterns (model selection based on prompt complexity, cost optimization based on user tier) require custom Workers. Build the advanced version.
months.gate: A complete AI middleware layer deployed: auth, caching, transformation, and fallback. Measurable cache hit rate, documented fallback behavior, observable PII redaction. The middleware is reusable across multiple AI applications, not coupled to one.

quarters.subtitle: Five production deployments. Optimization pass. "AI at the Edge" architecture guide published.

months.title: Build the flagship — five production Workers AI deployments
months.why: M6 shipped the first production edge AI app. By M10 the goal is five total production deployments — different use cases, different patterns, all running at the edge. Five is the number that proves the patterns generalize. The goal is breadth across the edge AI stack, not one polished demo.
weeks: Inventory existing deployments: M3 Workers AI work, M5 edge RAG, M6 first production app. That is three. M10 needs two more. Pick two use cases that exercise patterns not yet shipped — maybe a Workflows-based batch pipeline and an AI middleware proxy.

Build deployment 4: a use case that exercises Workflows + Workers AI for a real batch processing pipeline. Document ingestion, summary generation across thousands of documents, scheduled retraining triggers. The pattern Cloudflare's edge async makes possible.

Build deployment 5: an AI middleware proxy that sits in front of Anthropic and OpenAI for a real client or internal use case. Auth, caching, transformation, fallback all working. The deployment that proves the M9 middleware patterns work in production.

Cross-deployment observability: a unified dashboard showing health, latency, and cost across all five deployments. The pattern that makes operating multiple edge AI apps tractable rather than chaotic.
months.gate: Five production Workers AI deployments live. Cross-deployment observability dashboard. Each deployment exercises a different pattern (inference-only, RAG, stateful, async, middleware). The breadth is the proof the patterns generalize.

months.title: Performance, observability, cost optimization
months.why: Five production deployments running. Some are fast and cheap; others are likely neither. M11 is the optimization pass — measure everything, optimize the hot paths, control the cost. Edge cost compounds differently than centralized cost; per-request economics demand different discipline.
weeks: Latency optimization across all five: measure p50, p95, p99 for each. Identify the slowest deployment and the slowest path within it. Optimize one component at a time, re-measure, document the delta. The edge advantage is sub-100ms — anywhere a deployment exceeds 200ms is an optimization target.

Cost optimization: per-deployment cost analysis, identifying the most expensive call patterns, applying AI Gateway caching where caching hit rate could be high. Workers AI cost vs API provider cost — for each deployment, is the cheapest model still good enough?

Observability deepening: structured logging, distributed tracing across multi-service deployments, alert thresholds that fire before users notice. The "we know there's an issue before the user reports it" capability that distinguishes production-grade from demo-grade.

Documentation: every deployment has a README with architecture, key decisions, runbook for common failures, cost expectations. The documentation that lets a future-you (or a teammate) maintain the system without rediscovering everything.
months.gate: All five deployments meeting documented latency and cost targets. Observability dashboards alerting before issues become user-visible. Each deployment has a complete README with architecture, runbook, and cost model. The production-grade bar is met across the portfolio.

months.title: Publish "AI at the Edge" guide and brand integration
months.why: Twelve months of edge AI work. Five production deployments. The published architecture guide is what turns the body of work into brand asset. "AI at the Edge: When and how to choose Cloudflare for AI workloads" is the artifact that joins the Partner Network listing and gets cited by other practitioners building in the same space.
weeks: Draft the architecture guide: when does edge AI win? When does it lose? The decision framework other practitioners need: workload latency requirements, geographic distribution, cost model, vendor lock-in considerations. Specific examples from your five deployments.

Polish and publish: long-form post or Substack standalone, GitHub repo with the example code from your deployments (sanitized), architecture diagrams. Cross-link to the Partner Network profile and the AIaaS service offerings.

Cloudflare community presence: contribute to the Workers Discord, answer questions on the Cloudflare community forums, submit a talk to a Workers community event or Cloudflare Connect. The presence that turns "I built things on Workers" into "I am known in the Workers community."

Year retrospective: what changed in your understanding when edge became a paradigm? What does Y2 look like — deeper specialization in one Cloudflare service, contribution to open-source Cloudflare tooling, or branching into edge ML training (Constellation)? The retro feeds the Personal Brand arc Q4 work.
months.gate: The "AI at the Edge" architecture guide published. GitHub repo with example code public. Active presence in Cloudflare community (Discord/forums/event submission). Cloudflare AI stack added to the Partner Network capability listing. The arc work is now leverage, not just deployments.

book.sub: 12 months. One book chosen at M1 — memoir or practitioner, never both. Spine, structure, sample chapters in Q1. Full manuscript first draft in Q2. Two structural edits and professional review in Q3. Publication path decided. Final production locked in Q4. The book exists in the world as a real artifact by M12, with sustained distribution and a written Y2 plan.

quarters.subtitle: The fork decision. Structure. First chapters drafted to publishable quality.

months.title: The fork — memoir or practitioner book
months.why: The single most common reason book projects fail is not lack of skill or time — it is the practitioner trying to write two books at once. The memoir and the practitioner book serve different audiences, require different voices, and live in different markets. M1 forces the irreversible choice that makes the next 11 months possible. Picking is the work.
weeks: The audit: read the existing memoir draft and the existing practitioner notes side by side. Which one has more pages? Which one has more energy? Which one would you regret not finishing in three years? The answers usually surprise you. Write them down.

The market test: for each candidate book, write a one-paragraph pitch and send it to three readers. The memoir pitch to three people who knew Phillis or the era. The practitioner pitch to three peers or potential readers. Watch which responses are genuine vs polite — the gap is real signal.

The constraint test: for each candidate, define what success looks like at M12. Memoir success — published, reviewed by people who knew the story, the diagnostic-instinct spine landed cleanly. Practitioner success — shipped, creates Partner Network pull-through, the central framework cited by name. Specific and dated.

Make the decision. Write it down. Date it. The decision document goes into your project files and becomes the reference for every "should I include this?" moment over the next 11 months. The other book is explicitly deferred to Y2+ with no shame and no exception clauses.
months.gate: One book chosen with documented reasoning, market-test responses, and M12 success criteria. The deferred book is named and dated as a Y2+ commitment. The fork is closed.

months.title: Structure — spine, chapter map, voice, sample
months.why: Most book drafts that stall do so because the structure was never solidified. Writing chapter 3 before knowing what chapter 7 contains produces chapter 3 that does not earn its place. M2 is the structural blueprint — boring to produce, expensive to skip. The book is built on this skeleton.
weeks: The spine — the single sentence the entire book serves. For memoir: "Construction, Not Recovery" as the diagnostic-instinct engine of a built life. For practitioner: the central framework that organizes everything else. Write it. Test it against three readers. Refine until they paraphrase it back correctly.

Chapter map — title, 2-3 sentence summary, target length, the role each chapter plays in advancing the spine. Memoir: typically 12-18 chapters at 4-6K words. Practitioner: typically 8-12 chapters at 5-8K words. Do not write — just map.

Voice and reader spec — explicit definition of who reads this and what voice meets them. For memoir: who and why does the story matter to them? For practitioner: which stage of practitioner does this book serve and what voice earns their attention? Written specification, not vibes.

One sample chapter — not chapter 1, which carries the opening burden. Pick one from the middle. 5-8K words at target quality. The first chapter you write tells you whether the spine, structure, voice, and reader are all working. Adjust the structural spec based on what the writing reveals.
months.gate: Full chapter map with per-chapter spine role. Voice and reader specification written. One sample chapter drafted at publishable quality. The structural foundation is real, not theoretical.

months.title: First three chapters polished to sample-quality
months.why: M2 produced one chapter. M3 produces three at the same quality. Three chapters is what an agent or acquisitions editor wants to see; three chapters is what a self-publication launch needs as proof; three chapters is the volume at which voice consistency becomes a real discipline. The Q1 output is a sample package, not just a draft.
weeks: Chapter A — pick the chapter that most directly carries the spine. Draft to first-pass quality, ~5-8K words. The "if a reader only ever reads one chapter, this is the one" criterion.

Chapter B — pick the chapter that most directly tests voice in difficult territory. For memoir: a hard emotional terrain chapter. For practitioner: a chapter where the framework actually has teeth and breaks easy intuition. Draft fully.

Chapter C — pick the chapter that proves the book has more than one mode. If A and B were both intense, C is reflective. If A and B were both technical, C connects to the human. Drafted at first-pass quality.

Self-edit pass across all three: voice consistency, structural integrity per chapter, the spine through-line visible across all three. Send to one trusted reader for honest reaction. Not "is this good?" — "what is this book about, and would you read more?"
months.gate: Three chapters drafted at sample quality (~15-24K words total). Read by one trusted reader with feedback that confirms (or course-corrects) the spine, voice, and direction. The Q2 draft has a quality bar to maintain, not invent.

quarters.subtitle: Full manuscript first draft completed. Chapters 4 through end at first-pass quality.

months.title: Manuscript draft — chapters 4-7
months.why: Q1 produced the spine and the sample. Q2 is the long middle — the months that separate writers who produce books from writers who produce three-chapter samples. The discipline of "draft pace" matters more than the discipline of "draft quality" in this quarter. Quality comes in Q3 editing; volume comes in Q2 drafting.
weeks: Chapter 4 — drafted to first-pass quality. Word target hit. Aim for ~1.5-2K words per writing session, 3-4 sessions per week.
Chapter 5 — drafted. Track pace honestly. If chapter 5 takes longer than chapter 4, the spine or structure has a problem that surfaces. Diagnose now, not in Q3.
Chapter 6 — drafted. Mid-quarter checkpoint: read all six chapters in one sitting. Does the cumulative arc work? Where is repetition? Where does the voice drift?
Chapter 7 — drafted. Weekly word count for the month documented. The pace data is the predictor for whether the book finishes in Q2 or slips into Q3.
months.gate: Chapters 4-7 drafted at first-pass quality. Cumulative read-through completed. Weekly word count documented as pace data for the remaining drafting months.

months.title: Manuscript draft — chapters 8-11
months.why: M5 is the make-or-break month. Either the draft pace from M4 holds and the book is on schedule, or it does not and the M12 launch is at risk. The honest assessment in week 1 of this month determines whether the rest of the arc remains realistic or needs re-scoping.
weeks: Honest pace assessment from M4 data. If on track, continue. If 20%+ behind, decide: extend the draft into Q3 (push edit/pitch right), cut a chapter, or accept reduced word counts per chapter. Decide explicitly — drift is the worst option.
Chapter 8 — drafted. The decision from week 1 is operating now.
Chapter 9 — drafted. Mid-point of the long-middle stretch.
Chapter 10 — drafted. If the book has 12 chapters, you are 2 from finish. If 18 chapters, you are 8 from finish — re-confirm Q3 timeline.
months.gate: Chapters 8-11 drafted. Explicit decision documented if pace required scope or schedule adjustment. The path to M6 completion is realistic, not aspirational.

months.title: Manuscript first draft completed + read-through
months.why: Q2 closes with the full first draft existing as a single artifact. The first draft is bad. That is normal. The achievement is having all of it written, in order, available to edit as a whole. The M6 read-through is the diagnostic for what Q3 editing actually needs to address.
weeks: Remaining chapters drafted to completion. If the book has more than 12 chapters and you are still drafting in M6, the M5 decision should have addressed this — re-confirm scope honestly.
Full read-through, ideally in one or two sittings. Print or e-reader, not laptop. Read as a reader, not a writer. Take notes on what works, what drags, what is repeated, what is missing.

Read-through notes synthesized into an edit plan. Three categories: structural problems (chapter order, redundancy, missing chapters), voice problems (drift, inconsistency, lapses), content problems (factual issues, unclear passages, weak transitions). Each item rated by severity.

Quarter break — one full week away from the manuscript. The book needs distance before edit-mode begins. Use the week for any non-book work that has accumulated. Resist the urge to "just touch one chapter." Distance is the work.
months.gate: Complete first-draft manuscript existing as one artifact. Read-through completed with an edit plan documenting structural, voice, and content issues by severity. A one-week deliberate distance from the manuscript taken.

quarters.subtitle: Two structural edit passes. Professional editor engaged. Pitch process or self-pub setup.

months.title: Edit pass 1 — structural revision
months.why: The first edit is not line-level. It is structural. Are the chapters in the right order? Are there chapters that should not exist? Are there chapters that should exist but were missed? The structural edit is where the book actually becomes a book, rather than a sequence of draft chapters in chronological order.
weeks: Chapter order audit — does the current sequence serve the spine? Move or merge chapters as needed. Some chapters die in this week. That is normal and correct.
Missing chapters — what is the read-through revealing as a gap? Write or sketch the new chapter that addresses the gap. Most first drafts need 1-3 new chapters during structural edit.
Redundancy cuts — where does the manuscript say the same thing twice? Cut the weaker passage every time. Most manuscripts lose 8-15% of their word count to redundancy cuts.

Structural read-through #2 — does the book hang together now? If not, another structural pass is needed before line edits. Do not move forward until the structure is right; line editing on a broken structure is wasted work.
months.gate: Edit pass 1 complete. Structural read-through #2 confirms the book hangs together. Word count and chapter map updated to reflect the revised structure.

months.title: Edit pass 2 — line edits + professional editor engaged
months.why: M7 fixed the structure. M8 fixes the prose. Line edits are slower than structural edits — each chapter takes longer, even though each change is smaller. This is also the month to engage a professional editor — the outside read that catches what self-editing cannot.
weeks: Engage a professional editor — developmental, copy, or both depending on what M7 revealed needs. For memoir, often developmental. For practitioner book, often copy edit + technical reviewer. Budget $2-5K for serious work. The editor reads while you continue line edits.
Line edits — first half of the book. Voice consistency, sentence rhythm, paragraph flow, transitions. The kind of editing that benefits from reading aloud.
Line edits — second half of the book. Pace is critical here; line editing tends to slow as fatigue accumulates. Schedule shorter sessions to maintain quality.
Editor feedback received and triaged. Critical changes implemented; cosmetic changes queued for later passes. A revised manuscript ready for the pitch process.
months.gate: Edit pass 2 complete across the full manuscript. Professional editor engaged with feedback received and major issues addressed. Manuscript ready for the M9 pitch process.

months.title: Pitch process — agent queries or self-pub decision
months.why: M9 is where the book moves from manuscript to publication path. For memoir, the question is usually traditional vs hybrid publication. For practitioner book, the question is often O'Reilly/Manning vs Substack-as-book vs self-pub. The decision is not aesthetic — it is strategic and depends on what role the book serves in the larger portfolio.
weeks: Publication path decision — for the chosen book, what is the right home? Memoir: agent + traditional, hybrid press, or self-pub via KDP and IngramSpark? Practitioner: technical publisher, established platform, or self-pub? Decide based on what role the book serves, not on prestige alone.

Traditional path: agent query letter, comp titles list, synopsis, and 50-page sample. Query 8-15 agents over 2-3 weeks. Self-pub path: cover designer engaged, ISBN obtained, KDP and IngramSpark accounts set up.

Traditional path: continue queries and track responses. Most queries get no response or polite passes. One or two requests for a full manuscript is a positive signal at this stage. Self-pub path: interior design and layout finalized, ARC copies prepared.

Decision tree branching: if traditional path gets a serious request, accommodate the agent's timeline. If queries are not landing or self-pub is the path, the M10-M12 sequence is now self-pub-driven. Document the path clearly so M10 starts without ambiguity.
months.gate: Publication path chosen. Either active agent queries with at least one full-manuscript request, or self-publication infrastructure (cover, ISBN, accounts) in place. The M10-M12 sequence is now path-specific, not theoretical.

quarters.subtitle: Final production. Pre-launch positioning. Public launch. The book exists in the world.

months.title: Final production — manuscript locked
months.why: Q4 is no longer a writing quarter. The book is essentially done; the work is now production and positioning. M10 locks the manuscript, finalizes design, and sets up the pre-launch positioning. The temptation to keep revising is the largest threat in Q4 — name it and resist it.
weeks: Final edit pass — proofread quality, not structural quality. Typos, formatting, citation consistency. Most issues found here are small. If significant structural issues surface, the M11 launch is at risk — push the launch by a month rather than ship a broken book.

Design and layout finalized. Cover (final), interior design, back cover copy, author bio. For traditional path, the publisher drives most of this; for self-pub, you drive it. Either way the M10 close has the package ready.

Pre-launch positioning — the book's landing page (your site or the publisher's), the launch announcement structure, the ARC list for early reviewers. The audience that will receive the book on day one is built in M10, not M11.

ARC distribution — advance review copies sent to 20-50 readers who can produce reviews, blurbs, or social distribution at launch. The most important ARC recipients are not the most famous; they are the ones who will actually read and respond.
months.gate: Manuscript locked. Design and layout final. Landing page live with pre-order or sign-up. ARC distribution to 20-50 readers complete. The book is ready to launch.

months.title: Launch — release week and distribution
months.why: The release is one week of intense activity that has been building for 10 months. The launch is not "marketing" in the abstract — it is the deliberate, structured set of actions across one to two weeks that determines whether the book lands or disappears. M11 is operational, not creative.
weeks: Launch week minus 1 — final landing-page polish, launch-day email to the existing audience pre-drafted, social posts queued, podcast or interview appearances scheduled where possible.

Launch week — book goes live. Launch-day email to The Prompt subscribers and LinkedIn network. Social posts across the week, not all on day 1. Personal thank-yous to the ARC reviewers who actually reviewed. The first week is the bulk of first-month sales.

Post-launch week — capture every review, every mention, every distribution. Respond personally to readers who reach out. The week-after-launch is where you discover what the book is actually about for readers — sometimes different from what you intended.
First-month numbers reviewed honestly. Sales (or downloads, for self-pub), reviews, distribution. What is the book doing in the world? The honest assessment shapes M12 and Y2.
months.gate: Book launched publicly. Launch-week distribution executed across owned and earned channels. First-month numbers documented honestly. The book exists in the world as a real artifact.

months.title: Post-launch positioning and Y2 plan
months.why: The book exists. M12 is about what happens next — sustained distribution rather than launch burst, the conversations the book enables, the Y2 work the book funds or unlocks. Most authors stop at launch. The ones who get long compounding from a book treat M12 onward as just as important as the launch week.
weeks: Sustained distribution — speaking engagements, podcast appearances, guest essays in venues that drive the book's audience. The book is the credential; the speaking is the distribution. Book at least 3 speaking or interview slots in the next 90 days.

Partner Network and Intinc integration — the book updates your Partner Network listing, your LinkedIn bio, the Intinc internal positioning. The credential is leveraged across every existing channel, deliberately, not assumed.

Y2 plan written — what does the next year look like with this book in the world? Is the deferred book now Y2? Is the work shift toward speaking or workshops based on the book? Is there a Y2 book sequel or follow-on? The plan is written, not assumed.

Year retrospective — what changed when the book existed? What did you learn about your own writing, your own discipline, your own readers? The retrospective feeds the Personal Brand arc Q4 work and becomes a Prompt edition or LinkedIn post.
months.gate: Sustained distribution plan executing. Book integrated into Partner Network and personal-brand assets. Y2 plan written. Retrospective published. The book is now a compounding asset, not a launch event.

course.sub: 12 months. From curriculum content to a real course business — Maven cohort or self-paced platform, four paid cohorts shipped, alumni community, marketing engine operating, $50-200K Y1 gross revenue. The Teaching arc built the curriculum; this arc turns it into the first business that does not require Kyle in every billable hour.

quarters.subtitle: Course thesis, audience definition, curriculum architecture, first lessons validated with beta students.

months.title: Course thesis and audience definition
