months.why: The Teaching arc built curriculum content. The Course arc turns it into a business — and the business begins not with lessons but with a clear thesis about who pays for this course and why. Most failed courses have great curriculum and no audience. M1 is the audience-and-thesis work that most course creators skip and pay for later.
weeks: The thesis statement: in one sentence, what does the course teach, to whom, and what changes in their work or career after completion? The sentence is hard. The sentence is the work. Test it against five potential students — they should be able to paraphrase it back accurately.

Audience interviews — five conversations with people who match the target student profile. Not pitches. Discovery interviews using the JTBD methodology from the Strategy arc M2: "walk me through the last time you tried to learn this..." Document what surprises you about their actual constraints, budgets, and learning preferences.

Competitive landscape: every other course teaching adjacent content — Maven cohorts, Udemy courses, YouTube channels, bootcamps, individual coaches. What are they charging? What are they leaving out? Where is the underserved gap that your specific perspective fills? Write the landscape.

Positioning document: thesis, audience, competitive position, and the specific "why this course, why now, why from you" pitch. Three pages, written, dated. Every later decision references this document. Without it, course development drifts toward "everything I know" rather than "what this specific audience needs."
months.gate: A written positioning document with thesis statement, audience interview synthesis, competitive landscape, and explicit differentiation. Five potential students can paraphrase the thesis back accurately. The course has a reason to exist beyond "I have knowledge to share."

months.title: Curriculum architecture — syllabus and lesson plan
months.why: M1 produced the thesis. M2 produces the curriculum that delivers on the thesis. The architecture matters more than any single lesson — a great lesson in a broken curriculum produces a frustrated student; a decent lesson in a clear curriculum produces a satisfied one. M2 is the architecture work that prevents M4 platform decisions from becoming structural rewrites.
weeks: Learning outcomes — what specifically can a student do at the end of the course that they could not do at the beginning? Outcomes are skills demonstrated, not topics covered. "Understand RAG" is not an outcome; "Design and deploy a production RAG system with eval metrics" is. Write 4-6 specific outcomes.

Module structure — how do the outcomes break into modules? Most cohort-based courses are 4-8 weeks with one module per week. Self-paced courses can be 6-12 modules. Pick the format based on the M4 platform decision (preliminary), and structure outcomes into modules.

Lesson plan per module — for each module, list the 4-8 lessons that build to the module outcome. Each lesson has a specific learning objective. Lessons are 15-45 minutes of content; modules are 2-4 hours of work for students including exercises.

Exercise design — for each module, the practical exercise that proves the outcome was achieved. The exercise is more important than the lesson; students learn from doing, not from watching. Document exercise design with specific success criteria.
months.gate: Complete curriculum architecture: learning outcomes, module structure, per-module lesson plans, and per-module exercises with success criteria. The course is now a buildable artifact, not a teaching concept.

months.title: First lessons built and beta-tested
months.why: The curriculum architecture is theoretical until students actually engage with the lessons. M3 builds the first module to delivery quality and runs it past 5-10 free beta students. The beta is not for the students' benefit — it is for the data on what actually works, what bores, what confuses, what lands.
weeks: Build module 1 to delivery quality — videos recorded, exercises drafted, written materials produced. The first module is the test of the production workflow. Most courses underestimate how long lesson production takes; the first module reveals the real number.

Recruit 5-10 beta students from M1 audience interviews and adjacent networks. Free access in exchange for honest feedback and willingness to engage with exercises. The recruitment is structured; "anyone want to try my course?" produces the wrong audience.

Run beta cohort through module 1 — synchronous if cohort-based, async if self-paced. Observe what students actually do, where they get stuck, which exercises produce real learning, which feel like busywork. Document patterns, not just feedback.

Beta retrospective and architecture revision — what worked? What needs restructuring? What does the curriculum architecture from M2 need to change based on real student data? Adjust the M4-onwards plan before committing to platform and pricing.
months.gate: Module 1 built to delivery quality and beta-tested with 5-10 students. Documented patterns of what worked vs what needs adjustment. Curriculum architecture updated based on beta data, not assumptions.

quarters.subtitle: Platform decision. Pricing model. Full curriculum built. First paid cohort soft-launched at $5-15K revenue.

months.title: Platform decision, pricing, sales funnel
months.why: The course economics live or die on these three decisions: where it runs, what it costs, how students find it. M4 is the decision month — preliminary signals from beta inform real platform commitment, real pricing, and the funnel that turns interest into enrollment.
weeks: Platform decision tree: Maven (cohort-based, built-in audience, 10-15% rev share, premium positioning), Teachable/Thinkific (self-hosted, full control, lower price points), Substack-as-course (audience-driven, lower production overhead), or fully custom (most control, most operational burden). Pick based on cohort vs self-paced, audience, and operations capacity.

Pricing model: cohort courses typically $500-2,500. Self-paced typically $99-500. Premium / executive variants $2,500-10K. The price signals positioning as much as the price extracts revenue. Underpriced courses are often perceived as lower value than fairly-priced ones. Decide based on positioning, not on "what feels comfortable."

Sales funnel architecture: landing page, email capture, nurture sequence, sales page, checkout. Each is its own discipline. Most course creators build a funnel that works for them but doesn't convert strangers. Borrow proven structures (Maven's built-in funnel, or established self-pub frameworks like the "About → Free Resource → Email → Pitch" sequence).

Launch date set for M6 cohort — backwards-plan from the date. Marketing window is M5 (lead generation), M6 first 2 weeks (sales push), M6 last 2 weeks (cohort starts). Without a date, the launch perpetually slides; with a date, the work shapes around the constraint.
months.gate: Platform chosen and configured. Pricing set. Sales funnel built end-to-end with at least a landing page, email capture, and checkout flow live. Launch date for M6 cohort set and committed.

months.title: Full curriculum built + lead generation
months.why: M5 has two parallel tracks: finish building the curriculum, and start generating leads for the M6 launch. Curriculum-only months produce great content that no one buys. Marketing-only months produce demand for a product that doesn't exist. M5 is the discipline of running both simultaneously.
weeks: Curriculum production track: modules 2-N built to delivery quality. The M3 beta calibrated production pace; M5 is execution at that pace. If pace is slower than projected, reduce module count rather than reduce module quality.

Lead generation track: weekly content on the platform where the audience lives (LinkedIn for B2B/practitioner, YouTube for skills, Twitter for community). Each piece of content references the course landing page. The goal is 200-500 email subscribers by M6 launch.

Curriculum production: continued. Mid-month checkpoint: is curriculum on track for M6 first-week-of-cohort delivery? If module N is at risk, decide now to defer it to "bonus" content or pull it from the cohort scope.

Lead generation: continued + waitlist activation. Email subscribers get a waitlist signup with early-bird pricing. The waitlist conversion is typically 5-15% — calibrate launch expectations against waitlist size, not raw subscriber count.
months.gate: Curriculum built to cohort-ready quality across all modules. Email subscriber base of 200-500 with a waitlist of 30-100 names. The M6 launch has the product to ship and the audience to ship it to.

months.title: First paid cohort soft launch — $5-15K revenue
months.why: The first paid cohort is the validation moment. Real students paying real money for the actual course. Most courses fail to launch at all — building forever, polishing forever, never charging. M6 is the discipline of launching when the course is good enough, not perfect.
weeks: Launch week — landing page live with pricing, email sequence active, sales push to waitlist and email list. Target: 10-20 paid enrollments for the first cohort. The first cohort is intentionally small; small cohorts produce better student outcomes and better feedback.

Cohort week 1 — first module delivered, students engaged, first exercises completed. Observe everything. The first cohort's experience tells you what marketing claims need to match and what curriculum claims need adjustment.

Cohort weeks 2-3 — continued delivery. Daily or weekly check-ins with students. Document what questions come up repeatedly, what exercises produce learning, where students get stuck. The data is the product roadmap.

Cohort close + retrospective. What worked? What did students actually achieve? What do they say in NPS surveys and unprompted feedback? The retrospective shapes M7 cohort #2 — every iteration should be measurably better than the last.
months.gate: First paid cohort completed with 10-20 students paying $5-15K total revenue. Documented retrospective with student outcomes, NPS, and specific curriculum/delivery adjustments for M7 cohort #2.

quarters.subtitle: Cohort #2 + #3 with marketing system operational. Revenue compounds. Course-market fit signals emerge.

months.title: Cohort #2 with marketing system spinning up
months.why: M6 proved the course can be sold. M7 builds the marketing engine that sells it repeatedly. Without an engine, each cohort requires the same heroic launch effort. With an engine, cohorts launch more efficiently and grow predictably. M7 is the systematizing work most course creators avoid because it is less satisfying than teaching.
weeks: Marketing system audit: what worked in M6 launch? Specific channels, specific posts, specific email sequences. Document the conversion data — landing page conversion %, email open rates, waitlist-to-purchase conversion. The data is the system.

Content engine: a sustainable weekly content cadence that drives leads without burning out the creator. 1-2 LinkedIn posts per week, one long-form piece per month, occasional video. The cadence is calibrated to sustain across the year, not just spike for cohort #2.

M6 cohort alumni: testimonials, case studies, referrals. The first cohort is the strongest marketing asset for cohort #2. Capture testimonials with specifics ("after the course I built X" beats "the course was great"). Alumni referrals are typically the highest-conversion channel.
Cohort #2 launch — target 20-30 students, $10-25K revenue. Marketing system carries more of the load than in M6. The creator-time-per-enrollment ratio should be measurably lower.
months.gate: Marketing system documented and operational. Cohort #2 launched with 20-30 students and $10-25K revenue. Creator-time-per-enrollment measurably lower than M6 (the engine is doing more of the work).

months.title: Cohort retrospective and product-market fit signals
months.why: Two cohorts is enough data to start reading PMF signals honestly. Are students completing the course? Are they getting outcomes? Are they referring others? Are repeat-buy signals (advanced course, coaching, community) present? M8 is the honest assessment that determines whether to scale, refine, or rebuild.
weeks: Aggregate retrospective: completion rates, outcome rates, NPS, referral rates, repeat-purchase signals. Compare M6 and M7 cohorts honestly. What is the trend? PMF signals are improving completion, improving NPS, increasing referrals.
Course refinement based on data: which modules need work? Which exercises don't produce learning? What gaps did both cohorts surface? The refinement is data-driven, not preference-driven.

Alumni community design: an alumni Slack or Discord, periodic alumni events, a referral program. The alumni community is both a retention asset and a marketing asset. Most course businesses neglect this — those who don't compound faster.

Strategic decision: scale (cohort #3 larger), refine (smaller cohort #3 with improved curriculum), or pivot (different audience or different format). The decision is documented, not drifted. Sometimes the right answer is "this course is not the right business" — M8 is when that signal would surface.
months.gate: Aggregate retrospective document with completion, outcome, NPS, and referral data from M6 and M7 cohorts. Course refinements implemented. Alumni community structure live. Documented strategic decision for M9 cohort #3.

months.title: Cohort #3 — revenue compounds
months.why: M9 is the cohort where the marketing system, the alumni network, and the iterated curriculum compound. This is the cohort that proves the course is a real business, not just three one-off launches. Target revenue: $15-30K, with meaningfully higher cohort size and meaningfully better student outcomes.
weeks: Cohort #3 launch — marketing system operating at higher efficiency. Alumni referrals contributing meaningfully (20%+ of enrollments). Waitlist from continued content engine. Target 30-50 students.

Cohort delivery — operational discipline now mattering as much as teaching quality. Multi-cohort overhead (alumni community + active cohort + waitlist for next cohort + content engine) is real. The systems work designed in M7 carries this.

Mid-cohort signals — are completion rates improving? Are alumni continuing to engage? Is the course delivering on the M1 thesis at increasing scale? The signals confirm or contradict the M8 strategic decision.
Q3 close: $30-70K total revenue across three cohorts. Cohort #3 metrics documented. Year-end revenue projection updated based on M10-M12 cohort pace. The course is provably a business by Q3 close.
months.gate: Cohort #3 completed with 30-50 students and $15-30K revenue. Total Q3 revenue: $30-70K across three cohorts. Documented compounding from alumni referrals and content engine. The course is operationally a business.

quarters.subtitle: Cohort #4. Year 1 gross revenue $50-200K. Y2 strategic decision: scale, sustain, or sunset.

months.title: Cohort #4 — operational discipline at scale
months.why: Cohort #4 tests whether the business holds together at higher volume. Three cohorts done well looks promising; four cohorts done well with sustained quality and continued alumni engagement is a business. M10 is the operational discipline month — systems holding up, not just being demonstrated.
weeks: Cohort #4 launch with mature marketing system. Target 40-60 students. The marketing system should produce enrollments with less creator-direct involvement than M6. If creator time per enrollment is not trending down, the system isn't actually a system.

Multi-cohort operations: cohort #4 delivery + alumni community + content engine + cohort #5 marketing. The operational load is real. Either the creator is doing the work, or a TA / community manager is supporting. Document what is creator-only vs delegatable.

Quality discipline: cohort #4 student outcomes need to match or exceed cohort #1 outcomes. Quality regression at scale is the failure mode. Compare M10 student NPS and outcome data against M6 explicitly.

Pricing review: is the price still right? Most successful courses increase prices in year 1 by 30-100% as positioning strengthens. The increase signals confidence and filters for serious students. Decide for M11 cohort #5 pricing.
months.gate: Cohort #4 completed with 40-60 students and quality metrics matching or exceeding M6 baseline. Multi-cohort operations stable. Pricing decision for M11 documented.

months.title: Y2 strategic decision — scale, sustain, or sunset
months.why: M11 is the binary decision point. Four cohorts of data, four iterations of the curriculum, a marketing engine, an alumni community. The honest assessment determines whether this is a Y2 business worth scaling, a sustainable Y2 income stream worth maintaining, or a Y1 experiment that should sunset before consuming Y2 energy.
weeks: Aggregate Y1 data: total revenue, total students, completion rate, NPS, referral rate, creator-hours invested, dollar-per-creator-hour. The dollar-per-hour number is the honest signal of whether this is leverage or hidden labor.

Three Y2 scenarios written: (1) Scale — higher prices, larger cohorts, possible team hire, $200-500K target. (2) Sustain — same cadence, modest growth, $100-200K target. (3) Sunset — wind down after one final cohort, archive curriculum, redirect energy. Each scenario with specific tradeoffs documented.

Decision conversation with trusted advisor (Daniel, a peer course creator, or a business coach). The decision is consequential enough to deserve outside perspective. The conversation is structured, not just "what do you think?"
Y2 decision documented and committed. The decision shapes M12 work and the Personal Brand arc Q4 work. The decision is binding for Y2 with one review point at Y2 Q2.
months.gate: Y1 aggregate data documented. Three Y2 scenarios written with tradeoffs. External advisor conversation completed. Y2 decision (scale, sustain, or sunset) documented and committed with one review point scheduled.

months.title: Year retrospective + brand integration
months.why: M12 closes the year by integrating the course into the broader portfolio. Year 1 gross revenue is one number; what the course did for Partner Network credibility, brand authority, AIaaS service line credibility, and personal growth is a separate set of values. M12 makes those values explicit and integrates them across the portfolio.
weeks: Y1 financial close: gross revenue, costs (platform fees, contractor costs, marketing), net revenue, taxes set aside. The financial picture is documented for tax purposes and for honest portfolio assessment.

Brand integration: the course is now a credential on LinkedIn, in Partner Network listings, in AIaaS service line pitches, in The Prompt author bio. The credential is leveraged everywhere it can be, deliberately.

Alumni assets: testimonials curated, case studies written, alumni network documented as a referral and advisory asset for future work. The alumni are the most valuable Y2 asset regardless of the M11 decision.

Year retrospective published as a Prompt edition or LinkedIn long-form post. What changed when the course existed? What did you learn about teaching, marketing, operations, and yourself? The retrospective is both closure and the bridge to Y2.
months.gate: Y1 financial close documented. Brand integration complete across LinkedIn, Partner Network, AIaaS, and The Prompt. Alumni network formalized as an asset. Year retrospective published. The course is now portfolio infrastructure, not a single launch.

saas.sub: 12 months. From "I shipped an app" to "I run a SaaS business." MVP validated with design partners, Stripe billing live, first 3-10 paying customers, growth channel identified and scaled, $5-50K MRR by year-end. The first business in your portfolio where the deliverable is software earning recurring revenue, not consulting hours.

quarters.subtitle: Idea validation. Customer concentration decision. MVP shipped to 5-10 design partners.

months.title: Idea validation and the customer concentration check
months.why: The Full-Stack arc shipped three apps; one likely has paying customers. This arc takes the strongest candidate (or starts fresh) and turns it into a real SaaS business. M1 is the validation work — and more importantly, the customer concentration decision that will shape everything. Building for one specific client produces a different product than building for the market.
weeks: Idea audit — for the candidate product, write the problem statement, target user, and current alternatives. Compare against the Strategy arc M2 audience-interview methodology. If the product was built on assumptions rather than interviews, M1 is where that gets caught and addressed.

Customer interviews — 8-12 conversations with potential users. Document their actual pain, current workarounds, and willingness to pay. The "willingness to pay" question is the hard one: most interview subjects say yes when asked abstractly. The validation is in observing them pull out a credit card or commit to a pilot.

The concentration decision: build for one anchor client (consulting-style, $50-200K ARR from one customer) or build for the market (SaaS-style, 50+ customers at $50-500/month MRR). The math, the operations, the product, and the exit options all change based on this single decision. Decide explicitly.

Positioning document — for the chosen concentration path, write the positioning. For anchor-client: who is the client, what do they pay for, what does success look like at M12. For market: what segment, what price point, what acquisition channel, what does $5-50K MRR look like at M12.
months.gate: A written validation document with 8-12 customer interviews documented, an explicit customer-concentration decision (anchor vs market), and a positioning document for the chosen path. The product has validated demand or has had its M1 reset before building further.

months.title: MVP design and tech stack decision
months.why: M1 validated the demand. M2 designs the MVP — the minimum product that delivers the core value, nothing more. Most failed SaaS products spent M2-M6 building features that were not needed and missing features that were. The MVP discipline is in resisting the urge to build everything you could build in favor of building only what proves the thesis.
weeks: MVP scope definition: the single user journey that delivers the core value. Everything else is out of scope. Write it as a user story: "User Y can do X in less than Z minutes, producing outcome W." If the MVP cannot be described in one user story, the scope is too large.

Tech stack decision — Next.js + Vercel + Supabase + Stripe is the default. Use it unless there is a specific reason to deviate. Most SaaS arcs fail from over-engineered stacks; the default stack ships products that earn revenue. Document the stack and the reason for any deviation.

Wireframes and key flows — not pixel-perfect designs, but clear flows. The login flow, the core feature flow, the billing flow. The wireframes communicate the product to the next month's build, not to investors or users.

Architecture sketch: database schema, API surface, deployment plan, third-party services (Stripe for billing, Supabase Auth for auth, Resend for email, PostHog for analytics). Architecture documented in one diagram. If the architecture cannot fit in one diagram, the MVP is too complex.
months.gate: MVP scope defined in one user story. Tech stack decided (likely Next.js + Vercel + Supabase + Stripe). Wireframes complete for core flows. Architecture sketched in one diagram. The build for M3 is now well-defined, not exploratory.

months.title: Build first version and ship to 5-10 design partners
months.why: M3 is the build month. The MVP gets built end-to-end and shipped to design partners — early users who get free or heavily-discounted access in exchange for feedback and willingness to be cited as customers later. Design partners are the bridge between "I built something" and "people pay for this."
weeks: Core build — the single user journey from M2 implemented end-to-end. Skip everything that is not on the user journey. The build should feel constrained; if it feels like there's room to add features, the user journey was scoped too small.
Production deployment — domain, SSL, basic analytics, error monitoring (Sentry), email transactional (Resend). The infrastructure that lets real users use the product in production conditions.

Design partner recruitment — from M1 interview pool, reach out to 5-10 specific people. Offer free or $20-50/month access for the first 6 months in exchange for usage and feedback. Sign a simple agreement; design partners are a real commitment on both sides.

Onboarding the partners — direct, white-glove. Walk each through the product personally. Document where they get stuck, what they ask about, what they don't use. The friction data is the M4 product roadmap.
months.gate: MVP shipped to production. 5-10 design partners onboarded with documented usage patterns and friction points. The product is real, not a demo. The next quarter's work is informed by design-partner data.

quarters.subtitle: Auth and billing infrastructure. First 3-10 paying customers. $500-2K MRR. Retention systems live.

months.title: Auth, billing infrastructure, production readiness
months.why: The MVP shipped without payment in M3 — design partners are free. M4 builds the auth and billing layer that turns design partners into paying customers and lets the product accept revenue from new signups. The infrastructure is not glamorous, but it is the difference between a product and a business.
weeks: Auth refinement — Supabase Auth wired up with email/password and optionally Google OAuth. Password reset flow, email verification, session management. The auth layer is invisible when it works and catastrophic when it doesn't; spend the week getting it right.

Stripe billing integration — products and prices configured in Stripe, checkout flow built, webhook handler for subscription events, customer portal for self-service management. Most billing bugs are in webhook handling; test thoroughly.

Production hardening — error monitoring tightened, database backups configured, rate limiting on API endpoints, abuse prevention. The infrastructure that prevents the first paying customer from hitting a broken product.

Convert design partners to paid plans — for the partners who continued using the product, present the pricing and the upgrade path. Some convert immediately; some need a few weeks. The conversion rate is data: if under 30% convert, the pricing or value prop needs adjustment.
months.gate: Auth and billing infrastructure live and tested. At least 30-50% of design partners converted to paying plans. Production monitoring catches errors before customers report them. The product can accept revenue from anyone, not just design partners.

months.title: First paying customers — $500-2K MRR
months.why: M5 is the first revenue month. Real customers paying real money for the product. The number is small ($500-2K MRR is 3-10 customers at $50-500/month), but the validation is real. M5 is also when retention becomes the most important metric — keeping the first customers is harder and more valuable than acquiring them.
weeks: Acquisition push 1: warm network. LinkedIn audience, The Prompt subscribers, Partner Network contacts. The warm network is the easiest source of first customers and the hardest source of scalable customers. Use it for the first 5-10 paying customers; don't expect it to scale.

Onboarding optimization — for each new paying customer, observe their first 7 days. Where do they get stuck? What do they need help with? Most SaaS products lose 40-60% of new customers in the first week from poor onboarding. The first 10 customers reveal the patterns.

Customer support discipline — every support request, every email, every confused user gets responded to within 24 hours, ideally within 4. The first 10 customers should feel like they have a hotline to the founder. The support work is also product research.

MRR tracking — formal MRR calculation, churn tracking, customer count, average revenue per customer. The metrics dashboard is built in M5 and refined every month. Without the dashboard, decisions get made on vibes; with it, decisions get made on data.
months.gate: 3-10 paying customers generating $500-2K MRR. Onboarding optimized based on first-week observation patterns. Customer support response time under 24 hours. MRR/churn/customer count dashboard live.

months.title: Retention systems and product-market fit signals
months.why: Acquisition without retention is a leaky bucket. M6 builds the retention systems that keep customers around long enough to compound. Onboarding, activation, regular engagement, churn prevention — each is a discipline. M6 is also when PMF signals start to emerge or fail to emerge. The honest reading determines what Q3 looks like.
weeks: Onboarding system formalized — email sequence for new signups, in-product onboarding flow, "first value" milestone defined and measured. Most customers churn because they never reached first value. The system is designed to get them there in days 1-3.

Activation metric defined — the specific action that predicts long-term retention. For most SaaS products, activation is a specific feature used N times in the first M days. Pick the metric, measure it, optimize for it.
Churn analysis — for any customer who churned in M5, document why. Exit surveys, manual outreach, pattern recognition. The churn data is the highest-signal product research available.

PMF assessment — Sean Ellis test ("how disappointed would you be if you could no longer use this?"), retention curves (do retention curves flatten or keep dropping?), word-of-mouth signals (are customers referring others?). The aggregate signal is honest, not aspirational.
months.gate: Onboarding system formalized with measurable first-value milestone. Activation metric defined and tracked. Churn analysis documented for any churned customers. Aggregate PMF signal assessed honestly with documented evidence.

quarters.subtitle: Growth channel experiments. Winning channel identified and scaled. $3-10K MRR by Q3 close.

months.title: Growth channel experiments — 3-5 channels tested
months.why: The warm network is exhausted by M7. Growth now requires real channels — predictable, repeatable sources of new customers. M7 is the experimentation month: try 3-5 channels in parallel, measure honestly, and let the data identify the winner. Most SaaS arcs fail in Q3 not because nothing works but because nothing was tested rigorously enough to know what works.
weeks: Channel hypothesis — list 3-5 candidate growth channels for your specific product and customer. Common candidates: SEO content (long lead time but compounds), paid ads (fast but expensive), partnerships (high effort but high conversion), product-led growth (built-in virality), community-driven (slow but durable). Pick based on customer interview data, not preference.

Channel #1 and #2 — first two channels launched in parallel. Each gets its own small budget, its own measurement, its own owner (likely you). Document the funnel: impressions → signups → activated → paid. The funnel data is the channel's signal.
Channel #3 — third channel launched. By now, channels #1 and #2 have early data. The third channel is calibrated against what's working and what's not.

Mid-quarter assessment — for each channel, calculate cost per acquired customer (CAC) and revenue lifetime value (LTV). The LTV:CAC ratio is the channel's viability signal. Under 3:1, the channel is borderline. Under 2:1, the channel is not viable at scale. Cut channels honestly.
months.gate: 3-5 growth channels tested with documented funnel data. CAC and LTV calculated per channel. Channels rated by LTV:CAC ratio. The viable channels are identified and the non-viable ones cut.

months.title: Identify winning channel and double down
months.why: M7 produced data on multiple channels. M8 picks the winner and scales it. Most SaaS businesses succeed with one dominant channel and use others as supplementary. M8 is the focus month — go deep on the one channel that works rather than maintaining diluted effort across multiple.
weeks: Channel selection — based on M7 data, pick the channel with the best LTV:CAC ratio and the most scalable mechanics. The decision is data-driven, not preference-driven. Sometimes the winning channel is the one you didn't expect.

Channel doubling-down — for the chosen channel, increase budget, increase frequency, increase quality. If SEO: more content. If paid ads: more spend. If partnerships: more outreach. The discipline is in committing fully to the channel that works rather than hedging.

Conversion optimization — landing pages, signup flow, onboarding all optimized for the specific customers coming from the chosen channel. Different channels convert differently. The channel-specific optimization is where the compounding happens.

Operational systems — the chosen channel run as a system, not as heroics. Content calendar, ad management cadence, partnership pipeline. The systems are what allow scale without proportional time increase.
months.gate: Winning channel identified and committed. Channel-specific conversion optimization complete. Operational systems for the channel documented and running. The channel is scaling, not just being tested.

months.title: $3-10K MRR with channel compounding
months.why: M9 is the revenue compounding month. The winning channel is operating, customers are signing up consistently, retention is holding from the M6 systems, and MRR is meaningfully higher than M6. $3-10K MRR is not a unicorn, but it is the threshold where the business starts looking real.
weeks: Channel scaling — continued investment in the winning channel. New content, new ads, new partnerships, whatever the channel is. The scaling is calibrated to LTV:CAC sustainability, not to maximize short-term growth at the expense of unit economics.

Customer success motion — for new customers from the channel, the onboarding-to-activation flow runs reliably. Some customers need extra support; build the playbook for that. The customer success motion is what turns acquisition into retention.

Pricing review — by M9, you have enough data to assess whether pricing is right. Are customers complaining about price? Are they paying without question? Most SaaS products underprice in year 1. The M9 review is the moment to adjust.

Q3 close metrics — total customers, MRR, churn rate, LTV:CAC, customer lifetime value. The numbers shape the M10-M12 work. If MRR is at the low end ($3K), Q4 is about validating the model. If MRR is at the high end ($10K), Q4 is about scaling further.
months.gate: $3-10K MRR by Q3 close. Channel-driven acquisition operating consistently. Customer success motion preventing the kind of churn that would offset acquisition. Pricing reviewed and adjusted based on M5-M9 data.

quarters.subtitle: Operational maturity. Strategic Y2 decision: scale, lifestyle business, or sunset. $5-50K MRR target.

months.title: Operational maturity and customer success automation
months.why: M10 is when the business stops being heroic and starts being operational. Customer support has a system, not just direct founder response. Onboarding is automated where possible and white-glove where required. The business runs without Kyle in every customer interaction. M10 is the work that determines whether the SaaS scales or stays at "lifestyle business" tier.
weeks: Customer support tiering — what gets answered by docs / AI / automation, what gets answered by you. The tiering reduces founder-time-per-customer as the customer base grows. Most SaaS arcs fail to scale here.
Onboarding automation — for the most common customer profile, the onboarding is fully automated and produces activation reliably. White-glove onboarding reserved for high-value customers only.

Documentation and self-service — the help center, the knowledge base, the in-product help. Customers who can self-serve don't generate support tickets. The documentation is an investment with high return.
Operational dashboard — MRR, churn, NPS, support response time, infrastructure costs all visible in one place. The dashboard is the daily-check artifact that prevents drift.
months.gate: Customer support tiered with clear automation/AI/human boundaries. Onboarding automated for the common case. Self-service documentation comprehensive. Operational dashboard tracking all key metrics in one view.

months.title: Y2 strategic decision — scale, lifestyle, or sunset
months.why: M11 is the binary moment. Twelve months of data. Real customers, real revenue, real operations. The honest assessment of "what is this business going to be in Y2?" determines whether to invest harder, optimize for sustained cash flow, or wind down. Most SaaS founders default to "scale" without honest examination; the discipline is in considering all three paths seriously.
weeks: Y1 aggregate analysis — total revenue, total customers, churn rate, LTV, CAC, founder hours, dollar-per-founder-hour. The financial picture is documented honestly. The dollar-per-hour number is the honest signal of leverage vs labor.

Three Y2 scenarios written: Scale (raise prices, expand product, possibly raise capital, $50-500K MRR target) — Lifestyle (sustain current cadence, modest growth, $20-50K MRR ceiling, low ops burden) — Sunset (wind down, sell to existing customers or strategic acquirer, redirect energy). Each scenario with specific tradeoffs.

External advisor conversation — an investor, a peer founder, or a strategic advisor. The decision is consequential enough to deserve outside perspective. The conversation is structured around the three scenarios.

Y2 decision documented and committed. The decision is binding for Y2 with one explicit review point in Y2 Q2. The other two scenarios are explicitly closed — the lifestyle business owner isn't secretly trying to raise capital; the scaling business isn't taking the foot off growth.
months.gate: Y1 aggregate analysis with dollar-per-hour calculated honestly. Three Y2 scenarios documented with tradeoffs. External advisor conversation completed. Y2 decision committed with one review point scheduled.

months.title: Year retrospective and portfolio integration
months.why: M12 closes the year by integrating the SaaS into the broader portfolio. Whether the Y2 decision is scale, lifestyle, or sunset, the SaaS becomes portfolio infrastructure — case study, credential, Partner Network asset, brand artifact. M12 makes those integrations explicit rather than implicit.
weeks: Y1 financial close — revenue, costs, taxes set aside, net to founder. The financial picture is documented for tax purposes and honest portfolio assessment.

Case study production — what the SaaS taught about product, customers, growth, operations. The case study becomes Partner Network credibility, AIaaS service line credibility, and a Brand arc Q4 flagship piece.
Brand integration — the SaaS is now a credential in your LinkedIn bio, Partner Network listing, Customization Service positioning. The credential is leveraged everywhere.

Year retrospective published as a Prompt edition or long-form post. What changed when you built a real SaaS? What did you learn about product, customers, marketing, and yourself? The retrospective is both closure and the bridge to Y2.
months.gate: Y1 financial close documented. Case study produced and integrated. Brand assets updated everywhere. Retrospective published. The SaaS is portfolio infrastructure regardless of Y2 path.

partner.sub: 12 months. From Partner Network listing to Partner Network as primary revenue channel. Niche selection at M1, three case studies in Q2, active referral generation in Q3, multiple engagements running in Q4. Target: $200-500K annual revenue routed through Partner Network or Partner-adjacent referrals. The lowest-risk Lane B arc because the demand already exists — the question is positioning.

quarters.subtitle: Partner Network profile optimized. Niche selection. Initial visibility. First inbound conversations.

months.title: Niche selection — what use case do I want to be called about?
months.why: The Partner Network listing exists from Series 2 capstones, but generalist listings produce generalist results. M1 forces a deliberate niche choice — the specific use case, industry, or problem you want clients to find you for. Generalists compete on price and availability. Specialists compete on fit. The niche choice determines which conversations the Partner Network produces.
weeks: Niche audit — list the 5-8 use cases you have demonstrable depth in (Copilot Studio implementation, agentic eval, MCP servers, regulated-industry AI, voice agents, fullstack AI products, etc.). For each, rate: depth on a 1-5 scale, market demand on a 1-5 scale, fit with Intinc positioning on a 1-5 scale, and your genuine interest in doing more of this work on a 1-5 scale.

The niche decision — pick 1-2 niches based on the audit. Three is too many for a 12-month positioning sprint. One can work if the niche has enough demand. The decision is binding for the year — re-niche-ing in M6 produces a year with no clear positioning. Document the decision and the reasoning.

Competitive landscape for the chosen niche — who else lists in this niche? What do their profiles say? What are they not saying that you could? The Partner Network ecosystem is small enough that the competition can be mapped specifically, not abstractly.

Niche-specific value proposition — three to five sentences that articulate why a client in this niche would choose you over the alternatives. The value prop is tested against three peers or potential clients before being finalized. If they cannot paraphrase it back, it is not done.
months.gate: A documented niche selection with depth/demand/fit/interest ratings. A niche-specific value proposition tested with three external readers. The competitive landscape for the chosen niche mapped specifically. The positioning is now concrete, not aspirational.

months.title: Partner Network profile rewritten for the niche
months.why: M1 chose the niche. M2 rewrites the Partner Network listing, your LinkedIn bio, your kylerosebrook.com positioning, and anywhere else the niche needs to be reflected. The profile work is the visible artifact that turns the M1 decision into something a search engine, an Anthropic Partner team member, or a potential client can actually find.
weeks: Partner Network listing rewrite — title, description, specializations, case study placeholders. The listing is read by humans in the Anthropic Partner team and (implicitly) by their internal routing. Every word earns its place. Submit the revision and confirm it goes live.

LinkedIn headline and About rewrite — the niche is now the primary positioning, not a secondary specialty. Most LinkedIn profiles try to do everything; this one does one specific thing very well. Document and ship.

kylerosebrook.com positioning — the personal site reflects the niche where relevant. Lane discipline is maintained (kylerosebrook.com and FlashFusion remain distinct), but the niche-relevant credentials are surfaced.

Secondary surfaces — the bio on The Prompt, the bio in any speaking engagements, any other places your professional positioning shows up. Consistency across surfaces signals serious positioning, not casual experimentation.
months.gate: Partner Network listing rewritten and live. LinkedIn and personal site positioning updated. Consistent niche positioning across all professional surfaces. The niche is now visible everywhere a client might find you.

months.title: First inbound activation and tracking system
months.why: M3 is the activation month. The positioning exists; now the question is whether it produces inbound. M3 also builds the tracking system that lets you distinguish "Partner Network sourced" from "warm network sourced" from "direct outreach sourced" — the data that drives the next 9 months of decisions.
weeks: Outreach to Anthropic Partner team — a specific, professional message to the relevant Partner team contact introducing the niche positioning and asking what specifically helps them route relevant work to you. Most Partners never do this; the ones who do get measurably more routing.

Inbound tracking system — a spreadsheet, Notion database, or CRM with fields for source, niche fit, conversation stage, outcome. Every inbound conversation gets logged. Without tracking, the Q3 channel analysis is impossible.

First conversations — the existing warm network is the first inbound source. Reach out to 5-10 contacts who could refer Partner-relevant work, with the explicit niche framing. Document the conversations in the tracking system.

Q1 close — by end of M3, the positioning is live, the tracking system is running, and at least one Partner-relevant conversation has happened (warm or inbound). The "no signal yet" outcome is also data — it tells you what M4-M6 marketing work is needed.
months.gate: Anthropic Partner team outreach completed with documented response. Inbound tracking system live. At least one Partner-relevant conversation logged. The infrastructure for evaluating Partner-sourced work is operational.

quarters.subtitle: Three case studies published. Specializations claimed. Depth demonstrated publicly. Inbound starts.

months.title: First case study — the foundational proof
months.why: Case studies are the most undervalued and underused Partner Network asset. Most Partners list their company; few publish detailed case studies of their work. The asymmetry is real: a single well-written case study outperforms ten LinkedIn posts in terms of inbound conversion. M4 produces the first one.
weeks: Case study target selection — pick the engagement (Intinc internal, Customization Service deliverable, Series 1 or 2 arc capstone) that most directly demonstrates the M1 niche. Get permission from the relevant stakeholder. If permission is unclear, anonymize but keep specifics.

Case study structure — problem, approach, what was built, results, key learnings. The format matters less than the specifics. Most case studies fail by being too abstract; this one succeeds by being specific. Word target: 1,500-3,000 words plus visuals.

Drafting — the case study is written in your voice, not corporate marketing voice. The reader should feel like they are getting honest reflection from a practitioner, not a sales pitch. The "what didn't work" section is included; it builds credibility.

Publishing — case study published on kylerosebrook.com (or FlashFusion site if more relevant), linked from Partner Network listing, announced on LinkedIn with a specific angle (not "I published a case study" but "here's what we learned about X"). The publishing is the leverage event.
months.gate: First case study published with specifics, results, and key learnings. Linked from Partner Network listing and announced on LinkedIn with a specific framing. The first piece of niche depth evidence is now public.

months.title: Second case study and specialization claims
months.why: One case study is a data point. Two case studies on related themes start to look like a specialization. M5 produces the second case study and claims the specializations on Partner Network — Anthropic's formal way of saying "this Partner is specifically capable of X."
weeks: Second case study target — different engagement, same or adjacent niche. The repetition matters: showing depth across multiple engagements is what differentiates a specialist from someone who did the work once.

Specialization claims on Partner Network — Anthropic Partner Network has formal specialization designations. Apply for the relevant ones for your niche. The application is typically lightweight but produces durable signal.
Second case study published — same publishing motion as M4, refined based on what worked the first time. By M5, you have a publishing rhythm, not a one-off launch.

Cross-linking — both case studies cross-reference each other. The pattern is visible: "this practitioner has done this kind of work multiple times." LinkedIn announcement of the second case study explicitly references the first.
months.gate: Second case study published. Formal Partner Network specialization claims submitted. Cross-linking between case studies in place. The depth claim is now backed by two pieces of public evidence.

months.title: Third case study and Q2 close metrics
months.why: Three case studies in three months is the volume that turns case studies from "occasional content" into "evidence base." M6 also closes the quarter with honest metrics: is the Partner-sourced inbound starting to come, or is the positioning still invisible? The honest read shapes Q3.
weeks: Third case study target and draft — another related engagement. By M6, the format and voice are muscle memory; production is faster than M4.

Third case study published and cross-linked with the first two. The case study library on your site is now a real asset; potential clients researching you find three pieces of depth evidence in a row.

Inbound conversation review — over Q1-Q2, how many Partner-relevant conversations have happened? From what sources? Document patterns. If Partner Network itself is not generating inbound yet, what is driving the conversations that are happening?

Q2 close metrics — number of inbound conversations, source breakdown, conversion-to-discovery-call rate, deals in pipeline. The metrics are honest and inform Q3. If the metrics are weak, Q3 needs more aggressive direct outreach. If strong, Q3 scales what is working.
months.gate: Three case studies published. Documented inbound metrics with source breakdown. A Q3 plan that responds to actual data, not assumptions about what Partner Network would do.

quarters.subtitle: Active referral generation. First Partner-sourced revenue. Direct outreach to specific opportunities.

months.title: Active referral generation — the warm network worked
months.why: Inbound from Partner Network is passive; it takes 6-12 months to compound. Active referral generation is the higher-leverage M7 work — explicit conversations with the warm network about who they could refer you to. Most Partners never ask. The ones who do measurably outperform.
weeks: Referral outreach list — 20-30 people in your warm network who could plausibly refer Partner-relevant work. The list is specific: not "everyone I know" but "people whose work intersects with the niche."

Referral conversations — direct, specific messages to the list. Not "do you know anyone who needs help" but "here is the specific kind of work I am taking on, who comes to mind?" The specificity produces 5x the response rate of generic asks.

Follow-through on referrals received — every referral that comes in is responded to within 24 hours. Most referrals die in slow founder response. The discipline of "drop everything for a referral" is what makes the referral channel work.

Referral tracking — every referral logged with source, fit, conversation stage, outcome. The tracking reveals which referral sources are highest quality. By M9, you will know which 3-5 people in the warm network are your best referrers.
months.gate: Referral outreach completed to 20-30 warm contacts with documented responses. At least 3-5 active referrals generated. Tracking system showing source quality patterns. The referral channel is now active, not passive.

months.title: First Partner-sourced or Partner-adjacent engagement closed
months.why: M8 is the month where the positioning produces revenue, not just conversations. The first Partner-sourced engagement (or Partner-adjacent referral) closes — billable work that came specifically from the Partner Network positioning, not from existing warm network. The first close is the validation moment.
weeks: Pipeline review — from Q1-Q2 conversations and Q3 referrals, what deals are in pipeline? List them, rate likelihood, identify next action for each. The pipeline review surfaces deals that are close but stalled.

Close work — actively close the highest-likelihood deal in pipeline. Proposal, pricing, contract, kickoff. The close work is unglamorous but specific. Most pipeline deals die from founder neglect, not from buyer rejection.

First engagement kickoff — the deal closes and the work begins. The execution is in scope of the niche, demonstrating the M1 thesis was right. The engagement itself becomes the M11 case study candidate.

Pipeline replenishment — closing one deal empties the pipeline. M8 also seeds the next pipeline through continued referral outreach and content. The discipline is in maintaining pipeline at the same time as executing on closed work.
months.gate: First Partner-sourced or Partner-adjacent engagement closed and kicked off. Pipeline replenished with 3-5 new conversations. Documented learnings about what specifically drove the close (positioning, case studies, referral, niche fit).

months.title: Direct outreach to specific opportunities
months.why: Inbound + referral is the foundation; direct outreach is the accelerant. M9 adds deliberate outbound work targeting specific opportunities in the niche — companies you know need this work, conversations you can initiate without waiting for inbound. The mature Partner positioning combines all three channels.
weeks: Target list — 30-50 companies or contacts that map specifically to the niche. Not "all consulting prospects" but "specifically these companies because of these specific signals." The list quality determines the response rate.

Outreach sequences — multi-touch, niche-specific outreach with the case studies as proof points. Most outbound is generic; niche-specific outbound with concrete depth evidence converts measurably better. Sequence over 2-3 weeks.

Response handling — every response (positive, negative, neutral) gets logged. Negative responses are also data; they reveal positioning gaps or wrong-fit prospects. Positive responses convert to discovery calls.

Mid-quarter pipeline review — by mid-M9, the combined channels (Partner inbound + warm referrals + direct outbound) should be generating 3-5 active conversations per month. If under, the next month adjusts which channel gets more investment.
months.gate: Direct outreach campaign executed against 30-50 targets with documented response rates. Combined channel pipeline of 5-10 active conversations. The Partner positioning is now producing predictable conversation flow, not occasional luck.

quarters.subtitle: Closed engagements compound. $200-500K annual run-rate. Y2 plan: deepen niche or expand specializations.

months.title: Multiple engagements running and operational maturity
months.why: M10 is the operational test. Multiple engagements running simultaneously means context-switching cost, calendar management, quality maintenance across deliverables. The discipline that prevents quality drift while running 2-4 engagements in parallel is the difference between a real Partner business and a one-deal-at-a-time freelance practice.
weeks: Engagement portfolio review — what is in flight? Quality of each? Risk of slippage on any? The review is honest, not optimistic. Most quality issues compound silently before becoming visible; the M10 review catches them early.

Operational systems — calendar discipline (focus blocks per engagement), communication discipline (per-client async cadence), invoicing discipline (monthly, not deal-end). The systems are what allow scale without proportional founder time.

Quality discipline — for each active engagement, the deliverable quality bar is maintained even as engagement count grows. If quality drifts on any engagement, the engagement count is too high. The discipline is in reducing count before quality breaks.

Pipeline maintenance — even with multiple engagements running, the pipeline continues to be fed. Stopping pipeline work because "you have enough" is the failure mode that produces Q1-of-Y2 deal droughts. Pipeline work continues at 20-30% of the cadence even during heavy execution months.
months.gate: 2-4 engagements running simultaneously with documented quality maintenance. Operational systems for multi-engagement work in place. Pipeline maintained despite execution load. The Partner business is now operationally mature.

months.title: $200-500K annual run-rate and Y2 strategic decision
months.why: M11 is the run-rate and strategic-decision month. By M11, the trailing-12-months Partner-sourced revenue should be in the $200-500K range depending on niche and engagement size. The exact number matters less than the trajectory — is this scaling, sustaining, or stalling? The Y2 decision flows from the honest read.
weeks: Y1 financial close — Partner-sourced revenue, Partner-adjacent revenue, total revenue, average engagement size, time-to-close. The data is documented for tax purposes and strategic clarity.

Three Y2 scenarios written: Deepen (same niche, larger engagements, premium positioning, $300-600K target) — Expand (add a second niche, build out specializations, $400-800K target) — Sustain (current cadence, stable revenue, focus on quality of life, $250-400K target). Each scenario with specific tradeoffs.

Strategic conversation with Daniel and external advisor — the decision is consequential. Daniel's perspective on how the Partner work intersects with Intinc and Head of AIaaS path. External advisor (peer Partner, Anthropic Partner team contact, business mentor) on what the data suggests.
Y2 decision documented and committed. The decision shapes M12 work and the Personal Brand arc Q4 work. The decision is binding for Y2 with one explicit review point in Y2 Q2.
months.gate: Y1 financial picture documented honestly. Three Y2 scenarios with tradeoffs written. Strategic conversations completed with Daniel and external advisor. Y2 decision committed.

months.title: Year retrospective and portfolio integration
months.why: M12 closes the year by integrating the Partner Network work into the broader portfolio. The case studies, the engagements, the referral network, the positioning all become Brand arc content, AIaaS service line credibility, and Y2+ infrastructure. M12 makes the integrations explicit.
weeks: Fourth case study published — from a Q3 or Q4 engagement. The case study library is now four deep; the depth claim is no longer fragile.

Brand integration — the Partner Network track record is now featured on LinkedIn, on kylerosebrook.com, in Intinc internal positioning, in any other professional surface. The credential is leveraged everywhere it can be.

Referral network formalization — the 5-10 highest-quality referrers from Q3-Q4 are explicitly thanked, possibly with a small gift or a formal referral acknowledgment. The relationships are Y2 infrastructure; treat them as such.

Year retrospective published — what changed when the Partner Network became the primary channel? What did you learn about positioning, niches, referrals, closing? The retrospective is both closure and Y2 strategic context.
months.gate: Fourth case study published. Brand integration complete across all surfaces. Referral network relationships formalized. Year retrospective published. The Partner Network is now portfolio infrastructure, not a single-year experiment.

regulated.sub: 12 months. From SecAI+/CAISP-credentialed AI security practitioner to the person healthcare CIOs, federal contractors, and financial services compliance teams call when they need AI deployed under genuine regulatory constraint. HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, GDPR-AI, ISO/IEC 42001 as fluent dialects. Reference architectures, three case studies, a published practitioner\'s guide.

quarters.subtitle: The four compliance frameworks mastered as language and as architectural constraint.

months.title: HIPAA + HITECH for AI workloads
months.why: HIPAA is the most common regulatory framework for AI in healthcare, and the most misunderstood by AI practitioners. M1 builds genuine HIPAA fluency: what PHI is, what BAA agreements require, what the Security Rule says about technical safeguards, and how AI workloads (training data, inference logs, model outputs) intersect with the rule. Most AI practitioners can fake HIPAA in conversation; the specialist actually knows it.
weeks: HIPAA Privacy Rule and Security Rule fundamentals from primary source documents — HHS guidance, not blog posts. Privacy Rule defines what PHI is and how it can be used. Security Rule defines the technical, physical, and administrative safeguards. Read both. Take notes. The primary sources are dense but they are what compliance teams cite.

Business Associate Agreements (BAA) for AI vendors — when a BAA is required, what it must contain, what happens when one is missing. Most AI tools (OpenAI, Anthropic via Bedrock, Claude through AWS) have specific HIPAA-eligible configurations. Learn which products under which conditions are HIPAA-eligible and which are not.

AI-specific HIPAA considerations — training data PHI contamination, inference logs containing PHI, model outputs that might constitute PHI, the de-identification standard (Safe Harbor and Expert Determination). These are the questions that come up in actual healthcare AI deployments and that most practitioners cannot answer correctly.

HIPAA breach scenarios — when does an AI deployment failure constitute a breach? The 500-individual threshold for HHS reporting, the state-level breach notification laws that often go further. Map specific AI failure modes (inference log leak, training data exposure, prompt injection extracting PHI) to specific breach reporting obligations.
months.gate: Verified HIPAA fluency — able to answer specific questions about PHI handling, BAA requirements, Security Rule technical safeguards, and AI-specific failure modes without reference to a blog post. The first compliance dialect is now in your fingers.

months.title: FedRAMP + ATO for AI in federal contexts
months.why: FedRAMP is the federal cloud security framework, and AI in federal contexts is increasingly significant — DOD, civilian agencies, federal contractors. FedRAMP is more bureaucratic than HIPAA and rewards practitioners who can navigate the language. M2 builds the FedRAMP fluency that turns "we cannot work with you" responses into "we can work with you under these conditions" responses.
weeks: FedRAMP baseline (Low, Moderate, High) and the authorization process — how cloud services become FedRAMP-authorized, what the JAB and agency authorization paths look like, what an ATO (Authority to Operate) is. The vocabulary matters more than the depth at this stage.

AI services in FedRAMP — Azure OpenAI Service in Government Cloud, AWS Bedrock with FedRAMP-eligible configurations, the specific authorization status of each major AI vendor in federal contexts. Most practitioners assume "the cloud is FedRAMP" without knowing which specific service in which specific region under which specific configuration.

NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) — the framework most federal AI deployments cite. The four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), what each requires, how it maps to actual technical implementation. Federal AI work increasingly references AI RMF; specialists know what each function entails.

CMMC and AI in DoD contexts — for defense industrial base contractors using AI, the CMMC framework adds another layer. Understanding when CMMC applies, what level (1, 2, 3), and what AI deployment patterns satisfy each level is specialized knowledge that produces measurable engagement value.
months.gate: Verified FedRAMP and federal AI fluency — able to navigate authorization status of major AI services, cite NIST AI RMF functions accurately, and articulate CMMC implications for AI in DoD contexts. The federal compliance dialect is now operational.

months.title: SOC 2 + ISO 27001 + GDPR-AI
months.why: M3 covers the broader compliance landscape — SOC 2 (the de facto enterprise audit standard), ISO 27001 (international), and GDPR's AI-specific implications. Most enterprise clients cite these even when they are not the primary regulatory framework. The specialist navigates all of them, not just the primary one.
weeks: SOC 2 Type I vs Type II audits, the five Trust Service Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy), how AI workloads are typically scoped. SOC 2 is the audit most B2B AI vendors pursue first; understanding what auditors look for is specialized knowledge.

ISO 27001 ISMS framework, ISO 27017 (cloud-specific), ISO 27018 (PII in cloud), and the new ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems, published 2023). ISO/IEC 42001 in particular is the first AI-specific international management system standard — early specialization here is rare and valuable.

GDPR Article 22 (automated decision-making), the right to explanation, Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) for AI systems, the EU AI Act intersection with GDPR. Most US-based AI practitioners avoid GDPR; the regulated-AI specialist embraces it because European and global clients require it.

Cross-framework mapping — when a deployment must satisfy HIPAA + SOC 2 + GDPR simultaneously, where do the requirements align, where do they conflict, what controls satisfy multiple frameworks at once? The cross-framework expertise is what enterprise clients actually need; single-framework expertise is commoditized.
months.gate: Verified fluency across SOC 2, ISO 27001/27017/27018/42001, and GDPR-AI. Cross-framework mapping for at least one realistic deployment scenario documented. The four major compliance dialects are now operational, not theoretical.

quarters.subtitle: AI architectures that satisfy each framework. Reference patterns built. Compliance posture documented.

months.title: HIPAA-compliant AI architecture patterns
months.why: M1 built the HIPAA fluency. M4 builds the actual architectures — the specific deployment patterns that satisfy HIPAA Security Rule technical safeguards while delivering AI value. The architecture is the deliverable that turns compliance knowledge into engagement value. Without architectures, you can talk about HIPAA; with them, you can deliver under HIPAA.
weeks: HIPAA-compliant RAG architecture — Azure OpenAI in HIPAA-eligible configuration, AI Search with private endpoints and security trimming, audit logging through Purview or equivalent, BAA in place. The end-to-end pattern that satisfies the Security Rule for a HIPAA RAG deployment. Build it as a reference architecture diagram.

PHI de-identification in AI pipelines — the technical patterns for Safe Harbor de-identification at ingestion, the Expert Determination pathway, the residual risk management. Most HIPAA AI deployments fail at de-identification; the architecture that handles it correctly is rare.

Audit logging and access controls for HIPAA AI — every inference logged with user identity, every training data access logged, every model output logged. The audit infrastructure that a HIPAA breach investigation would require. Build the logging architecture explicitly.

Incident response runbook for HIPAA AI failures — when inference logs leak, when training data is exposed, when prompt injection extracts PHI. The 60-day breach notification clock starts; the runbook tells the client what to do. The runbook is itself a deliverable.
months.gate: A documented HIPAA-compliant AI reference architecture (RAG end-to-end), a de-identification pipeline pattern, audit logging architecture, and incident response runbook. The HIPAA architecture is now a reusable engagement artifact.

months.title: FedRAMP + federal AI architecture patterns
months.why: M5 builds the federal equivalent — AI architectures for FedRAMP-authorized environments. The constraints are different (Government Cloud regions, specific service authorizations, additional logging requirements), and the architecture patterns that work in commercial cloud often do not translate directly.
weeks: Azure Government Cloud AI architecture — Azure OpenAI Service in Gov Cloud, AI Search in Gov Cloud, networking patterns that satisfy FedRAMP Moderate or High. The architecture is similar to commercial but with specific service variants and additional control overlays.

AWS GovCloud AI architecture — Bedrock availability in GovCloud, ITAR considerations, the differences from commercial AWS. For DoD contractors, GovCloud is often required; the architectural pattern that delivers AI value in GovCloud is specialized knowledge.

NIST AI RMF as architectural framework — the four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) translated into specific architectural and operational requirements. Most federal AI engagements require an AI RMF artifact; learning to produce one is specialist territory.

Continuous monitoring and POAM management — FedRAMP requires continuous monitoring and Plan of Action & Milestones (POAM) management. For AI workloads, the monitoring includes model drift detection, training data integrity, inference quality drift. The continuous monitoring architecture is the long-tail FedRAMP requirement.
months.gate: A documented FedRAMP-compliant AI reference architecture (Azure Gov Cloud or AWS GovCloud), NIST AI RMF artifact template, and continuous monitoring architecture for federal AI workloads. The federal architecture is now a reusable engagement artifact.

months.title: Financial services and ISO/IEC 42001 architecture patterns
months.why: M6 builds the architectures for the remaining major regulated industries — financial services (FFIEC, OCC, FINRA guidance for AI) and the emerging ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system pattern. Financial services AI is a meaningful market with specific regulatory expectations; ISO/IEC 42001 is the new international standard that enterprise clients will increasingly require.
weeks: FFIEC and bank regulatory AI guidance — OCC Bulletin 2021-7 (model risk management), the FFIEC Authentication guidance and AI, the SR 11-7 model risk framework. Financial services AI must satisfy these even though they are guidance, not regulation in the same sense as HIPAA. Architecture patterns that document model risk explicitly are specialist territory.

AI architecture for financial services — model risk management overlay (independent validation, performance monitoring, challenger models), fair lending considerations, the explainability requirements that regulators increasingly expect. The architecture incorporates the model risk management discipline that bank examiners look for.

ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management System architecture — the published standard's requirements for AI governance, AI policy, AI risk management, AI impact assessment. The architecture that implements ISO/IEC 42001 is rare because the standard is new (2023). Early specialists here have a window to establish positioning.

Cross-framework architecture summary — at end of Q2, produce a single reference document that maps the four frameworks against the architectural patterns. The document becomes a Q3 marketing artifact and the foundation for the M11 published guide. The Q2 capstone is this synthesis.
months.gate: Documented architectures for financial services AI (model risk management overlay) and ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system. Cross-framework architecture summary produced. Four reference architectures now exist as reusable engagement artifacts.

quarters.subtitle: First regulated-industry engagement (audit, advisory, or implementation). External reviewer validation. Pipeline.

months.title: First regulated-industry engagement secured
months.why: M7 is where the specialization produces revenue. The first regulated-industry engagement comes from positioning, network, or Partner Network referral — and the engagement validates that the M1-M6 work translates into market demand. Most specialization arcs fail here, by either not pursuing the first engagement actively enough or by accepting non-regulated work and breaking the niche discipline.
weeks: Engagement pipeline activation — outreach to specific regulated-industry contacts (healthcare CIOs/CISOs, financial services AI leads, federal contractors), Partner Network referral requests, Intinc internal opportunities. The pipeline is built deliberately, not waited for.

Engagement format options — compliance-focused AI audit (1-2 weeks, $15-30K), advisory engagement (4-8 weeks, $30-80K), implementation engagement (8-16 weeks, $80-250K). The format depends on client need and your appetite. Document the three options as separate service line offerings.

First engagement closed — proposal, contract, kickoff. The engagement is in scope of the regulated-AI niche. Document the close, the price, the format, and the specific compliance framework(s) in scope.

Engagement execution begins — the engagement uses the M4-M6 architectures and frameworks. The execution itself produces real artifacts (audit report, advisory deliverable, or implementation) that become Q4 case study material.
months.gate: First regulated-industry engagement closed and kicked off. Service line offerings documented for the three engagement formats. Engagement execution in progress with reference architectures applied.

months.title: External reviewer validation — the credential that compliance teams trust
months.why: M8 is the credibility-validation month. Regulated-industry buyers do not trust self-claimed expertise; they trust credentialed expertise. M8 secures an external validation — an industry certification, a published framework, a recognized credential, or a documented review by a known compliance authority — that turns "I know HIPAA" into "I am credentialed in HIPAA AI."
weeks: Credential option assessment — HCISPP for healthcare information security, CCSP for cloud security, CIPP for privacy, ISACA AI security credentials. Each has different time investment and recognition. Pick one based on which most directly serves the niche choice.

Credential pursuit — exam prep or formal certification process. Some credentials require documented experience hours; document your existing Series 1-2 work as evidence. The credential is the multi-week commitment.

Alternative validation — published framework or guide submitted to a respected venue (IAPP, HCISPP community, ISACA Journal, a HIMSS or FinTech Connect publication). The published artifact serves as credential-adjacent validation. Submit during this month.

External review by compliance authority — a compliance officer, a HIPAA Security Officer, or a federal cybersecurity contact reviews your reference architectures and provides documented feedback. The review is itself credential-adjacent — "reviewed by X authority" carries weight.
months.gate: Active credential pursuit (exam scheduled or in process) OR published framework submission OR documented external review by a recognized compliance authority. The expertise is now validated by something other than self-claim.

months.title: Pipeline expansion and second engagement
months.why: M9 is where one engagement becomes a practice. The first engagement winding down produces a case study candidate; the M7 pipeline work and the M8 credential together produce the second engagement. Two regulated-industry engagements in one year is the volume that signals "this is what they do" rather than "they did one of these."
weeks: First engagement wrap-up — final deliverables, client signoff, payment collection, retrospective notes for the case study. The engagement closes cleanly and produces an explicit client testimonial or case study permission.
Pipeline review — what conversations are in flight from M7 outreach and M8 credential surface area? Rate likelihood, identify next action for each. The pipeline shapes the M10-M11 work.
Second engagement closed — same niche, possibly different framework focus or different engagement format. Close, contract, kickoff. The second close is the signal that the first was not luck.
Continued pipeline development — even with one engagement winding down and another beginning, the pipeline work continues. Q4 close-month engagement requires Q3 pipeline work.
months.gate: First engagement closed with client testimonial or case study permission. Second regulated-industry engagement closed and kicked off. Pipeline maintained for Q4 close possibilities. Two engagements is now the floor, not the ceiling.

quarters.subtitle: Three case studies published. Specialization visible in market. Y2 strategic decision on depth or breadth.

months.title: Case studies published — three regulated-industry artifacts in market
months.why: M10 is the case study production month. Three case studies from Q3 engagements (sanitized to client comfort) are published with the compliance framework specifics highlighted. The case studies turn the specialization from claim to evidence — the most durable Partner Network and direct-pipeline asset.
weeks: First case study published — from the first engagement, with client permission. Specific to the framework (HIPAA, FedRAMP, financial services, or ISO/IEC 42001), specific to the architecture pattern used, specific about the results delivered. The framework specificity is what differentiates this case study from generic AI consulting case studies.

Second case study published — from the second engagement or from anonymized Q1-Q2 internal work. Cross-references the first case study; the pattern of regulated-industry expertise becomes visible across multiple artifacts.
Third case study published — either from a third engagement or from a synthesized cross-engagement learning piece. By M10 close, three published artifacts demonstrate regulated-AI specialization.

Distribution — case studies cross-posted in IAPP, HIMSS, HCISPP community, FedRAMP-adjacent newsletters, ISACA Journal. The distribution venues are niche-specific and produce higher inbound quality than generic LinkedIn posts.
months.gate: Three regulated-industry case studies published with specific compliance framework and architecture content. Distributed across niche-specific venues. The specialization is now backed by three pieces of public evidence.

months.title: Published framework or guide — the credential-adjacent asset
months.why: M11 publishes the comprehensive framework or guide that the M1-M10 work has produced — "Practitioner's Guide to HIPAA-Compliant AI Architecture" or "FedRAMP for AI Workloads" or a cross-framework synthesis. The published guide is the highest-leverage asset for inbound; it produces conversations for years after publication.
weeks: Guide scope decision — single framework deep (one compliance framework, comprehensive treatment) vs cross-framework practical (the four frameworks, how to navigate clients that span multiple). The depth choice depends on the M11 cumulative engagement profile.

Guide drafting — synthesis of M1-M10 work. The cross-framework architecture summary from M6, the case study patterns from M10, the credentialed perspective from M8. 8,000-15,000 words plus reference architectures. The guide is substantial.

Polish and review — external review by the M8 compliance authority contact, by a peer practitioner, by a sample target reader. The review catches positioning issues, technical errors, and gaps. Implement feedback before publication.

Publication — on kylerosebrook.com (or FlashFusion site), with PDF download, with submission to relevant industry publications. The guide is positioned as a definitive practitioner reference. The aspiration is for the guide to be cited and referenced by other practitioners for 2-3 years after publication.
